docs.title: Welcome to Celldega's Documentation
docs.text:
Celldega Landscape visualization of a human skin cancer Xenium dataset obtained from 10X Genomics.

Celldega is a spatial and single-cell analysis and visualization library developed by the Spatial Technology Platform at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. Explore large spatial datasets, including datasets with over 1 billion transcripts, and single-cell atlases with over a million cells, alongside analysis workflows using scverse tools such as Scanpy and Squidpy.

  • Getting Started
  • Installation
  • GitHub Repository

docs.title: Atera
docs.text: Visualize 10x Atera whole-transcriptome data in Celldega. The Atera Kidney Landscape-Clustergram tutorial explores 399,120 cells and over 1 billion transcripts in a human kidney section with linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Yearbook views, including cell-type composition around glomeruli.

docs.title: Visium HD Colorectal Cancer Tutorial Video
docs.text: This video shows how to link a Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich to analyze a Visium HD human colorectal cancer dataset. Follow along in the Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich tutorial.

docs.title: 3D Developing Mouse Brain
docs.text: Explore 3.8 million cells from 43 aligned Xenium sections of an E15.5 mouse brain as a 3D CellCloud. Open the interactive CellCloud gallery using compact Parquet DegaFiles, or follow the visualization notebook using AnnData Zarr on Hugging Face to link CellCloud with a Clustergram.

docs.title: bioRxiv Preprint
docs.text: Our preprint, Celldega: Integrated Toolkit for Visualization and Analysis of Spatial Data, is available on bioRxiv.

docs.title: About
docs.text:
Celldega is named after a bodega, a small shop with all the essentials that is part of the fabric of a neighborhood.

Celldega is open source and available on GitHub.

docs.title: Jupyter Notebook Examples
docs.text: These example notebooks demonstrate how to use Celldega to analyze and visualize spatial and single-cell data. Each notebook is designed to be run in a Jupyter environment and showcases different features of the library.

docs.title: Spatial Transcriptomics Tutorials
docs.text:
Comprehensive tutorials that walk through complete workflows:

  • Atera Kidney Landscape-Clustergram - Direct Scanpy and AnnData steps for default clusters, linked dotplot Clustergrams, and cell-type composition across podocyte-defined glomerular gradients
  • Atera Brain Hippocampus H&E Landscape-Matrix - Non-diseased fresh-frozen hippocampus with an aligned post-run H&E image: switch the Landscape and Yearbook between fluorescence and H&E, and link the default clusters to a pre-clustered Matrix, Clustergram and Enrich
  • Atera Breast Cancer FF H&E Landscape-Matrix - Fresh-frozen breast cancer with an aligned post-run H&E image, a cell Yearbook, and default clusters linked to a pre-clustered Matrix, Clustergram and Enrich
  • Atera Colorectal Cancer H&E Landscape-Matrix - Fresh-frozen colorectal cancer with an aligned post-run H&E image, a cell Yearbook, and default clusters linked to a pre-clustered Matrix, Clustergram and Enrich
  • Atera Breast Cancer Landscape-Clustergram - Loads a precomputed Scanpy clustering (or optionally recomputes it) and creates linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich widgets
  • Atera Breast Cancer Neighborhood Exploration - Continues the Atera tutorial with hextile niches linked to cell-type composition and alpha-shape overlap linked to a separate Landscape
  • Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich - Uses Scanpy and plain AnnData to summarize a clustered Visium HD colorectal cancer sample (signatures, fraction expressing, marker genes) and explores it in linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich widgets, ready for interactive annotation
  • Scanpy-Squidpy Xenium Pancreas - Full analysis workflow using Scanpy and Squidpy with Xenium data

docs.title: 3D Spatial Transcriptomics
docs.text:
Explore the Broad–Allen E15.5 developing mouse brain across 43 aligned Xenium sections. Follow these notebooks in order, or open the visualization notebook directly to use the already hosted DegaFiles:

  1. Broad–Allen Mouse Brain: Preprocessing and Alignment — align sections using cluster-centroid landmarks and neighborhood overlap, compare the results, and write named CellCloud DegaFiles variants.
  2. Broad–Allen Mouse Brain: Visualization — explore a 2D section, compare cluster composition across slices, and link the 3D CellCloud to a gene-expression Clustergram.

docs.title: Single Cell Tutorials
docs.text:
Tutorials that explore single-cell RNA-seq data with UMAP Landscapes linked to Clustergrams:

  • Chromium PBMC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich - Clusters the 10x Chromium PBMC 3k dataset with Scanpy and explores it from Hugging Face: a UMAP Landscape that reads the AnnData Zarr store in the browser, a Clustergram of each cluster's rank_genes_groups markers loaded from a Matrix Zarr store, and a single-cell Clustergram of the same markers linked to its own Landscape, each with Enrich
  • Tabula Sapiens Atlas Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich - Explores the 1.1-million-cell Tabula Sapiens atlas from AnnData Zarr stores on Hugging Face: a UMAP Landscape with cell-type signature estimates as you zoom, a cell-type marker Clustergram and Enrich linked to it, and a plasma-cell subset with its own signatures

docs.title: Brief Notebooks
docs.text:
Focused examples demonstrating specific features:

  • Landscape View Xenium - Basic Landscape visualization of Xenium data
  • Landscape from a Local Server - Viewing locally stored DegaFiles in a Landscape with dega.viz.get_local_server()
  • Atera Pre-process - Making DegaFiles from a 10x Atera output bundle with dega.pre.main and viewing them in a Landscape
  • Atera Pre-process with H&E - Downloading a 10x Atera bundle with its post-run H&E image, making DegaFiles (one file per tile for GitHub, or row groups for Hugging Face), and adding the aligned H&E with dega.pre.add_aligned_he
  • Atera Kidney Yearbook Review - Find large endothelial cells with podocyte (NPHS2) transcripts using dega.select, review their portraits, and get the selected IDs
  • CellCloud Thick MERFISH - 3D orbit-camera CellCloud view of thick-tissue MERFISH data
  • Landscape-Heatmap Visium-HD - Combined Landscape and heatmap visualization
  • UMAP-Cluster Pancreas Xenium - UMAP clustering with Xenium pancreas data
  • Custom Segmentation - Using custom cell segmentation with Celldega
  • Gradient Neighborhood Pancreas Islets - Building inward/outward gradient rings around pancreatic islets and profiling cell-type proportion and hormone expression with distance from the islet edge

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
Install Celldega and its dependencies:

pip install celldega

For full analysis workflows, you may also need:

pip install scanpy squidpy

Out[5]: id rank score 0 lahifclf-1 0 149.862610 1 jmlonpne-1 1 144.399109 2 enbjaomo-1 2 143.721802 3 lgojfnkd-1 3 138.122849 4 mcaabbga-1 4 133.472092

The counts support this reasoning. The two cell types are close: 87% of endothelial cells have a podocyte within 20 µm (centroid to centroid). NPHS2 is podocyte-specific: outside podocytes and endothelial cells, only 0.2% of cells have at least 2 NPHS2 counts, but 26% of endothelial cells (1,091 of 4,118) do. Endothelial cells with podocin transcripts are also larger than other endothelial cells (median 52 vs. 40 µm², about the size of a podocyte), consistent with some being merged with a podocyte. The query keeps those larger than 90% of endothelial cells (at least 70 µm²): 232 candidates, of which the 100 largest are shown.

EMCN is the endothelial marker here because it is both strong and specific: at least 2 counts in 91% of glomerular endothelial cells (and 98% of the 100 candidates), compared with 48% for FLT1 (VEGF receptor 1). VWF, a common endothelial marker, is low in glomerular capillaries (0.1 counts per cell on average in cluster 20). The query itself identifies endothelial cells by their cluster.

docs.title: Atera kidney: review candidate cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text:
Use a tissue-wide Landscape for context, then send candidate cell IDs to a paginated Yearbook. Select the portraits that deserve a closer look and get their IDs back in Python.

Why glomerular endothelial cells and podocytes? In the glomerulus, podocytes wrap their foot processes around capillaries lined by endothelial cells, so the two cell types sit right next to each other. They are otherwise very different cells with distinct expression profiles: EMCN (endomucin) marks endothelial cells and NPHS2 (podocin) marks podocytes, and podocin is not expected in an endothelial cell. An endothelial cell that contains podocin transcripts is therefore a potential doublet: an endothelial cell and a podocyte segmented as one cell (a segmentation merge), or a few transcripts from a neighboring podocyte assigned to the wrong cell. These are review candidates, not doublet calls: marker counts alone cannot distinguish technical artifacts from biology.

The data are the public 10x Genomics Atera WTA FFPE human non-diseased kidney dataset. We use the same prepared DegaFiles as the Atera kidney tutorial. The analysis downloads cell IDs and positions, cluster labels, two sparse gene vectors, and cell areas (about 30 MB in total); the viewers stream images and spatial tiles as needed.

This example requires Celldega 0.28.0a6 or later: pip install --pre "celldega>=0.28.0a6".

docs.title: 1. Inspect the tissue context¶
docs.text: This Landscape shows the whole section with its original default clusters. In the glomeruli, cluster 16 contains podocytes and cluster 20 glomerular endothelial cells. Type NPHS2, EMCN (comma-separated) in the gene search box to show both markers' transcripts at once; the Yearbook below will focus on a small set of cells.

docs.title: 2. Select large endothelial cells that contain podocin transcripts with dega.select¶
docs.text:
Build a small AnnData with EMCN and NPHS2 counts, the default cluster labels, and the cell area for all 399,120 cells. This pinned DegaFiles export uses numeric row positions in its sparse gene files; the observation index below preserves the original cell IDs from cell_metadata.parquet. Cell areas come from the obs table of the annotated counts H5AD; only the cell IDs and areas are read over HTTP, not the whole 1.31 GiB file.

Selector.attr(...) and Selector.gene(...) build predicates, & combines them, and selector.samplers.rank(...) orders the matching cells. These thresholds are exploratory settings that you can change. See the Select API for more query and sampling options.

docs.title: 3. Review portraits across pages¶
docs.text: Pass the candidate cell IDs to Yearbook. Click the checkbox at the lower right of a portrait to select that cell. To view both markers, type NPHS2, EMCN in the Yearbook's gene search box; only those genes' transcripts are shown, each in its own color. A single boundary enclosing two nuclei suggests a segmentation merge; NPHS2 transcripts concentrated along the edge an endothelial cell shares with a podocyte suggest spillover.

docs.title: 4. Get the selected cell IDs¶
docs.text: yearbook.selected_cells returns the IDs of the cells you selected. Run this cell in a live notebook after selecting portraits.

docs.title: Optional: sample high-count cells using observation metadata¶
docs.text:
A second dega.select example combines an obs threshold with seeded random sampling. The annotated counts H5AD contains total_counts in obs. If you already downloaded it for the full kidney tutorial, the code below reads only metadata in backed mode, not the count matrix. It deliberately does not download that 1.31 GiB file just for this example.

Cells in the highest 1% of total counts are another review queue, not a doublet classification. To inspect this alternative, replace review_selection = candidate_review with review_selection = high_count_review in the Yearbook cell and rerun it.

docs.title: Atera Pre-process¶
docs.text:
Make DegaFiles from a 10x Atera output bundle. Atera is Xenium-class, so dega.pre.main detects an Atera bundle (by its experiment.spatial file) and runs the Xenium pipeline with Atera readers; view the result with technology="Xenium".

Requires the pre-processing extra (pip install "celldega[pre]", which needs libvips). Each region is one bundle folder, e.g. data/atera/EA_s3_broad_DX002/, containing experiment.spatial, cells.zarr.zip, transcripts.zarr.zip, cell_feature_matrix.zarr.zip, and morphology_2d/.

A large Atera WTA region (~430k cells, 3.4 billion transcripts) takes about an hour, peaks around 55 GB of memory, and produces ~20 GB of DegaFiles.

landscape_alpha Out[8]:

From these cell-cluster neighborhoods we can derive brand-new ones. A gradient is anchored to an existing neighborhood, so we pass the islet (endocrine) cluster's alpha shape to dega.nbhd.calc_gradient, which grows concentric rings around it and returns a new neighborhood GeoDataFrame — one ring per row, ordered inner-most to outer-most. We step every 50 µm in both directions, out to 400 µm, so the gradient reaches well into the surrounding tissue.

To stop the outward rings from overhanging into empty regions near the edges of the section, we clip them to a tissue boundary. We just hand calc_gradient the original adata via clip_reference — it extracts the cell coordinates and computes a tissue alpha shape on the fly, so the caller never has to dig out spatial arrays. clip_alpha can be coarse (a large value such as 200 µm) since we only need the overall tissue outline. The geometry is already in microns, so we leave is_pixel_space=False (the default).

Inward erosion stops automatically once a small islet erodes away, so there are fewer inward rings than outward ones.

    islet_alpha,              # the islet neighborhood
    direction="both",         # "outward", "inward", or "both"
    bin_width=50,             # ring width in microns
    max_dist=400,             # reach well outside the islets
    clip_reference=adata,     # clip outward rings to a tissue alpha shape (from adata)
    clip_alpha=200,           # coarse tissue outline is fine
)

docs.title: Gradient Neighborhoods: profiling the pancreatic islet microenvironment¶
docs.text:
This notebook demonstrates the gradient neighborhood workflow in celldega.nbhd. From a region of interest (ROI) we build concentric rings that step outward into the surrounding tissue and inward into the ROI, then measure how cell-type composition and gene expression change with distance from the ROI boundary.

Here the ROI is the set of pancreatic islets in a Xenium human pancreas section. We:

  1. Load a pre-clustered Xenium AnnData (Leiden clusters + spatial coordinates).
  2. Identify the endocrine / islet cluster from hormone markers.
  3. Define a neighborhood per cell cluster with alpha shapes, then build inward + outward gradient rings around the islet neighborhood with dega.nbhd.calc_gradient.
  4. Quantify the cell-type proportion and mean hormone expression gradient per ring.
  5. Visualize the alpha shapes and rings as static plots, a gene Clustergram, and a linked Landscape + Clustergram for interactive exploration.
  6. Optionally keep the rings and their results together in a NeighborhoodCollection.

It's a small but complete vertical slice of celldega: a dead-simple way to define neighborhoods (alpha shapes), a method to derive new ones (gradients), neighborhood-level AnnData summaries (calc_nbhd_by_pop / calc_nbhd_by_gene), and visualization (Landscape + Clustergram).

The dataset is the public Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs.h5ad and the matching DegaFiles landscape (see the Scanpy-Squidpy Xenium Pancreas tutorial for how this AnnData was produced).

docs.title: 2. Identify the islet (endocrine) cluster¶
docs.text: Pancreatic islets are marked by the endocrine hormones INS (β-cells), GCG (α-cells), SST (δ-cells), and PPY (PP-cells). We score each Leiden cluster by mean hormone expression and pick the clear winner. (In this dataset that is cluster 9 — but the score keeps the example robust if the clustering is ever re-run and the labels change.)

docs.title: 3. Define neighborhoods with alpha shapes — one per cell cluster¶
docs.text:
An alpha shape is a concave hull that wraps a point cloud. It's a refreshingly simple way to turn cells of a given type into a spatial neighborhood: no parameters to tune beyond a single length scale. dega.nbhd.alpha_shape_cell_clusters runs this for every Leiden cluster at once, and filter_alpha_shapes keeps a single value.

That length scale is inv_alpha (= 1 / alpha), and because the cell coordinates are in microns, inv_alpha is itself in microns — it's the characteristic gap the hull is allowed to bridge. A smaller value hugs the points tightly (more, smaller pieces); a larger value smooths over gaps. We use a uniform inv_alpha = 25 µm across all clusters, so each cluster becomes a MultiPolygon of its spatial domains. Keeping it small means the islets stay cleanly separated rather than getting bridged together into larger blobs.

docs.title: View all cell-cluster alpha shapes on the Landscape¶
docs.text: Passing the alpha-shape GeoDataFrame to nbhd= is all that's needed — the widget reads the micron_to_image_transform.csv from the DegaFiles base_url and converts the micron geometry to pixels itself, coloring each neighborhood by its cluster. Setting landscape_state="nbhd" reveals the neighborhood layer in the initial view (the same way landscape_state="umap" opens on the UMAP). The result is a tissue-wide map of every cell-type domain at a glance.

docs.title: Static plot — islets and their gradient rings¶
5. Quantify the gradient¶
docs.text:
Because the rings are a neighborhood GeoDataFrame, the calc_nbhd_by_* functions summarize each ring directly, returning rings × features AnnData:

  • calc_nbhd_by_pop → cell-type proportion per ring (here, the islet-cell fraction).
  • calc_nbhd_by_gene → mean expression per ring (here, the islet hormones).

Rings with fewer than 5 cells have no estimate; we reindex to every ring (filling them with 0) so the gradient axis stays complete.

docs.title: Static plots — composition and expression vs. distance from the islet edge¶
6. Clustergram of the gradient gene feature space¶
docs.text: The neighborhood-by-gene AnnData is a matrix of rings × genes, so we can cluster it as a heatmap to see which genes share a gradient profile. We keep the 40 most variable genes across the rings, transpose to genes × rings, and build a dega.clust.Matrix (row-z-scored) and a Clustergram. We set col_entity="nbhd" so the columns (rings) can link to the Landscape in the next section. Genes separate into an islet-enriched block (high inside, e.g. INS / GCG / SST) and an acinar block (high outside), while the rings order into an inward vs. outward split. (We build the Clustergram here and display it linked with the Landscape below.)

docs.title: 7. Linked Landscape + Clustergram¶
docs.text:
dega.viz.landscape_clustergram places the gradient Landscape and the Clustergram side by side and links them. Passing nbhd=gdf_grad is all the Landscape needs — it converts the micron ring geometry to pixels using the DegaFiles transform, each ring keeps its gradient color (reds inward, blues outward), and landscape_state="nbhd" shows the rings on load.

Because the clustergram's columns are the gradient rings (col_entity="nbhd") and the Landscape's neighborhood names are the same ring labels, clicking a ring column in the heatmap highlights that ring on the tissue (and toggles on the NBHD layer) — letting you read expression and spatial position together.

docs.title: 8. Optional: keep the results together in a NeighborhoodCollection¶
docs.text:
Everything above used plain objects: a GeoDataFrame of rings and the AnnData results. When you want the rings, their per-ring tables, and ring-to-ring relations kept aligned in one object (to save them together, or to subset them all at once), store them in a NeighborhoodCollection.

The collection only stores data. The celldega.nbhd functions do the computation and return plain objects, which we store with add_mod (per-ring tables) and add_relation (ring-to-ring matrices). Rings that fell below min_cells are zero-filled on the collection's ring axis.

docs.title: Cell size and continuous rotation¶
docs.text:
cell_size sets the default cell diameter in microns, assuming the centroid coordinates are in microns. Change cell_size=10.0 below and rerun the notebook to try another default.

In the interactive preview, the CELL slider multiplies this diameter: its midpoint is 1× (10 µm here), the minimum is 0×, and the maximum is 2× (20 µm here). Drag vertically or horizontally to rotate continuously, including past the poles where vertical rotation previously stopped.

The saved documentation preview uses the JavaScript bundle served by this local docs site. Reexecuting the notebook uses your locally built frontend.

docs.title: Landscape from a Local Server¶
docs.text: Celldega's widgets run in the browser and load DegaFiles (the output of dega.pre.main) over HTTP. To view DegaFiles stored on your own machine, start a local file server with dega.viz.get_local_server() and point the Landscape's base_url at it.

docs.title: Serve local DegaFiles¶
docs.text:
get_local_server() starts a background HTTP server (with CORS enabled) rooted at the notebook's working directory and returns its port. Build base_url from that port plus the path to your DegaFiles folder, relative to the working directory:

from pathlib import Path

path_dega_files = Path("data/Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs")

port = dega.viz.get_local_server()
base_url = f"http://localhost:{port}/{path_dega_files.as_posix()}"

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    technology="Xenium",
    base_url=base_url,
    height=500,
)

landscape

The server runs for the lifetime of the kernel. Run this in a live Jupyter session: the static documentation page cannot reach your localhost.

docs.title: The same view from GitHub¶
docs.text: Any static host that serves the DegaFiles folder works the same way. Below, the same Landscape is created from DegaFiles pushed to a GitHub repository, so it also renders on this page. Only base_url changes.

import re
from importlib.metadata import version
from urllib.request import urlopen

import numpy as np

# The H&E image selector and Matrix.read_zarr need Celldega 0.28.2 or newer.
installed = tuple(int(x) for x in re.findall(r"\d+", version("celldega"))[:3])
if installed < (0, 28, 2):
    raise RuntimeError(
        f"This notebook needs celldega>=0.28.2 but {version('celldega')} is installed. "
        'Run: pip install -U "celldega>=0.28.2", then restart the kernel.'
    )

SAMPLE = "Atera_v1_WTA_S4A_Brain_Hippocampus_ND_FF"

# DegaFiles for the Landscape and Yearbook: GitHub (one file per tile)
BASE_URL = "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/broadinstitute/celldega_atera-wta-ff-human-nd-brain/main"
# The Matrix (pre-clustered AnnData-Zarr) is hosted on Hugging Face only.
MATRIX_URL = f"{HF_BASE}/{SAMPLE}/cgm/default_clusters"

# Atera centroids are in microns; this matrix maps microns to image pixels.
with urlopen(f"{BASE_URL}/micron_to_image_transform.csv") as response:

docs.title: Atera human brain hippocampus (non-diseased, fresh frozen) with aligned H&E: Landscape, Yearbook and a Matrix-linked Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Explore the pre-processed 10x Genomics Atera WTA dataset Atera_v1_WTA_S4A_Brain_Hippocampus_ND_FF with Celldega:

  1. a wide Landscape of the whole tissue with its default clusters,
  2. a Yearbook of individual cells (query by cluster and gene),
  3. a linked Landscape and Clustergram of the default clusters, drawn from a Matrix whose clustering was pre-computed, with an Enrich widget for gene-set enrichment of selected genes.

Each Landscape and the Yearbook can show either the fluorescence morphology image or the dataset's post-run H&E image, aligned to it with the 10x Genomics alignment matrix. Cells, transcripts and clusters stay in place on both backgrounds, so expression can be compared directly with tissue histology.

The Matrix is a clusters x genes object with pre-clustered results stored in an AnnData-Zarr (dendrograms, dot-plot sizes, marker-ranked views, and value attributes). It is loaded here, not computed, so the Clustergram appears right away. The Clustergram is the visualization of that Matrix.

Data (all public):

What Where DegaFiles (fluorescence and aligned H&E images, cells, transcripts, expression) GitHub repository celldega_atera-wta-ff-human-nd-brain (one file per tile) Matrix with pre-clustered results (AnnData-Zarr) Hugging Face only: Atera/Atera_v1_WTA_S4A_Brain_Hippocampus_ND_FF/cgm/default_clusters.zarr (and a single-file .zarr.zip) Original 10x data Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Brain (sample Atera_v1_WTA_S4A_Brain_Hippocampus_ND_FF, Atera Onboard Analysis 1.1.1)

Dataset: Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Brain, Atera In Situ Gene Expression Dataset by Atera Onboard Analysis v1.1.1, 10x Genomics, (2026, November 3). The original data are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see the 10x citation guidelines). Changes made for Celldega: the Atera output bundle was converted to DegaFiles with dega.pre.main, the post-run H&E image was resampled onto the morphology image with 10x's alignment CSV using dega.pre.add_aligned_he, and the default-cluster Matrix was computed as described at the end of this notebook. The Atera pre-processing with H&E notebook shows these steps.

Requirements: pip install "celldega>=0.28.2". The Matrix is read with anndata/zarr, which Celldega already depends on. Scanpy is only needed to re-create the Matrix (see the end of this notebook).

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text:
Explore the full tissue and its default clusters. This full-width Landscape is a separate widget from the linked view below, so selections and resizing in one leave the other independent.

Switch to H&E: click FLR (fluorescence) next to SPATIAL IMG at the top left and choose H&E. Choose FLR again to return to the DAPI, boundary, RNA and protein channels.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same default clusters as the Landscape. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with the largest default cluster (21) ranked by CLDND1, a strong marker of that cluster. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells. The Yearbook has the same FLR / H&E selector next to IMG, so the portraits can also be shown on the H&E image.

docs.title: Load the Matrix with pre-clustered results¶
docs.text:
The default-cluster Matrix was computed once and saved as an AnnData-Zarr, so loading it is fast and needs no Scanpy. It holds:

  • values: log1p CPM of each gene per default cluster (pseudo-bulk signatures of all cells), z-scored per gene for display;
  • dot sizes: the fraction of each cluster's cells expressing each gene;
  • marker-ranked views: the DIM slider shows the top 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75 or 100 markers per cluster (ranked with scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups, Wilcoxon, on all cells); all genes remain available;
  • value attributes: each cluster column has n_cells, and each gene row has total_counts and mean_counts over all cells.

Matrix.read_zarr restores the clustering exactly as saved; nothing is re-clustered.

docs.title: Linked Landscape and Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Pass the pre-clustered Matrix to Clustergram and link it to a Landscape. Click a gene row to show its spatial expression, or a cluster column to select that cluster's cells. The DIM slider changes how many top markers per cluster are shown; the dot plot encodes mean expression by color and fraction of cells expressing by size. This Landscape has its own FLR / H&E selector, independent of the overview above.

enrich=True adds an Enrich widget beside the Clustergram: select genes (for example a branch of the row dendrogram, or genes picked in the Landscape) to run gene-set enrichment, and use its controls to choose the gene-set library, such as CellMarker for cell-type annotation.

docs.title: How the Matrix was made¶
docs.text:
The Matrix was pre-computed from the Atera cell_feature_matrix and the dataset's default Leiden clustering with standard scverse tools. The steps, in outline:

import anndata as ad, scanpy as sc
from celldega.pre.atera import read_atera_cbg, read_atera_clusters

cells = ad.AnnData(...)            # raw counts + default cluster in cells.obs["cluster"]
# keep clusters with at least 100 cells

# pseudo-bulk signatures from ALL cells (no subsampling)
signatures = sc.get.aggregate(cells, by="cluster", func=["sum", "count_nonzero"])
signatures.obs["n_cells"] = cells.obs["cluster"].value_counts().reindex(signatures.obs_names)
signatures.X = signatures.layers["sum"].astype("float32")
signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"] = (
    signatures.layers["count_nonzero"] / signatures.obs["n_cells"].to_numpy()[:, None]
)
sc.pp.normalize_total(signatures, target_sum=1e6)
sc.pp.log1p(signatures)
signatures.var["total_counts"] = ...   # sum of raw counts per gene over all cells
signatures.var["mean_counts"] = ...    # mean raw counts per gene per cell

# marker ranking on all cells, as in the Scanpy clustering tutorial
ranked = ad.AnnData(cells.X.copy(), obs=cells.obs[["cluster"]].copy(), var=cells.var.copy())
sc.pp.normalize_total(ranked)
sc.pp.log1p(ranked)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(ranked, groupby="cluster", method="wilcoxon", n_genes=ranked.n_vars)
signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"] = ranked.uns["rank_genes_groups"]

matrix = dega.clust.Matrix(
    signatures, col_attr=["cluster", "n_cells"], row_attr=["total_counts", "mean_counts"],
    name="default_clusters",
)
matrix.set_size_matrix(ad.AnnData(signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"],
                                  obs=signatures.obs.copy(), var=signatures.var.copy()))
matrix.norm("row", by="zscore")
matrix.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100])

matrix.write_zarr("default_clusters.zarr")                 # AnnData-Zarr, read with Matrix.read_zarr
matrix.write_dega_files("path/to/DegaFiles", name="default_clusters")  # parquet for the browser

Cluster colors are taken from the DegaFiles so the Clustergram and Landscape agree.

docs.title: Atera breast cancer Landscape + Clustergram + Enrich¶
docs.text:
This tutorial uses celldega>=0.26.0. It demonstrates the handoff from a precomputed Scanpy analysis plus published cell type annotations to Celldega: Scanpy provides normalized expression and UMAP coordinates, the cell types and colors come from 10x Genomics' own annotation of this dataset. Scanpy calculates expression signatures and marker rankings in plain AnnData objects; Celldega builds the all-gene hierarchy and linked interactive widgets. The first run downloads the raw 10x file and runs the Scanpy filtering, normalization, PCA, neighbors, and UMAP steps once, saving the result. Later runs load the saved AnnData and go straight to Celldega.

Data source: broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data. Downloads use a direct Hugging Face /resolve/main/ URL through Python's standard library, so huggingface_hub is not a notebook dependency. Cell types are from 10x Genomics' WTA_Preview_FFPE_Breast_Cancer_cell_groups.csv.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: If the processed AnnData is already on disk it is loaded directly. Otherwise the raw file is downloaded (if needed) and processed with Scanpy.

docs.title: Load or compute the Scanpy preprocessing¶
docs.text: Keep all genes and preserve raw counts in layers["counts"] for aggregation and detection fractions. Normalize and log-transform X for UMAP and marker testing. The saved preprocessing is also used by the neighborhood exploration tutorial; signatures and marker rankings are calculated below on each run. Cell types are added from the 10x annotation in the next section.

docs.title: 10x cell types¶
docs.text: The 10x cell groups CSV is small (one row per cell: cell_id, group, color), so it is read straight from the URL and propagated onto adata.obs by cell id. The 10x colors are stored as adata.uns["cell_type_colors"] (Scanpy's palette convention), so Scanpy, the Landscape, and the Clustergram all share them.

docs.title: Landscape¶
docs.text: Start with a full-width, 700px-high tissue view. landscape_overview is a separate widget instance from landscape, which is reserved for the linked Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich view below. Linking and resizing that view therefore leaves this overview at its original size.

docs.title: AnnData expression, fraction expressing, and marker ranks¶
docs.text: sc.get.aggregate summarizes raw counts per 10x cell type. Normalize the sums to log1p-CPM for dot colors and divide nonzero-cell counts by group size for dot sizes. Run sc.tl.rank_genes_groups directly on the log-normalized cell-level adata.X. Its standard Scanpy results are stored in signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"]; the signatures AnnData contains all genes, their best-scoring cell type, and the same category colors as the Landscape.

docs.title: Clustergram over all genes¶
docs.text:
The full expression matrix is hierarchically clustered. Marker-ranked views are additional slider levels; they do not replace or prefilter the all-gene matrix.

Columns are colored by 10x cell type with the same palette as the Landscape. Rows are colored by a gene-level grouping derived from those cell types: each gene is assigned to the cell type where it scores highest in rank_genes_groups (signatures.var["cell_type_marker"]). Double-click a category name to reorder by it.

docs.title: Yearbook: visually query individual cells¶
docs.text:
Yearbook displays a grid of tissue portraits centered on individual cells, so you can compare their morphology and local surroundings side by side. Use its query controls to select cells by cluster or cell type, gene expression, or both. A cell-type query samples cells from that group; adding a gene ranks the matching cells by expression, highest first.

This example starts with Myeloid Cells ranked by LST1 expression. Eight portraits are shown per page, with up to 48 cells available through the paging controls. Change the cell type or gene in the Yearbook to explore another population. These queries run in the browser and also work in the saved documentation page.

docs.title: Atera human breast cancer (fresh frozen) with aligned H&E: Landscape, Yearbook and a Matrix-linked Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Explore the pre-processed 10x Genomics Atera WTA dataset Atera_v1_WTA_S4C_Breast_Cancer_FF with Celldega:

  1. a wide Landscape of the whole tissue with its default clusters,
  2. a Yearbook of individual cells (query by cluster and gene),
  3. a linked Landscape and Clustergram of the default clusters, drawn from a Matrix whose clustering was pre-computed, with an Enrich widget for gene-set enrichment of selected genes.

Each Landscape and the Yearbook can show either the fluorescence morphology image or the dataset's post-run H&E image, aligned to it with the 10x Genomics alignment matrix. Cells, transcripts and clusters stay in place on both backgrounds, so expression can be compared directly with tissue histology.

The Matrix is a clusters x genes object with pre-clustered results stored in an AnnData-Zarr (dendrograms, dot-plot sizes, marker-ranked views, and value attributes). It is loaded here, not computed, so the Clustergram appears right away. The Clustergram is the visualization of that Matrix.

Data (all public):

What Where DegaFiles (fluorescence and aligned H&E images, cells, transcripts, expression) GitHub repository celldega_atera-wta-ff-human-breast-cancer (one file per tile) Matrix with pre-clustered results (AnnData-Zarr) Hugging Face only: Atera/Atera_v1_WTA_S4C_Breast_Cancer_FF/cgm/default_clusters.zarr (and a single-file .zarr.zip) Original 10x data Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Breast Cancer (sample Atera_v1_WTA_S4C_Breast_Cancer_FF, Atera Onboard Analysis 1.1.1)

Dataset: Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Breast Cancer, Atera In Situ Gene Expression Dataset by Atera Onboard Analysis v1.1.1, 10x Genomics, (2026, November 5). The original data are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see the 10x citation guidelines). Changes made for Celldega: the Atera output bundle was converted to DegaFiles with dega.pre.main, the post-run H&E image was resampled onto the morphology image with 10x's alignment CSV using dega.pre.add_aligned_he, and the default-cluster Matrix was computed as described at the end of this notebook. The Atera pre-processing with H&E notebook shows these steps.

Requirements: pip install "celldega>=0.28.2". The Matrix is read with anndata/zarr, which Celldega already depends on. Scanpy is only needed to re-create the Matrix (see the end of this notebook).

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text:
Explore the full tissue and its default clusters. This full-width Landscape is a separate widget from the linked view below, so selections and resizing in one leave the other independent.

Switch to H&E: click FLR (fluorescence) next to SPATIAL IMG at the top left and choose H&E. Choose FLR again to return to the DAPI, boundary, RNA and protein channels.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same default clusters as the Landscape. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with the largest default cluster (5) ranked by MGST1, a strong marker of that cluster. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells. The Yearbook has the same FLR / H&E selector next to IMG, so the portraits can also be shown on the H&E image.

docs.title: Load the Matrix with pre-clustered results¶
docs.text:
The default-cluster Matrix was computed once and saved as an AnnData-Zarr, so loading it is fast and needs no Scanpy. It holds:

  • values: log1p CPM of each gene per default cluster (pseudo-bulk signatures of all cells), z-scored per gene for display;
  • dot sizes: the fraction of each cluster's cells expressing each gene;
  • marker-ranked views: the DIM slider shows the top 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75 or 100 markers per cluster (ranked with scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups, Wilcoxon, on all cells); all genes remain available;
  • value attributes: each cluster column has n_cells, and each gene row has total_counts and mean_counts over all cells.

Matrix.read_zarr restores the clustering exactly as saved; nothing is re-clustered.

docs.title: Linked Landscape and Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Pass the pre-clustered Matrix to Clustergram and link it to a Landscape. Click a gene row to show its spatial expression, or a cluster column to select that cluster's cells. The DIM slider changes how many top markers per cluster are shown; the dot plot encodes mean expression by color and fraction of cells expressing by size. This Landscape has its own FLR / H&E selector, independent of the overview above.

enrich=True adds an Enrich widget beside the Clustergram: select genes (for example a branch of the row dendrogram, or genes picked in the Landscape) to run gene-set enrichment, and use its controls to choose the gene-set library, such as CellMarker for cell-type annotation.

docs.title: How the Matrix was made¶
docs.text:
The Matrix was pre-computed from the Atera cell_feature_matrix and the dataset's default Leiden clustering with standard scverse tools. The steps, in outline:

import anndata as ad, scanpy as sc
from celldega.pre.atera import read_atera_cbg, read_atera_clusters

cells = ad.AnnData(...)            # raw counts + default cluster in cells.obs["cluster"]
# keep clusters with at least 100 cells

# pseudo-bulk signatures from ALL cells (no subsampling)
signatures = sc.get.aggregate(cells, by="cluster", func=["sum", "count_nonzero"])
signatures.obs["n_cells"] = cells.obs["cluster"].value_counts().reindex(signatures.obs_names)
signatures.X = signatures.layers["sum"].astype("float32")
signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"] = (
    signatures.layers["count_nonzero"] / signatures.obs["n_cells"].to_numpy()[:, None]
)
sc.pp.normalize_total(signatures, target_sum=1e6)
sc.pp.log1p(signatures)
signatures.var["total_counts"] = ...   # sum of raw counts per gene over all cells
signatures.var["mean_counts"] = ...    # mean raw counts per gene per cell

# marker ranking on all cells, as in the Scanpy clustering tutorial
ranked = ad.AnnData(cells.X.copy(), obs=cells.obs[["cluster"]].copy(), var=cells.var.copy())
sc.pp.normalize_total(ranked)
sc.pp.log1p(ranked)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(ranked, groupby="cluster", method="wilcoxon", n_genes=ranked.n_vars)
signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"] = ranked.uns["rank_genes_groups"]

matrix = dega.clust.Matrix(
    signatures, col_attr=["cluster", "n_cells"], row_attr=["total_counts", "mean_counts"],
    name="default_clusters",
)
matrix.set_size_matrix(ad.AnnData(signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"],
                                  obs=signatures.obs.copy(), var=signatures.var.copy()))
matrix.norm("row", by="zscore")
matrix.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100])

matrix.write_zarr("default_clusters.zarr")                 # AnnData-Zarr, read with Matrix.read_zarr
matrix.write_dega_files("path/to/DegaFiles", name="default_clusters")  # parquet for the browser

Cluster colors are taken from the DegaFiles so the Clustergram and Landscape agree.

docs.title: Atera breast cancer neighborhood exploration¶
docs.text:
Continue from the Atera Landscape–Clustergram tutorial. Run its data preprocessing first; this notebook reuses the saved cell list, 10x cell types and tissue coordinates. Requires celldega>=0.26.0.

Two views explore the same sample at 75 µm: cell-type composition niches from hextiles, and overlap of cell-type alpha-shape footprints. Niche labels belong to hextiles; no niche attribute is added to individual cells.

docs.title: Hextile niches¶
docs.text:
Count cell types in each tile, discard tiles with fewer than five cells, and cluster square-root proportions (Hellinger representation) with Celldega's Matrix.cluster and cut_tree. Eight niches is an exploratory resolution. The Composition bars pool cell counts across retained tiles of each niche. The broad biological names describe this 75 µm, eight-niche result; the table retains the original IDs and leading cell types so you can check them. These are composition labels, not validated histological regions. Review the names if you change the tile size or clustering resolution.

Click a column label to highlight every individual hextile of that niche. Click a row label to show that cell type across the tissue, irrespective of niche. Column dendrogram selections highlight groups of niches. The polygons remain separate hextiles, so you can also select one directly in the Landscape.

docs.title: Alpha-shape overlap¶
docs.text:
Make one footprint per cell type, retaining disconnected patches within its MultiPolygon. ALPHA_SCALE_UM is the inverse-alpha shape scale in microns, not a tile diameter. Empty footprints are omitted.

Calculate intersection areas with dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_overlap, then column-normalize with Matrix.norm: each column sums to one, including self-overlap on the diagonal. A value is a share of the column's summed intersection areas, not the fraction of its unique area covered by a cell type; overlapping footprints can count the same area more than once.

Click any matrix tile, including a zero, to highlight both footprints and inspect their spatial overlap or separation. Row/column labels select one footprint; dendrogram selections highlight groups with similar overlap profiles. These footprints describe spatial mixing of cell types, not cell–cell contacts.

docs.title: Atera human colorectal cancer (fresh frozen) with aligned H&E: Landscape, Yearbook and a Matrix-linked Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Explore the pre-processed 10x Genomics Atera WTA dataset Atera_v1_WTA_S4B_Colorectal_Cancer_FF with Celldega:

  1. a wide Landscape of the whole tissue with its default clusters,
  2. a Yearbook of individual cells (query by cluster and gene),
  3. a linked Landscape and Clustergram of the default clusters, drawn from a Matrix whose clustering was pre-computed, with an Enrich widget for gene-set enrichment of selected genes.

Each Landscape and the Yearbook can show either the fluorescence morphology image or the dataset's post-run H&E image, aligned to it with the 10x Genomics alignment matrix. Cells, transcripts and clusters stay in place on both backgrounds, so expression can be compared directly with tissue histology.

The Matrix is a clusters x genes object with pre-clustered results stored in an AnnData-Zarr (dendrograms, dot-plot sizes, marker-ranked views, and value attributes). It is loaded here, not computed, so the Clustergram appears right away. The Clustergram is the visualization of that Matrix.

Data (all public):

What Where DegaFiles (fluorescence and aligned H&E images, cells, transcripts, expression) GitHub repository celldega_atera-wta-ff-human-crc (one file per tile) Matrix with pre-clustered results (AnnData-Zarr) Hugging Face only: Atera/Atera_v1_WTA_S4B_Colorectal_Cancer_FF/cgm/default_clusters.zarr (and a single-file .zarr.zip) Original 10x data Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Colorectal Cancer (sample Atera_v1_WTA_S4B_Colorectal_Cancer_FF, Atera Onboard Analysis 1.1.1)

Dataset: Atera In Situ Gene Expression, Fresh Frozen Human Colorectal Cancer, Atera In Situ Gene Expression Dataset by Atera Onboard Analysis v1.1.1, 10x Genomics, (2026, November 5). The original data are licensed under CC BY 4.0 (see the 10x citation guidelines). Changes made for Celldega: the Atera output bundle was converted to DegaFiles with dega.pre.main, the post-run H&E image was resampled onto the morphology image with 10x's alignment CSV using dega.pre.add_aligned_he, and the default-cluster Matrix was computed as described at the end of this notebook. The Atera pre-processing with H&E notebook shows these steps.

Requirements: pip install "celldega>=0.28.2". The Matrix is read with anndata/zarr, which Celldega already depends on. Scanpy is only needed to re-create the Matrix (see the end of this notebook).

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text:
Explore the full tissue and its default clusters. This full-width Landscape is a separate widget from the linked view below, so selections and resizing in one leave the other independent.

Switch to H&E: click FLR (fluorescence) next to SPATIAL IMG at the top left and choose H&E. Choose FLR again to return to the DAPI, boundary, RNA and protein channels.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same default clusters as the Landscape. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with the largest default cluster (3) ranked by CLDN4, a strong marker of that cluster. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells. The Yearbook has the same FLR / H&E selector next to IMG, so the portraits can also be shown on the H&E image.

docs.title: Load the Matrix with pre-clustered results¶
docs.text:
The default-cluster Matrix was computed once and saved as an AnnData-Zarr, so loading it is fast and needs no Scanpy. It holds:

  • values: log1p CPM of each gene per default cluster (pseudo-bulk signatures of all cells), z-scored per gene for display;
  • dot sizes: the fraction of each cluster's cells expressing each gene;
  • marker-ranked views: the DIM slider shows the top 1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75 or 100 markers per cluster (ranked with scanpy.tl.rank_genes_groups, Wilcoxon, on all cells); all genes remain available;
  • value attributes: each cluster column has n_cells, and each gene row has total_counts and mean_counts over all cells.

Matrix.read_zarr restores the clustering exactly as saved; nothing is re-clustered.

docs.title: Linked Landscape and Clustergram¶
docs.text:
Pass the pre-clustered Matrix to Clustergram and link it to a Landscape. Click a gene row to show its spatial expression, or a cluster column to select that cluster's cells. The DIM slider changes how many top markers per cluster are shown; the dot plot encodes mean expression by color and fraction of cells expressing by size. This Landscape has its own FLR / H&E selector, independent of the overview above.

enrich=True adds an Enrich widget beside the Clustergram: select genes (for example a branch of the row dendrogram, or genes picked in the Landscape) to run gene-set enrichment, and use its controls to choose the gene-set library, such as CellMarker for cell-type annotation.

docs.title: How the Matrix was made¶
docs.text:
The Matrix was pre-computed from the Atera cell_feature_matrix and the dataset's default Leiden clustering with standard scverse tools. The steps, in outline:

import anndata as ad, scanpy as sc
from celldega.pre.atera import read_atera_cbg, read_atera_clusters

cells = ad.AnnData(...)            # raw counts + default cluster in cells.obs["cluster"]
# keep clusters with at least 100 cells

# pseudo-bulk signatures from ALL cells (no subsampling)
signatures = sc.get.aggregate(cells, by="cluster", func=["sum", "count_nonzero"])
signatures.obs["n_cells"] = cells.obs["cluster"].value_counts().reindex(signatures.obs_names)
signatures.X = signatures.layers["sum"].astype("float32")
signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"] = (
    signatures.layers["count_nonzero"] / signatures.obs["n_cells"].to_numpy()[:, None]
)
sc.pp.normalize_total(signatures, target_sum=1e6)
sc.pp.log1p(signatures)
signatures.var["total_counts"] = ...   # sum of raw counts per gene over all cells
signatures.var["mean_counts"] = ...    # mean raw counts per gene per cell

# marker ranking on all cells, as in the Scanpy clustering tutorial
ranked = ad.AnnData(cells.X.copy(), obs=cells.obs[["cluster"]].copy(), var=cells.var.copy())
sc.pp.normalize_total(ranked)
sc.pp.log1p(ranked)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(ranked, groupby="cluster", method="wilcoxon", n_genes=ranked.n_vars)
signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"] = ranked.uns["rank_genes_groups"]

matrix = dega.clust.Matrix(
    signatures, col_attr=["cluster", "n_cells"], row_attr=["total_counts", "mean_counts"],
    name="default_clusters",
)
matrix.set_size_matrix(ad.AnnData(signatures.layers["fraction_expressing"],
                                  obs=signatures.obs.copy(), var=signatures.var.copy()))
matrix.norm("row", by="zscore")
matrix.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 2, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100])

matrix.write_zarr("default_clusters.zarr")                 # AnnData-Zarr, read with Matrix.read_zarr
matrix.write_dega_files("path/to/DegaFiles", name="default_clusters")  # parquet for the browser

Cluster colors are taken from the DegaFiles so the Clustergram and Landscape agree.

docs.title: Atera kidney: default clusters and glomerular gradients¶
docs.text:
Compare the dataset's 28 default Leiden clusters in a linked Landscape–dotplot Clustergram, then measure how cell-type composition changes with distance from podocyte-defined glomerular footprints.

Watch on YouTube

Default cluster 16 contains 5,172 cells, 96.7% with a supplied Podocyte annotation. We use its spatial nodules as candidate glomeruli, then summarize the supplied Azimuth coarse cell types inside and around them. The gradient uses all 399,120 cell centroids, including cells without a default cluster.

The workflow uses AnnData, GeoDataFrames, Scanpy, and the neighborhood module's geometry functions. There are no collection classes, inline helper functions, signature caches, or sub-clustering steps. Manual category tracks are disabled in the linked default-cluster view.

The data are the public Atera WTA FFPE human non-diseased kidney dataset from 10x Genomics, with over 1 billion transcripts. Use the dega environment on the atera_preprocess branch. DegaFiles are on GitHub; annotated raw counts are on Hugging Face. The count file is 1.31 GiB; allow several GiB of memory.

docs.title: Cell-type context for the default clusters¶
docs.text:
The supplied Azimuth coarse labels provide a guide to a few default clusters:

Default cluster(s) Main supplied cell-type annotation 2 B cells (76.9%) 11 Macrophages (77.9%) 15 T cells (65.9%) 16 Podocytes (96.7%), used for glomerular footprints below 21, 22, 24 Proximal-tubule epithelial cells (95–100%) 13 Endothelial cells (94.6%)

These annotations describe cluster composition; they do not rename or independently validate the default clusters.

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text: Explore the full tissue and its original default clusters. This full-width Landscape is a separate widget from the linked views below, so their selections and resizing leave this overview independent.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same default clusters as the Landscape above. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with cluster 16 (podocytes) ranked by NPHS2. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells.

docs.title: Default cluster signatures¶
docs.text:
All 28 default clusters pass the 100-cell minimum: 398,873 labeled cells; 247 unlabeled cells are excluded from the linked views. cells.X contains raw counts, and its original Leiden colors match the DegaFiles.

First aggregate counts and detection fractions into a clusters × genes AnnData. Dot colors will show log1p CPM, z-scored per gene; dot sizes will show the fraction of cells expressing each gene.

docs.title: Linked default-cluster view¶
docs.text: Pass the signatures AnnData to Matrix, and a second AnnData with detection fractions to set_size_matrix. Click a gene row to show spatial expression, or a cluster column to select its cells. The DIM slider changes the number of top markers per cluster; all 18,049 genes remain available.

docs.title: Podocyte-defined glomerular footprints¶
docs.text:
Use dega.nbhd.alpha_shape on cluster 16 at an inverse-alpha scale of 40 µm. Fill enclosed holes so the footprint includes the nodule interior, union any nested components, and retain components supported by at least 10 podocytes. These are candidate footprints, not histologically segmented glomeruli; the scale and support cutoff are exploratory settings.

At these settings, 119 footprints contain 4,430 of the 5,172 seed cells. The other seed cells do not define a retained footprint, but remain eligible for the composition counts.

SEED_CLUSTERS is a list so you can add other default clusters. Start with ["16"]: including a broadly distributed endothelial or stromal cluster without a spatial restriction can connect unrelated regions.

docs.title: Distance bands in a GeoDataFrame¶
docs.text:
dega.nbhd.calc_gradient returns 25 µm bands, measured from the footprint boundary: negative distances are inside, positive distances are outside, up to 200 µm. It unions the footprints before buffering, so neighboring glomeruli do not double-count the same surrounding tissue. Outward bands are clipped to a tissue alpha shape built from all cell centroids (inverse alpha 200 µm).

The resulting rings is a plain GeoDataFrame. The spatial check below shows the whole section and a zoom near its center. Black outlines delimit footprints; red bands lie inside and blue bands outside.

docs.title: Count cell types with a spatial join¶
docs.text:
Count each cell once, even on shared band boundaries: intersects includes hull vertices, and ties go to the more inward band. This matters because many seed podocytes are exactly on their footprint's boundary.

Use the supplied coarse annotations, keeping uncertain and unassigned cells in the denominator. No minimum cell-type size is imposed on the analysis. population is an AnnData with bands × cell types: proportions in X, integer counts in layers["counts"], and distances and sample sizes in obs. Cell-to-band assignments remain in spatial_cells.obs["glomerulus_band"]; cells outside the analyzed region have missing assignments.

docs.title: Cell-type composition versus distance¶
docs.text:
For display only, retain cell types reaching 2% in any band and combine the remaining types into Other. All individual categories remain in population. The upper panel shows the number of cells supporting each estimate; the lower panel shows proportions. Zero marks the footprint boundary.

These are pooled, cell-weighted proportions from one section, not averages over glomeruli or biological replicates. Deep inward bands sample only the larger footprints. Podocyte enrichment at the boundary is partly built into how the footprints were defined.

docs.title: Linked Landscape–Composition view¶
docs.text:
Composition accepts an AnnData directly. Set col_entity="nbhd" so its distance-band columns select the matching GeoDataFrame geometries in a separate Landscape. The row entity names the cell-type attribute shared with that Landscape; clicking a stacked segment highlights its cell type and distance band together.

cluster=False preserves distance order. The distance and cell-count tracks expose each band's metadata, and the PROP/COUNTS toggle compares proportions with cell counts. Cell colors match the static plot, including the display-only Other group. The complete, uncollapsed analysis remains in population. The wide overview and default-cluster view above stay independent.

docs.title: Reading this run¶
docs.text:
There are 149,833 unique cells across 11 bands (three inward and eight outward), with 52 supplied coarse labels represented. The deepest band contains 286 cells; the other bands contain 2,928–19,631 cells.

Within 0–25 µm outside the footprints, endothelial-labeled cells account for 16.3%, proximal-tubule-labeled cells 3.9%, and macrophages 7.0%. At 175–200 µm outside, those proportions are 8.3%, 21.1%, and 8.0%, respectively. Endothelial labels reach 44.1% in the deepest inward band. These changes describe the supplied annotations in this section; inspect the footprints and label confidence before interpreting them biologically.

The source counts, labels, and DegaFiles are unchanged. The following exports contain the full composition table, candidate footprints, distance bands, and an expression-free AnnData with cell coordinates and band assignments. They can be joined to the original expression AnnData by cell ID.

def download_if_missing(remote_filename, destination):
    """Download one public Hub file, with no HF client dependency."""
    if destination.is_file():
        return destination

    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    partial = destination.with_name(f"{destination.name}.part")
    url = f"{HF_RESOLVE_BASE}/{remote_filename}?download=true"
    request = Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "celldega-example-notebook"})
    print(f"Downloading {url}")
    try:
        with urlopen(request) as response, partial.open("wb") as output:
            shutil.copyfileobj(response, output, length=8 * 1024 * 1024)
        partial.replace(destination)
    except Exception:
        partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise
    return destination

        for cl in set(native[a]) & set(native[b]):
            ga = shapely.transform(native[a][cl], transforms[a].apply)

            inter = ga.intersection(gb).area
            union = ga.area + gb.area - inter
            ious.append(inter / union if union > 0 else 0.0)
        out.append(np.mean(ious) if ious else np.nan)
    return out

docs.title: Broad-Allen Developing Mouse Brain E15.5: Align¶
docs.text:
This tutorial uses celldega>=0.28. It shows how Celldega aligns serial sections into a 3D stack in two simple steps, using the Leiden clusters as landmarks:

  1. Cluster centroids: one landmark per (slice, cluster) at the cluster's centroid, then a rigid Procrustes fit chained out from the middle slice.
  2. Neighborhoods: one alpha shape per (slice, cluster); each slice's rigid pose is refined to maximize the overlap of matching shapes in nearby slices.

The aligned cells are then written as CellCloud DegaFiles, which the companion notebook Broad-Allen_Dev-Mouse-Brain_E15.5_Viz visualizes.

docs.title: The experiment¶
docs.text:
This dataset is being generated in collaboration with the Allen Institute. It is whole-brain spatial transcriptomics of a mouse embryo at E15.5. The brain was cut into 44 coronal sections, ordered from the front of the brain (slice 1, anterior) to the back (slice 44, posterior), with a section taken every 100 µm, and profiled with the 10x Xenium platform and a 480-gene panel. Cells were segmented from the images, which gives each cell a position (in µm) and a gene-count vector. After quality control the dataset holds about 3.8 million cells.

All cells from all slices were clustered together with Leiden using rapids-singlecell on Manifold.ai, so a cluster means the same thing in every slice. The clustered AnnData (raw counts, cell positions, slice numbers and Leiden labels) is hosted on Hugging Face: Allen-Broad_Dev-Mouse-Brain/E15.5/xenium_E15.5_clustered.h5ad (about 1.9 GB).

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text: The clustered AnnData is downloaded from Hugging Face, unless it is already on disk.

docs.title: 1. Load the cells¶
docs.text: Only the cell metadata, positions and UMAP are needed for alignment, so the AnnData is opened in backed mode and the count matrix stays on disk.

docs.title: 2. Leiden clusters¶
docs.text: We use the leiden_1.0 clusters. Because the clusters are shared across slices, the same cluster appears in neighboring slices and can serve as a landmark for alignment.

docs.title: 3. Select the cells to align¶
docs.text:
Two sets of cells are left out:

  • Slice 44, a small fragment at the end of the series that barely overlaps its neighbor and has poor clusters. Its position in the stack is left empty, so the remaining slices keep their true spacing.
  • A second, separate piece of tissue on slice 13 (flagged in extra_tissue_piece). Only the main piece is aligned.

docs.title: 4. Align, step 1: cluster centroids¶
docs.text: dega.align.calc_landmarks places one landmark per (slice, cluster) at the cluster's centroid. We also add a tissue-center landmark per slice. dega.align.calc_alignment_transform then fits a rigid Procrustes transform for each slice to its neighbors (within alignment_window slices), chained out from the middle slice. A cluster's centroid in one slice should land on top of the same cluster's centroid in the next.

docs.title: 5. Align, step 2: neighborhoods¶
docs.text:
A neighborhood here is the alpha shape of all cells of one cluster in one slice, computed in each slice's native frame. dega.align.neighborhood_alignment starts from the Procrustes pose and nudges each slice (a bounded rotation and translation) to maximize the overlap of matching neighborhoods in nearby slices. Centroids average away a region's shape and orientation; overlapping the shapes recovers it.

On a laptop the alpha shapes take a few minutes and the refinement about 15-20 minutes.

docs.title: 6. Compare the two steps¶
docs.text: For each pair of adjacent slices we compute the intersection-over-union (IoU) of each cluster's alpha shapes after alignment, averaged over the clusters the two slices share. Higher means matching regions overlap better.

docs.title: 7. Apply both alignments to every cell¶
docs.text:
Each slice's transform is applied to its cells. The position along the stack is (slice - reference) * 100 µm, so the dropped slice leaves a gap instead of shifting the later slices.

The plots show all slices stacked on top of each other (left) and from the side (right). After the neighborhood step the clusters line up more tightly from slice to slice.

docs.title: 8. Write the CellCloud DegaFiles¶
docs.text:
The DegaFiles for this dataset are already hosted on GitHub at broadinstitute/celldega_xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud, so you don't need to write them to follow the Viz notebook. The code below shows how they were made.

CellCloud draws every cell as a point in 3D. Its orbit camera spins around the vertical (data-Z) axis, so side_view_coords puts the stack along data-X (anterior on the left) and the dorsal-ventral axis along Z (dorsal up). Points are drawn in file order without depth sorting, so the cells are written anterior first and posterior last, to suit the Viz notebook's camera.

dega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset writes both alignments as named variants of one directory. The first call creates the directory, including the cluster colors and the counts of all 480 genes (cbg/, one file per gene). The second call only adds the centroids positions.

def side_view_coords(xy_um, stack_um):
    """(x, y, stack) -> (stack, x, y), centered on the origin, with dorsal up."""
    pts = np.column_stack([xy_um, stack_um])
    center = (pts.min(axis=0) + pts.max(axis=0)) / 2
    x, y, s = (pts - center).T
    return np.column_stack([s, x, y])


CELL_CLOUD_DIR = Path("DegaFiles/xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud_v2_1um")
CELL_CLOUD_ZARR = Path("data/xenium_E15.5_cellcloud_v2_1um.zarr")
draw_order = np.argsort(slices, kind="stable")  # posterior slices last

cloud = ad.read_h5ad(H5AD_PATH)[keep][draw_order].copy()  # raw counts in X
cloud.obs = cloud.obs[[CLUSTER_KEY]]
alignment_xyz = {
    name: side_view_coords(aligned_xy[name][draw_order], stack_um[draw_order])
    for name in ["neighborhood", "centroids"]
}
for name, xyz in alignment_xyz.items():
    cloud.obsm["spatial"], cloud.obs["Z"] = xyz[:, :2], xyz[:, 2]
    dega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset(
        cloud,
        CELL_CLOUD_DIR,
        name=name,
        z_key="Z",
        cluster_key=CLUSTER_KEY,
        write_base_metadata=(name == "neighborhood"),
        use_int_index=True,
        coordinate_resolution=1.0,
        compression="zstd",
        compression_level=6,
    )

# The same cells and alignments, as a self-contained AnnData Zarr alternative
cloud.obsm["spatial"] = alignment_xyz["neighborhood"]
dega.pre.write_point_cloud_zarr(
    cloud,
    CELL_CLOUD_ZARR,
    z_key=None,
    cluster_key=CLUSTER_KEY,
    alignments=alignment_xyz,
    coordinate_resolution=1.0,
)

Both writers use new output paths and refuse accidental replacement. Original cell IDs are retained once; repeated Parquet tables use numeric row IDs. Rounding is limited to positions (at most 0.5 µm per axis); raw expression and cluster labels are unchanged. See the CellCloud guide for either base_url= (DegaFiles) or zarr_url= (AnnData Zarr).

def download_if_missing(remote_filename, destination):
    """Download one public Hub file, with no HF client dependency."""
    if destination.is_file():
        return destination

    destination.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    partial = destination.with_name(f"{destination.name}.part")
    url = f"{HF_RESOLVE_BASE}/{remote_filename}?download=true"
    request = Request(url, headers={"User-Agent": "celldega-example-notebook"})
    print(f"Downloading {url}")
    try:
        with urlopen(request) as response, partial.open("wb") as output:
            shutil.copyfileobj(response, output, length=8 * 1024 * 1024)
        partial.replace(destination)
    except Exception:
        partial.unlink(missing_ok=True)
        raise
    return destination

docs.title: Broad-Allen Developing Mouse Brain E15.5: Viz¶
docs.text:
This tutorial uses Celldega 0.28.0a5 and the matching JavaScript package 0.28.0-alpha.5. It visualizes a 3D alignment of the serial sections. Install the pinned release below, restart the kernel if Celldega was already imported, then run the remaining cells. The companion Preprocessing and Alignment notebook shows the two-step workflow with dega.align and exports either compact DegaFiles with dega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset or AnnData Zarr with dega.pre.write_point_cloud_zarr. Here we:

  1. Visualize in 2D: a Landscape of one slice at full resolution.
  2. Explore the clusters in 3D: a wide Composition plot of the Leiden clusters in every slice introduces the clusters along the front-to-back axis. A CellCloud of all 3.8 million aligned cells, linked to a Clustergram of the 480-gene signatures of the clusters, then lets you explore them.

Using the linked widgets. Drag to orbit around the brain and scroll to zoom. Click a column of the Clustergram (a cluster) to highlight that cluster in 3D, or a row (a gene) to color the cells by its expression.

Watch on YouTube

docs.title: The experiment¶
docs.text:
This dataset is being generated in collaboration with the Allen Institute. It is whole-brain spatial transcriptomics of a mouse embryo at E15.5. The brain was cut into 44 coronal sections, ordered from the front of the brain (slice 1, anterior) to the back (slice 44, posterior), with a section taken every 100 µm, and profiled with the 10x Xenium platform and a 480-gene panel. Cells were segmented from the images, which gives each cell a position (in µm) and a gene-count vector. After quality control the dataset holds about 3.8 million cells.

All cells from all slices were clustered together with Leiden using rapids-singlecell on Manifold.ai, so a cluster means the same thing in every slice. The clustered AnnData (raw counts, cell positions, slice numbers and Leiden labels) is hosted on Hugging Face: Allen-Broad_Dev-Mouse-Brain/E15.5/xenium_E15.5_clustered.h5ad (about 1.9 GB).

The DegaFiles (the 3D CellCloud and the 2D Landscape of slice 35) are hosted on GitHub at broadinstitute/celldega_xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text:
The CellCloud reads a compact AnnData Zarr directly from Hugging Face by default. The same cells and alignments are available as compact Parquet DegaFiles on GitHub; only the data-source argument changes. The 2D Landscape reads slice 35's original DegaFiles from GitHub.

The clustered H5AD is downloaded only when running the Python analysis cells that calculate composition and gene signatures. The rendered documentation already contains those saved results.

docs.title: Choose DegaFiles or AnnData Zarr¶
docs.text:
The saved CellCloud uses AnnData Zarr. Both hosted sources contain the same 3.8 million cells, raw counts, cluster colors, and centroid/neighborhood alignments. The controls, linked Clustergram, and alignment="neighborhood" argument work with either source.

# AnnData Zarr: default for this example
CELL_CLOUD_SOURCE = {"zarr_url": CELL_CLOUD_ZARR_URL}

# Or use compact Parquet DegaFiles instead
CELL_CLOUD_SOURCE = {"base_url": CELL_CLOUD_DEGAFILES_URL}

Choose one configuration, then run the final CellCloud cell. No in-memory AnnData is needed by that widget: it reads positions and categories from the hosted source and fetches expression when a gene is selected.

Both exports round positions to the nearest 1 µm, preserving the original cell IDs and expression values. DegaFiles store original IDs once and use numeric row IDs in repeated tables. The AnnData Zarr uses CSC expression and compressed XYZ chunks; its original observation IDs stay in obs_names.

To reproduce the exports, use the preparation script. It writes new local paths and never uploads or replaces existing hosted data. The original H5AD and DegaFiles remain available.

The notebook pins CELLDEGA_ESM_VERSION="0.28.0-alpha.5" before importing Celldega, and its saved widgets use that same JavaScript release. The original analysis outputs are retained. For checkout development, run npm run build and start the kernel with CELLDEGA_LOCAL_ESM=1 to use a local bundle instead.

docs.title: 1. Visualize in 2D: a Landscape of one slice¶
docs.text:
A Landscape shows one slice at full resolution: the DAPI and cell-boundary images, the cell outlines, and the transcripts of every gene. Cells are colored by their Leiden cluster, and the UMAP of the slice's cells is available from the control panel. Here we show slice 35, in the posterior part of the brain.

The cells in the AnnData are named <slice>_<cell id>. cell_name_prefix=True drops the slice prefix so the names match the cell ids of the slice's Xenium output.

docs.title: Cluster composition across slices¶
docs.text: The composition plot shows, for every slice (one bar each, anterior to posterior), the share of cells in each Leiden cluster. It gives an overview of all clusters at once and shows which ones belong to which part of the brain along the front-to-back axis.

docs.title: Gene-expression signatures of the clusters¶
docs.text:
Matrix(adata, groupby=...) summarizes each Leiden cluster with scanpy: the mean log-normalized expression (sc.get.aggregate), the fraction of the cluster's cells expressing each gene, and the top marker genes of each cluster (sc.tl.rank_genes_groups).

Marker ranking works on log-normalized expression of every cell, which for 3.8 million cells needs far more memory than a laptop has. The signatures are therefore computed from a random sample of up to 20,000 cells per cluster (all cells of smaller clusters). For this dataset the sampled signatures correlate with those of all cells at r > 0.999 for every cluster.

docs.title: Linked 3D view¶
docs.text:
A CellCloud of every aligned cell, linked to the Clustergram. Click a column of the Clustergram to highlight that cluster in 3D, or a row to color the cells by that gene's expression.

The CellCloud holds both alignments of the same cells. Pass alignment="centroids" to see the result of step 1 alone.

The first load reads aligned positions and cluster metadata for all 3.8 million cells. Gene expression is fetched on demand. The hosted Zarr took a median 4.4 seconds to initialize and 1.08 seconds for first Dcx coloring in three trials; network conditions and caching affect these timings. The gallery uses compact Parquet and includes the comparison.

docs.title: Preprocess DegaFiles and Viz — Pancreas¶
docs.text:
A minimal end-to-end walkthrough of the Celldega pipeline on the public Xenium V1 Human Pancreas (FFPE) dataset: download the raw data (only if it isn't already present), run dega.pre.main to generate DegaFiles, then view the result in a Landscape widget.

Data source: https://www.10xgenomics.com/datasets/ffpe-human-pancreas-with-xenium-multimodal-cell-segmentation-1-standard

docs.title: 1. Download raw Xenium data (only if needed)¶
docs.text: Checks for the extracted data first, then the downloaded archive, and only curls / unzips what's missing — so re-running the notebook doesn't re-download ~9 GB every time.

docs.title: 2. Run preprocessing → DegaFiles¶
docs.text: dega.pre.main reads the raw Xenium output under data_root_dir/sample and writes the DegaFiles landscape bundle to path_dega_files.

docs.title: 3. Visualize the DegaFiles in a Landscape¶
docs.text: By default this renders the Landscape widget from a public GitHub-hosted copy of these same Pancreas DegaFiles, so the cell below works immediately — without waiting on steps 1–2 to download/preprocess anything.

docs.title: Using your own locally generated DegaFiles instead¶
docs.text:
To view the files you generated in step 2 (path_dega_files) rather than the GitHub-hosted copy, serve them from a local server and point base_url there instead of the URL above:

server_address = dega.viz.get_local_server()
base_url = f"http://localhost:{server_address}/{path_dega_files}"

landscape_ist = dega.viz.Landscape(
    technology="Xenium",
    base_url=base_url,
)

landscape_ist
