docs.title: Chromium PBMC 3k: Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich¶
docs.text:
Cluster the 10x Genomics Chromium PBMC 3k dataset with Scanpy, save the AnnData to Zarr, and explore it with Celldega:

  • Landscape reads the cells, clusters, UMAP, and per-gene expression straight from the AnnData Zarr store in the browser, with no DegaFiles. Color cells by a gene, or plot two genes against each other in the XY view.
  • Clustergram shows each cluster's rank_genes_groups markers, clustered hierarchically with Matrix and saved to Zarr too.
  • A single-cell Clustergram shows the same markers in every cell, so you can see how they vary within each cluster.
  • Enrich finds gene sets enriched in a Clustergram selection.

Like a baking show, the recipe comes first and the finished result comes out of the oven: the steps below were already run, and the notebook loads their output from Hugging Face.

This notebook needs Celldega 0.28 or later (pip install --pre celldega until 0.28.0 is released), zarr>=3, and anndata>=0.12,<0.13. The stores use Zarr format 3: an older Zarr 2 environment can report PathNotFoundError even when the URL is valid.

docs.title: The recipe: cluster with Scanpy¶
docs.text:
The standard Scanpy workflow on the 10x PBMC 3k dataset. The raw counts are kept in a layer: Landscape shows them, the same values DegaFiles store.

from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import scanpy as sc
import zarr

data_dir = Path("data/pbmc3k")
sc.settings.datasetdir = data_dir
adata = sc.datasets.pbmc3k()
adata.var_names_make_unique()

sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_genes=200)
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=3)
adata.var["mt"] = adata.var_names.str.startswith("MT-")
sc.pp.calculate_qc_metrics(adata, qc_vars=["mt"], percent_top=None, log1p=False, inplace=True)
adata = adata[(adata.obs["n_genes_by_counts"] < 2500) & (adata.obs["pct_counts_mt"] < 5)].copy()

adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata, target_sum=1e4)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.highly_variable_genes(adata, n_top_genes=2000)
sc.tl.pca(adata, mask_var="highly_variable", random_state=0)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata, n_neighbors=10, n_pcs=40, random_state=0)
sc.tl.umap(adata, random_state=0)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, flavor="igraph", directed=False, n_iterations=2, resolution=0.9, random_state=0)
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="leiden", method="wilcoxon", use_raw=False)
# Stores the cluster colors in adata.uns["leiden_colors"].
sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden", legend_loc="on data")

docs.title: The recipe: save the AnnData to Zarr for Landscape¶
docs.text:
Landscape reads one gene at a time from a column-compressed (CSC) copy of the counts: each gene's values are contiguous, so the browser fetches only that gene. The per-gene mean and max, used to rank the gene bars and scale cell colors, go in var. Consolidated metadata lets the browser open the store in one request.

adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.var["mean"] = np.asarray(adata.layers["counts_csc"].mean(axis=0)).ravel()
adata.var["max"] = adata.layers["counts_csc"].max(axis=0).toarray().ravel()

# Write every chunk, even all-zero ones: Hugging Face answers 403 rather than
# 404 for a missing file.
with zarr.config.set({"array.write_empty_chunks": True}):
    adata.write_zarr(data_dir / "pbmc3k.zarr")
zarr.consolidate_metadata(data_dir / "pbmc3k.zarr")

docs.title: The recipe: cluster the markers with Matrix¶
docs.text:
Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden") aggregates the cells of every gene into a dot plot (mean expression as color, the fraction of expressing cells as size) and reuses the rank_genes_groups markers. cluster(view="rank_genes_groups") adds a slider for the top markers per cluster, with the full transcriptome as its "all" stop. write_zarr saves the clustered result.

import celldega as dega

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden", col_attr=["leiden"], name="pbmc3k_leiden")
mat.norm("row", by="zscore")
mat.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 3, 5, 10, 25, 50, 75, 100, 200])
mat.write_zarr(data_dir / "pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr")

Both stores were then uploaded to a Hugging Face dataset:

hf upload broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data data/pbmc3k/pbmc3k.zarr pbmc3k/pbmc3k.zarr --repo-type dataset
hf upload broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data data/pbmc3k/pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr pbmc3k/pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr --repo-type dataset

docs.title: Out of the oven: explore from Hugging Face¶
docs.text:
zarr_url points the Landscape at the AnnData Zarr store. Python only passes the URL along: the browser reads the store's metadata, clusters, colors, and UMAP, and then fetches each gene's values when you select it, the same way it reads DegaFiles. So the Landscape also works in a saved, kernel-free notebook. Matrix.read_zarr loads the clustered markers without re-clustering.

Click a cluster or a gene to color the UMAP. To plot two genes against each other, select them (shift-click the gene bars) and click XY, or click XY and type them in the autocompleting X and Y inputs. Select Clustergram rows to run Enrich, and click a gene in Enrich to color the cells by it.

docs.title: Single-cell Clustergram¶
docs.text:
The Clustergram above summarizes each cluster as one column. To see how the markers vary from cell to cell, load the AnnData itself (about 25 MB from Hugging Face) and build a Matrix with genes as rows and individual cells as columns, colored by their Leiden cluster. The values are the log-normalized expression in adata.X, z-scored across cells for each gene. col_entity="cell" marks the columns as individual cells, so Clustergram selections highlight those cells in a linked Landscape.

The AnnData carries Scanpy's rank_genes_groups results, so cluster(view="rank_genes_groups") adds the same RANK slider for the top markers per cluster. The rows are each cluster's top 50 markers, the slider's "all" stop, which keeps the matrix small enough to cluster and display.

docs.title: Selected cells¶
docs.text:
With a running kernel, get_selected_cells() returns the IDs of the selected cells: a cluster, a Clustergram dendrogram selection, or the cells inside a drawn gate. Pass the AnnData loaded above to subset it to those cells:

selected = landscape.get_selected_cells(adata)

docs.title: Tabula Sapiens: the CELLxGENE Atlas UMAP and Cell-Type Signatures¶
docs.text:
CELLxGENE Discover's homepage sends you to Tabula Sapiens - All Cells in its Explorer: 1,136,218 cells from 28 organs of 24 donors, on the authors' UMAP. This notebook shows the same view in Celldega, the UMAP colored by cell type with the Explorer's colors, and adds what the Explorer lacks:

  1. The atlas UMAP, whose cell-type and gene bars follow the viewport as you zoom in.
  2. Cell-type signatures: the 180 cell types' expression in a Clustergram, linked to the UMAP and to Enrich, with a slider for the number of markers per cell type.
  3. Plasma-cell sub-clusters: the 27,349 plasma cells re-clustered on their own, in the same linked layout.

The stores were prepared once, by the pre-process notebook, which streams CELLxGENE's 45 GB h5ad. This notebook reads them from the Celldega Supporting Data on Hugging Face: the Landscapes fetch cells and genes in the browser, one gene at a time, so the 15 GB atlas store is never downloaded whole.

This notebook needs Celldega 0.28.0a2 or later (pip install --pre celldega until 0.28.0 is released), zarr>=3, and anndata>=0.12,<0.13.

Data and attribution. Tabula Sapiens - All Cells (Tabula Sapiens 2.0; dataset version 1c88f927-bcbb-4bb1-9881-281842945a2d), curated and distributed by CZ CELLxGENE Discover in the Tabula Sapiens collection under CC BY 4.0.

  • The Tabula Sapiens Consortium. Tabula Sapiens reveals transcription factor expression, senescence effects, and sex-specific features in cell types from 28 human organs and tissues. bioRxiv (2024). doi:10.1101/2024.12.03.626516 (the citation the Tabula Sapiens data release policy asks for with the 2.0 data; apparently published as Cell 189, 7212–7227 (2026), doi:10.1016/j.cell.2026.08.010).
  • The Tabula Sapiens Consortium. The Tabula Sapiens: A multiple-organ, single-cell transcriptomic atlas of humans. Science 376, eabl4896 (2022). doi:10.1126/science.abl4896

The stores are derived from that data: the expression is normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and log1p-transformed, and the cell-type signatures, marker ranks, and plasma-cell sub-clusters are our analyses, not the Tabula Sapiens Consortium's. The Hugging Face folder's README lists every change and includes the license and the full text of the Tabula Sapiens data release policy, which applies to any redistribution.

docs.title: 1. The atlas, as CELLxGENE shows it¶
docs.text:
The authors' X_umap, colored by cell_type. CELLxGENE Explorer has no author palette for cell types, so it spreads d3's rainbow over them in their stored order; the store holds the same colors. The UMAP's second coordinate increases upward, as in CELLxGENE and Scanpy. Landscape loads the cells, cell types, and UMAP when it opens, then fetches a gene's expression when you pick one in the gene bar. Expression is normalized to 10,000 counts per cell and log1p-transformed, as the Explorer shows it: Tabula Sapiens mixes 10x UMI counts with Smart-seq2 read counts, which are not comparable unnormalized.

Zoom in and the bars follow the viewport, as they do in a spatial dataset:

  • The cell-type bars count the cells in view, and points grow as you zoom.
  • The gene bars estimate expression in view by weighting each cell type's mean expression (gene_signature_url) by its cells in view; TRX turns purple to mark the estimate. It is blue when every cell is in view and the bars show the whole dataset.
  • In the current 0.28.0 development build, TRX is an indicator in UMAP/XY; clicking it leaves the estimate unchanged. The saved preview below uses an earlier prerelease and may still offer the former exact-expression action.

To color by organ or compartment instead, pass cluster_attr="tissue_in_publication" or "compartment": the store holds the authors' palettes for both, as the Explorer uses them.

docs.title: 2. Cell-type signatures, linked to the UMAP and Enrich¶
docs.text:
Each Clustergram column is a cell type and each row a gene: dot color is the gene's Z-scored mean log-normalized expression, dot size the fraction of the cell type's cells expressing it. The column bars show each cell type's color, its majority compartment, and its number of cells (n_cells): double-click an attribute's label to order the columns by it, e.g. by cell count.

The RANK slider sets how many top markers per cell type are shown, from 1 to 50 (at most 9,000 genes for 180 cell types) or all, each cell type's top 100 together. Markers are ranked by Welch's t-test, the t-test method of Scanpy's rank_genes_groups: each cell type against all other cells, computed exactly on all 1.1M cells.

A second Landscape of the same store sits next to the Clustergram, so each view has its own UMAP.

docs.title: 3. Plasma-cell sub-clusters¶
docs.text:
The 27,349 plasma cells, re-clustered on their own: a new UMAP and Leiden sub-clusters from the authors' batch-corrected scVI embedding, so cells group by biology rather than by donor or assay. Each Clustergram column is a sub-cluster, with its majority organ and cell count; markers are Scanpy's Wilcoxon test of each sub-cluster against the other plasma cells.

Things to look for: antibody isotype (IGHA1/IGHA2 with JCHAIN in the gut against IGHG1–IGHG4 in lymph node and spleen), proliferating plasmablasts (MKI67), and sub-clusters marked by stress (FOS, JUN) or mitochondrial genes, which are likely technical rather than new cell states.

Here the viewport signatures are computed on the fly: load the plasma cells' expression (about 400 MB), average it per sub-cluster with Scanpy, and pass the result as adata_sig, sent with the widget like adata.

docs.title: Selected cells¶
docs.text:
With a running kernel, get_selected_cells() returns the cell IDs of the selected cell type, Clustergram selection, or drawn gate. The atlas store's expression is 15 GB, so read only its obs table (about 1.1M rows) to look the cells up. The plasma-cell view uses the same cell IDs, so plasma_landscape.get_selected_cells() works too:

import zarr

obs = ad.io.read_elem(zarr.open_group(zarr_url, mode="r")["obs"])
selected = landscape_linked.get_selected_cells()
obs.loc[selected, CELL_ATTR].value_counts().head(10)

docs.title: Visium HD human colorectal cancer Landscape + Clustergram + Enrich¶
docs.text:
This tutorial explores a Visium HD human colorectal cancer (CRC) sample that was already segmented into cells and clustered with Scanpy (220,703 cells, 15 Leiden clusters). It shows the handoff from Scanpy to Celldega:

  1. view the clustered cells in their tissue context with a Landscape,
  2. summarize clusters in a plain AnnData: pseudobulk expression, the fraction of cells expressing each gene, and marker genes ranked per cluster,
  3. explore the result in a Clustergram linked to the Landscape and to Enrich (Enrichr gene-set enrichment),
  4. annotate clusters and genes interactively, and
  5. sub-cluster the Goblet cells and color the sub-clusters by their depth along the colonic crypts.

Watch on YouTube

Data source: broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data. Files are downloaded once through direct Hugging Face /resolve/main/ URLs, so huggingface_hub is not a notebook dependency.

docs.title: Data¶
docs.text:
Two files are used, each downloaded on first run and reused afterwards:

  • crc_cluster.h5ad (~1.6 GB): the Scanpy analysis, with log-normalized expression in X, Leiden clusters in obs["leiden"], and a UMAP.
  • crc_raw_feature_cell_matrix.h5 (~280 MB): Space Ranger's cell-segmented count matrix for the same sample, which supplies the raw counts the analysis file does not keep.

docs.title: Wide Landscape overview¶
docs.text: The Landscape loads pre-tiled image and segmentation data (LandscapeFiles) from base_url and takes cell metadata, including the Leiden clusters, from adata. This full-width overview is a separate widget from the linked views below, so their selections leave it unchanged.

docs.title: Look up cells with Yearbook¶
docs.text: Yearbook shows a grid of portraits centered on individual cells, using the same Leiden clusters as the Landscape above. Query by cluster, gene, or both: a cluster query samples its cells, and adding a gene ranks them by expression, highest first. This example starts with cluster 4 (Goblet cells) ranked by MUC2. Change the cluster or gene in the Yearbook controls to look up other cells.

docs.title: Landscape¶
docs.text: A second Landscape, linked below to the Clustergram and Enrich, with the full adata (including its UMAP).

docs.title: AnnData cluster signatures and marker genes¶
docs.text: Aggregate raw counts with sc.get.aggregate. The resulting AnnData holds log1p-CPM pseudobulk expression in X, detection fractions in layers["fraction_expressing"], and the shared cluster palette in obs["color"]. Run sc.tl.rank_genes_groups on cell-level log-normalized adata.X and copy its results into signatures.uns["rank_genes_groups"]. Each gene's best-scoring cluster colors its row.

docs.title: Clustergram¶
docs.text: The Matrix colors columns by cluster (col_attr=["leiden"]) and rows by each gene's best-scoring cluster (row_attr=["leiden_marker"]), using the same palette as the Landscape. All genes are hierarchically clustered; the marker-ranked views add DIM slider levels with each cluster's top 1, 2, 3, ... markers, each re-biclustered ahead of time. rank_dim=3 opens on the top 3 markers per cluster.

docs.title: Linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich¶
docs.text:
• Click a column (cluster) label to highlight that cluster in the Landscape and send its top marker genes to Enrich.
  • Click a gene (row) label to show that gene's expression in the Landscape.
  • Select a dendrogram cluster of genes to run enrichment on that gene set.
  • Drag the DIM slider to move between marker-ranked views and all genes.
  • Use the ROW / COL dropdowns in the control panel to switch which category the bar plots summarize, and hover a category to locate it in the matrix.
  • Annotate: select columns or rows (e.g. from a dendrogram) and assign a cell_type or info category. Annotations are colored in the matrix and summarized in the category bars.

docs.title: Sub-clustering Goblet cells along the crypt axis¶
docs.text:
Leiden cluster 4 (Goblet / mucin-secreting epithelial cells, 15,613 cells) lines the colonic crypts. Re-clustering these cells reveals epithelial states that may vary along the crypt axis. The ordering below is a working interpretation to check against tissue position and the full expression signatures.

The sub-clusters were calculated from cluster 4's raw counts:

goblet = sc.AnnData(adata[adata.obs["leiden"] == "4"].layers["counts"].copy())
sc.pp.normalize_total(goblet)
sc.pp.log1p(goblet)
sc.tl.pca(goblet)
sc.pp.neighbors(goblet, n_neighbors=30, metric="correlation")
sc.tl.leiden(goblet, flavor="igraph", resolution=1.0, random_state=0)
sc.tl.umap(goblet, min_dist=0.5, spread=2, random_state=0)
# Sub-clusters are then relabeled 0, 1, 2, ... from largest to smallest.

Here the precomputed result is downloaded instead. It has the same cell barcodes as adata, log-normalized expression in X, sub-clusters in obs["leiden"], and a sub-cluster UMAP.

Sub-clusters 3 and 6 remain excluded from this working selection. They retain Goblet-marker expression, so this exclusion needs review and is not a validated cell-type annotation. The remaining nine sub-clusters keep their original Leiden labels and UMAP coordinates.

docs.title: A speculative crypt orientation¶
docs.text: The sub-clusters are given a working order from the crypt base to the surface (CRYPT_ORDER below). This orientation is speculative: check it against tissue position and the full signatures in the Clustergram. crypt_depth is an ordinal label (9 at the proposed base to 1 at the surface), not a measured distance, and the colors are a display gradient. Sub-clusters 7 and 9 occupy separate crypts, so their positions on the axis are uncertain.

docs.title: Sub-cluster signatures and marker genes¶
docs.text:
The sub-clusters are summarized in an AnnData, the same way as the clusters above. Raw counts come from the main adata, which has the same cells and genes. This Clustergram retains the full gene space: use its DIM slider (0 = all genes) to explore it.

Each sub-cluster's crypt_depth is added as a numeric column attribute. Double-click its label in the Clustergram to order the sub-clusters from the crypt base (left) to the surface (right).

Genes get the same attribute: after the marker ranking, each gene takes the depth of its best-scoring sub-cluster (var["leiden_marker"]). Double-click the row attribute label to order marker genes from the crypt base (top) to the surface (bottom). Genes without a marker score have depth 0.

docs.title: Goblet sub-clusters in the tissue¶
docs.text: Only the retained cells are colored in this Landscape. Under the proposed orientation, purple indicates the crypt base and yellow the surface; the green crypts in the upper region are sub-clusters 7 and 9. Click a sub-cluster column in the Clustergram to highlight its cells in the tissue and send its top marker genes to Enrich. In the Landscape, switch to the UMAP view to see the sub-cluster embedding.

docs.title: Broad-Allen Developing Mouse Brain E15.5: 3D
docs.text:
Data source: Compact DegaFiles (Parquet) AnnData Zarr

Loading 3.8 million cells…

  • Dataset: 3.8 million cells from 43 coronal Xenium sections of a whole E15.5 mouse embryo brain, measured with a 480-gene panel.
  • Alignment: sections are aligned first by Leiden cluster centroids, then by neighborhood overlap. Colors show Leiden clusters.
  • Controls: drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. Select a cluster or gene to explore its distribution; see the CellCloud guide.
  • Data: generated in collaboration with the Allen Institute. Choose the AnnData Zarr on Hugging Face or compact DegaFiles on GitHub. The original DegaFiles remain available.
  • Prepare the stack: follow the preprocessing and alignment notebook.
  • Explore linked views: the visualization notebook introduces slice composition and links CellCloud to a Clustergram.

docs.title: Use DegaFiles or AnnData Zarr
docs.text:
Both hosted sources show the same cells, clusters, and alignments. This gallery defaults to compact Parquet DegaFiles; the visualization notebook uses AnnData Zarr. Use the source picker above to compare them. In Python, change only the source argument.

For this unreleased checkout, run npm run build and start the notebook kernel with CELLDEGA_LOCAL_ESM=1 before importing Celldega. This uses the new browser reader instead of an older published bundle.

import celldega as dega

options = dict(alignment="neighborhood", cluster_attr="leiden_1.0",
               rotation_x=20, rotation_orbit=-25, ini_zoom=-3.6, height=700)

from_zarr = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    zarr_url=(
        "https://huggingface.co/datasets/broadinstitute/Celldega_Supporting_Data/"
        "resolve/main/Allen-Broad_Dev-Mouse-Brain/E15.5/cellcloud_v2_1um.zarr"
    ),
    **options,
)

from_degafiles = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    base_url=(
        "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/cornhundred/celldega_xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud/"
        "8d3cd06fc1a478f386826c27ba0e900b40703a3a/xenium_E15.5_cell_cloud_compact"
    ),
    **options,
)

from_degafiles  # display this widget, or from_zarr

The compact DegaFiles are currently served from a fork while upstream PR #1 awaits merge. Both sources support cluster colors, gene-expression coloring, named alignments, and a linked Clustergram. See File Formats for their storage layout.

docs.title: Measured loading performance
docs.text:
Compact Parquet was slightly faster in our hosted comparison, so it is the gallery default. These are medians from three loads and first Dcx selections per source, using the same browser renderer and bypassing browser HTTP caching:

Source Initial load First Dcx coloring Initial transfer / requests Compact Parquet on GitHub 3.6 s 0.67 s 31.3 MB / 7 AnnData Zarr on Hugging Face 4.4 s 1.08 s 25.7 MB / 39

Parquet uses fewer requests, which can reduce time spent waiting on the network. Zarr transfers fewer bytes for the initial view. For Dcx, Parquet transfers 3.34 MB in one request, versus 3.43 MB across 28 requests for Zarr. We expect slightly faster loading with compact Parquet for this hosted example; network conditions and CDN caching can change the result. Timings include transfer, decoding, and rendering updates, and exclude the JavaScript bundle startup.

The complete exports are 494 MB for compact Parquet and 583 MB for Zarr, versus 4.59 GB for the original DegaFiles (9.3× and 7.9× smaller, respectively). Both use positions rounded to 1 µm and preserve original cell IDs and gene counts.

docs.title: Prepare your own copy
docs.text:
The preparation script builds new exports of these same cells and alignments, rounding positions to the nearest 1 µm and using numeric row indices for repeated cell references. Original cell IDs, gene counts, cluster labels, and colors are retained. It writes a new local directory and does not upload or change the hosted data:

python scripts/prepare_allen_mouse_brain_cellcloud.py --download

Run this from the checkout to produce the new local exports. Existing hosted files are not modified. The complete output directories can also be served from another static host.

Getting Started
docs.text: Celldega is a spatial and single-cell analysis and visualization library developed by the Spatial Technology Platform at the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. Use its linked views to explore spatial tissue data, single-cell UMAP/XY landscapes, expression patterns, and gene-set enrichment.

docs.title: Video Tutorial
docs.text: This narrated tutorial links a Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich to analyze a Visium HD human colorectal cancer dataset. Follow along in the Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich notebook.

docs.title: Visualization and supporting analysis
docs.text:
Celldega has two parts that work together:

  1. Interactive visualizations for human-in-the-loop analysis. Explore tissue, cells, and gene expression; select, draw, and annotate what you find; and bring those selections back into your analysis. See Visualizations.
  2. A Python back-end that performs the analysis behind the visualizations:
    • hierarchical bi-clustering of genes and cell groups for Clustergrams (clust);
    • creating tissue neighborhoods and calculating their attributes, such as cell-type composition and gene expression (nbhd);
    • Collections: data structures for higher-level biological entities, such as neighborhoods, samples, and sets of cells, that keep several feature spaces together (collection, dataset, set);
    • choosing and ranking cells to review in Yearbook (select);
    • fast alignment of serial sections into 3D for CellCloud and NeighborhoodCloud (align);
    • preparing instrument output as DegaFiles for the browser (pre).

The Python API overview shows how the modules feed the visualizations.

docs.title: What you can explore
docs.text:
Celldega provides:

  • Landscape: Explore tissue images, cells, transcripts, and neighborhoods, or switch to UMAP and gene-expression XY views
  • Matrix/Clustergram Visualization: View hierarchical clustering heatmaps linked to spatial data
  • Yearbook View: Visualize individual cells as "portraits" in a grid layout
  • CellCloud: Explore cells in 3D, from thick tissue or aligned serial sections
  • Neighborhood Analysis: Define and analyze tissue neighborhoods with alpha shapes and hextiles
  • Multi-dataset Support: Compare multiple datasets side-by-side

docs.title: Interacting with the Visualizations
docs.text:
Every Celldega visualization is interactive: scroll to zoom, drag to pan, hover for details, and click to select clusters, genes, or regions. Selections can also update other views. For example, clicking a gene in a Clustergram colors the cells that express it in a linked Landscape.

The Visualizations overview introduces the control panel that most visualizations share, and the two ways to use them: as notebook widgets with a Python back-end, or as JavaScript on a web page. Each visualization's page then describes its interactions in detail. The Celldega logo in every control panel opens that page: Landscape · Yearbook · CellCloud · NeighborhoodCloud · Clustergram · Composition · Enrich.

docs.title: Performance
docs.text: Celldega provides responsive exploration of spatial transcriptomics datasets with over 1 billion transcripts. Landscape loads data in spatial tiles: as you zoom in, it fetches and draws every transcript in view, so you can move from a whole tissue section to individual transcripts without waiting for the full dataset to load. The Celldega preprint benchmarks loading, transcript display, and interactive exploration on datasets of 10 million to 1 billion transcripts; Celldega displayed transcripts without delay and completed the exploration task at every size. See Technologies for the visualization approach.

docs.title: DegaFiles and AnnData Zarr
docs.text:
DegaFiles prepare spatial datasets for browser visualization, with image pyramids, cell metadata and boundaries, transcripts, expression, and cluster assignments. Landscape loads the tiles needed for the current view.

AnnData Zarr stores analysis inputs and complete clustered Matrix objects. A single-cell Landscape can also read cell metadata, UMAP coordinates, and per-gene expression directly from an AnnData Zarr store.

See File Formats for layouts, row-group storage within DegaFiles, and Matrix persistence before and after clustering.

docs.title: Visualizations
docs.text:
Each visualization is a notebook widget in dega.viz. Landscape and Clustergram also have JavaScript entry points for web pages.

Visualization What you explore Landscape Tissue images, cells, transcripts, and neighborhoods, or UMAP and gene-expression XY views Yearbook A grid of individual cell portraits CellCloud Cells in 3D, from thick tissue or aligned serial sections NeighborhoodCloud Tissue neighborhoods across slices in 3D Clustergram Hierarchically clustered heatmaps and dot plots Composition Cell-type proportions across groups Enrich Gene-set enrichment through Enrichr

See Visualizations for all views and how to use them together.

docs.title: Supported Technologies
docs.text:
Celldega works with spatial and single-cell data:

  • Spatial transcriptomics: Xenium, including Atera (10x Genomics); MERSCOPE (Vizgen); Visium HD (10x Genomics); and CosMx (NanoString). 3D data, such as aligned serial sections and thick-tissue MERFISH, display as point clouds.
  • Single-cell: any AnnData, such as 10x Chromium RNA-seq (PBMC 3k tutorial), a cell atlas (Tabula Sapiens), or RNA and surface protein measured in the same cells with CITE-seq (PBMC cell types).

docs.title: 1. Install Celldega
docs.text: pip install celldega

docs.title: 2. Explore a public Xenium dataset
docs.text:
Open a prepared Xenium human pancreas dataset, hosted as DegaFiles on GitHub, and link it to a Clustergram of each default cluster's mean gene expression:

import ipywidgets as widgets
import pandas as pd
import celldega as dega

base_url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/broadinstitute/celldega_Xenium_human_Pancreas_FFPE/"
    "main/Landscape_Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs_webp"
)

# Tissue image, cells, and transcripts, with neighborhood drawing turned on.
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(base_url=base_url, height=600, nbhd_edit=True)

# Genes by default clusters (mean counts per cell), from the same DegaFiles.
df_sig = pd.read_parquet(f"{base_url}/df_sig.parquet")
mat = dega.clust.Matrix(df_sig)
mat.norm(axis="col", by="total")
mat.norm(axis="row", by="zscore")
mat.cluster()
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat, width=500, height=500)

# Clicking a gene or cluster in the Clustergram updates the Landscape.
widgets.jslink((cgm, "click_info"), (landscape, "update_trigger"))
widgets.HBox([landscape, cgm])

Click NBHD, then SKTCH (or press S over the tissue), and drag to outline a region. The drawn neighborhood and its cells are then available in Python:

landscape.nbhd  # a GeoDataFrame of drawn neighborhoods

In Jupyter, dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm) builds the same linked layout; the explicit jslink above also works in Google Colab.

docs.title: 3. Pre-process Your Own Data
docs.text:
For Xenium data (see Visualize Your Own Data for a complete walkthrough):

import celldega as dega

# Pre-process the Xenium sample directory into DegaFiles
dega.pre.main(
    sample="xenium_outs",
    data_root_dir="/path/to",
    path_dega_files="/path/to/output",
    tile_size=250
)

docs.title: 4. Integrate with AnnData
docs.text:
Use an analyzed AnnData to supply cell annotations, cluster colors, and UMAP coordinates:

import anndata as ad
import celldega as dega

adata = ad.read_h5ad("your_analyzed_data.h5ad")

# Cell IDs in adata.obs_names must match the DegaFiles cell IDs.
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url="https://your-landscape-files-url",
    adata=adata,
    ini_x=10000,
    ini_y=10000,
    ini_zoom=-5
)
landscape

For a single-cell Landscape, use a cell-level AnnData Zarr with a CSC expression layer instead of base_url:

adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.write_zarr("cells.zarr")

single_cell = dega.viz.Landscape(
    zarr_url="cells.zarr",
    zarr_layer="counts_csc",
    cluster_attr="leiden",
)

This example assumes sparse counts in adata.layers["counts"]. See the Landscape guide for preparation, viewport summaries, and neighborhood selection.

docs.title: 5. Create a Clustergram
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

# Create a Matrix from AnnData
mat = dega.clust.Matrix(adata)
mat.cluster()

# Visualize as a Clustergram
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat, width=800, height=600)
cgm

Save a complete clustered Matrix with mat.write_zarr("matrix.zarr") and restore it with dega.clust.Matrix.read_zarr("matrix.zarr"). See the Matrix API for details.

docs.text:
1. Open Celldega-App and choose Atera Kidney to explore cells in tissue.
  2. Choose Tabula Sapiens for the atlas UMAP, or its linked example for the UMAP and cell-type marker Clustergram together.
  3. Search for a gene or select a cell-type column to explore the relationship between the cells and expression patterns.

These examples stream prepared data from GitHub or Hugging Face. The first load may take a moment while metadata and visualization data arrive.

The start screen provides public examples, Open Dataset…, Open Clustergram…, and Make DegaFiles….

docs.title: Open your own dataset
docs.text:
Choose Open Dataset… and select a local DegaFiles directory or enter its remote HTTP(S) URL. The directory should contain landscape_parameters.json; see DegaFiles preparation and hosting. Optionally attach an analyzed AnnData .h5ad to use its cell annotations or generate a grouped-expression Clustergram.

Use Browse… for a local directory or AnnData file, or paste the prepared dataset's remote URL.

docs.title: Generate and save a Clustergram
docs.text:
With an AnnData attached, choose Clustergram… and select Linked in this window or Clustergram in a separate window. The app offers to provision its matching Python analysis runtime when needed. Use File → Analysis Runtime… to set it up or rebuild an older runtime. Make DegaFiles… also uses that runtime to prepare raw Xenium or MERSCOPE output.

Generated results appear under Saved Clustergrams and can be reopened after quitting without rerunning the analysis. Save Matrix… exports the complete Matrix Zarr folder, and Open Clustergram… opens a saved folder. The saved object retains matrix values, dot sizes, metadata, colors, dendrograms, and precomputed views; see Matrix storage. Browser zoom, crops, and unsaved manual edits are not a saved session snapshot.

The app covers 2D spatial and UMAP/XY Landscapes, Clustergrams, and Yearbooks. For 3D spatial views, use the notebook CellCloud or NeighborhoodCloud guides.

docs.title: Screenshot and data sources
docs.text:
These original app screenshots were captured on macOS on November 3, 2026, using app 0.7.1 and Celldega.js 0.28.0-alpha.4. The Development badge identifies the clean source profile used for the captures. The image links are pinned to that revision; capture metadata records their versions and dimensions.

Tabula Sapiens data are from the Tabula Sapiens Consortium, distributed via CZ CELLxGENE Discover under CC BY 4.0. See the Tabula Sapiens gallery for the dataset version, processing notes, and publication citation.

docs.title: Celldega File Formats
docs.text:
Celldega uses two complementary storage approaches: DegaFiles prepare spatial data for interactive rendering, and AnnData Zarr stores analysis inputs and visualization data. CellCloud can read either format; AnnData Zarr also supports single-cell Landscape data and complete clustered Matrix objects. Both can be served over HTTP from a local server or cloud storage.

Format Contents Used by Landscape DegaFiles Image pyramids, cell centroids, tiled boundaries/transcripts, per-gene expression, and a manifest Landscape and Yearbook Point-cloud DegaFiles XYZ cell positions, categories, per-gene expression, and a manifest CellCloud Cell-level AnnData Zarr Cell metadata, optional UMAP or XYZ positions, and a CSC expression matrix Single-cell Landscape, CellCloud, and Python analysis Analysis AnnData Zarr Values, observation/variable metadata, and any layers or analysis annotations saved on the AnnData Python inputs to Matrix Clustered Matrix AnnData Zarr Values plus clustering, precomputed views, colors, metadata, and optional sizes Python Matrix/Clustergram and browser Clustergram Cell-type signature AnnData Zarr A small dense cell-type-by-gene matrix with units and grouping metadata UMAP/XY viewport expression estimates

See the Landscape guide for spatial and low dimensional embedding landscapes (UMAP/XY), and the Matrix Python API for analysis and persistence. For an end-to-end preparation and sharing workflow, see generating DegaFiles and hosting prepared data.

docs.title: DegaFiles
docs.text: DegaFiles are a directory of visualization-specific files written by the pre module. They complement an analysis AnnData or SpatialData object: microscopy images, spatial geometry, and expression are arranged for the browser to request the parts needed for its current view.

docs.title: Landscape layout
docs.text:
A typical dataset using individual tile files has this layout. Available image channels and segmentation variants depend on the input technology.

DegaFiles/
├── landscape_parameters.json
├── cell_metadata.parquet
├── cell_clusters/
│   ├── cluster.parquet
│   └── meta_cluster.parquet
├── cbg/
│   └── <gene>.parquet
├── meta_gene.parquet
├── df_sig.parquet
├── cell_segmentation/
│   └── <tile>.parquet
├── transcript_tiles/
│   └── <tile>.parquet
├── pyramid_images/
│   ├── <channel>.dzi
│   └── <channel>_files/<zoom>/<tile>.webp
└── micron_to_image_transform.csv
File or directory Role in Landscape landscape_parameters.json Technology, tile size, image channels/format, segmentation variants, and optional row-group or aligned H&E configuration cell_metadata.parquet Cell identifiers and centroid geometry used to position the cell scatter cell_clusters/cluster.parquet Default cell-to-cluster assignments cell_clusters/meta_cluster.parquet Cluster colors and whole-dataset cell counts cbg/<gene>.parquet Nonzero expression values for one gene, used for cell coloring and XY axes meta_gene.parquet Gene statistics such as mean, standard deviation, maximum, detection proportion, and color df_sig.parquet Genes by default clusters: mean counts per cell, also used for UMAP/XY viewport estimates cell_segmentation/ Spatially tiled cell-boundary polygons transcript_tiles/ Spatially tiled transcript coordinates and gene identities pyramid_images/ Deep Zoom metadata and image tiles at multiple resolutions micron_to_image_transform.csv Affine mapping from physical tissue coordinates to reference-image pixels

Some datasets use compact integer cell/gene identifiers. Readers resolve them against the dataset's name ordering; use the preprocessing writers to keep identifiers consistent across centroids, expression, boundaries, and transcripts.

docs.title: How Landscape reads DegaFiles
docs.text:
1. The Python widget supplies base_url and display options. Optional adata supplies cell attributes, cluster colors, and obsm["X_umap"]; its obs_names must match the DegaFiles cell IDs.
  2. The browser reads the manifest, centroid and cluster data, and gene metadata to initialize the view.
  3. Panning and zooming request image tiles at the appropriate resolution. Transcript and cell-boundary tiles load automatically at close zoom, or on demand through TRX at intermediate zoom.
  4. Selecting a gene reads its expression data to color cells. XY uses the same reader to position cells by the expression of its two axis genes.
  5. UMAP/XY viewport bars count visible cell types. With matching signatures, gene bars estimate local mean expression from those counts; selected-gene coloring and XY axes use actual cell expression.
import celldega as dega

port = dega.viz.get_local_server(file_server_root="data")
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url=f"http://localhost:{port}/DegaFiles",
    adata=adata,
    cluster_attr="cell_type",
)

The browser reads the hosted files directly. A separate analysis service is not required to render prepared datasets. Cross-origin hosting must allow browser requests; efficient row-group reads also require HTTP byte ranges.

Source: Python preprocessing, widget metadata/URL handling, browser initialization, viewport loading, and gene-expression loading.

docs.title: Row Group Storage Mode (Optional)
docs.text:
Row-group storage is an optional DegaFiles layout. It packs many logical tiles or genes into fewer Parquet files while retaining partial reads in the browser. This reduces the number of files to host and distribute.

Enable it during preprocessing:

dega.pre.main(
    sample="Xenium_Sample",
    data_root_dir="data/xenium_data",
    path_dega_files="data/DegaFiles",
    tile_size=250,
    use_row_groups=True,
    max_row_groups_per_file=400,
)

The input dataset is data/xenium_data/Xenium_Sample. Large outputs are split into chunk files; max_row_groups_per_file controls the gene/vector chunks, while image packing has its own chunk size.

DegaFiles/
├── landscape_parameters.json
├── cell_metadata.parquet
├── cell_clusters/
├── meta_gene.parquet
├── df_sig.parquet
├── cbg/chunk_<n>.parquet
├── transcripts/chunk_<n>.parquet
├── cell_segmentation/chunk_<n>.parquet
└── pyramid_images/
    ├── <channel>.dzi
    └── <channel>/chunk_<n>.parquet
Data Logical row group Browser lookup Transcripts One spatial tile Visible tile coordinates Cell boundaries One spatial tile The same spatial tile grid Cell-by-gene expression One gene Gene-to-row-group metadata Image pyramid One image tile Channel, zoom level, and tile coordinates

The manifest's use_row_groups flag selects the readers. tile_grid records the grid dimensions, and row_group_files lists each data type's directory, chunk files, and row-group counts. Image entries also contain zoom information. Readers also support older layouts with a single Parquet file per data type.

For spatial vector tiles, the logical index is tile_x * num_tiles_y + tile_y. Empty tiles retain their grid positions, and chunk metadata maps the logical index to a file and local row group. Parquet footer metadata supplies the byte ranges for that group's data.

The browser uses HTTP Range requests to read the required groups. Hosting must support byte ranges and, for cross-origin access, CORS. The readers require range-capable hosting; there is no general whole-file fallback. Celldega's local file server, viz.get_local_server, supports byte ranges from version 0.28.1. Larger chunks reduce file counts but increase footer and memory costs. Individual-tile DegaFiles remain supported, with use_row_groups=False.

Source: preprocessing options, tile reader, gene reader, and image reader.

docs.title: Adding an aligned H&E background
docs.text:
pre.add_aligned_he() adds an RGB image pyramid and an aligned_he manifest entry to existing DegaFiles:

dega.pre.add_aligned_he(
    "data/DegaFiles",
    "sample_he.ome.tif",
    alignment="sample_he_imagealignment.csv",
)

The supplied 3×3 affine maps H&E pixels into reference-image pixels. If the image already shares the reference grid, omit alignment. Landscape and Yearbook then expose an FLR/H&E (fluorescence/H&E) selector using the same cell and transcript overlays. See Add aligned H&E to DegaFiles for requirements and the example workflow.

Source: H&E importer and background selector.

docs.title: AnnData Zarr for a single-cell Landscape
docs.text:
Landscape(zarr_url=...) reads a cell-level AnnData Zarr instead of DegaFiles. This path uses technology="Chromium" and supports UMAP and XY.

AnnData location Meaning obs_names / var_names Cell IDs / gene names obs[cluster_attr] Cell categories used for colors and composition bars Other requested obs columns Cell attributes selected through cell_attr uns[f"{cluster_attr}_colors"] Optional palette in category order obsm["X_umap"] Optional UMAP coordinates CSC X or a CSC layer Expression fetched one gene at a time var["mean"], var["max"], var["color"] Optional gene statistics and colors

For a sparse counts layer:

import zarr

adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.write_zarr("cells.zarr")
zarr.consolidate_metadata("cells.zarr")

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    zarr_url="cells.zarr",
    zarr_layer="counts_csc",
    cluster_attr="cell_type",
)

The browser uses Zarrita to read Zarr v2 or v3. It loads cell/gene metadata, UMAP positions, and the CSC column pointers, then slices data and indices for requested genes. It does not load the entire cell-by-gene expression matrix. Without var["mean"], the initial gene ranking uses detection fraction; without var["max"], the maximum is computed when a gene loads.

Choose the layer with zarr_layer. Otherwise, CSC X is preferred, then the only discoverable CSC layer. Consolidated metadata permits layer discovery; an explicit zarr_layer also works without consolidation. Dense and CSR expression matrices need a CSC copy for this Landscape reader.

Pass an HTTP(S) URL or a local store beneath the working directory; Python serves local paths over HTTP. Python does not open the expression matrix. If adata is also supplied, its metadata, colors, and UMAP take precedence. Pass one of base_url or zarr_url.

Cell-type signature stores are separate from this cell-level store. They contain dense, finite, nonnegative means and uns["viewport_signature"] grouping/units metadata. See viewport estimates for adata_sig and gene_signature_url, including exact counts versus estimated expression.

Source: AnnData Zarr reader, Landscape entry point, signature reader, and viewport summaries.

docs.title: AnnData Zarr for CellCloud
docs.text:
CellCloud(zarr_url=...) reads a self-contained cell-level AnnData Zarr store as an alternative to point-cloud DegaFiles. Both sources support 3D positions, cluster colors, on-demand gene-expression coloring, named alignments, and links to a Clustergram.

AnnData location Meaning in CellCloud obs_names / var_names Original cell IDs / gene names obs[cluster_attr] Categories used to color cells uns[f"{cluster_attr}_colors"] Palette in category order obsm["spatial"] Default cell positions, shape (n_cells, 3), in microns obsm["spatial_<alignment>"] Optional named XYZ alignment in the same cell order CSC X or a CSC layer Sparse expression indexed by zero-based observation position var["mean"], var["max"], var["color"] Gene statistics and colors uns["cell_cloud"] Export metadata: alignment names, coordinate units, and optional rounding resolution

pre.write_point_cloud_zarr prepares this layout from an AnnData. It writes CSC expression, consolidated Zarr v2 metadata, and compressed position arrays; its default 1 µm rounding uses int32 coordinates. Original cell IDs remain in obs_names, while numeric row positions index expression. The writer requires a new output path unless overwrite=True is explicitly selected.

dega.pre.write_point_cloud_zarr(
    adata,
    "data/cells.zarr",
    cluster_key="cell_type",
    coordinate_resolution=1.0,
)

cell_cloud = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    zarr_url="data/cells.zarr",
    cluster_attr="cell_type",
)

The browser loads cell IDs, category labels and colors, positions, and CSC column pointers to initialize the view. Selecting a gene fetches only the chunks covering its sparse values and row indices. It does not load the entire expression matrix. A named alignment="neighborhood" reads obsm["spatial_neighborhood"]; omit alignment to use obsm["spatial"]. Use zarr_layer when the expression is in a CSC layer rather than X.

Pass an HTTP(S) URL, or a local store beneath the working directory; Python serves local paths over HTTP. Pass one of base_url or zarr_url per widget. See the CellCloud guide and 3D mouse brain example for equivalent DegaFiles and Zarr usage.

Source: point-cloud exporters, CellCloud Python widget, AnnData Zarr reader, and cell initialization.

docs.title: AnnData Zarr before and after Matrix clustering
docs.text: Both stages use AnnData's observations-by-variables orientation. A Matrix displays the transpose: genes/features are rows, and cells/groups are columns.

docs.title: Before clustering: save the analysis input
docs.text:
Save the AnnData used to construct a Matrix, including the layers and annotations needed for the analysis:

import anndata as ad
import celldega as dega

adata.write_zarr("matrix_input.zarr")
loaded = ad.read_zarr("matrix_input.zarr")
mat = dega.clust.Matrix(loaded)
mat.cluster()

For an already prepared, unclustered Matrix, mat.to_adata().write_zarr("matrix_values.zarr") saves its current values and row/column metadata. Rebuild it with Matrix(ad.read_zarr(...)). to_adata() does not preserve the Matrix's size matrix, colors, axis-entity settings, marker rankings, or clustering/view state. Save the original AnnData when its layers and analysis annotations are needed.

docs.title: After clustering: save the complete Matrix (experimental)
docs.text:
Matrix.write_zarr() requires cluster() first and preserves:

  • Values and the optional dot-size matrix.
  • Row and column metadata.
  • Dendrogram orders and linkages.
  • Precomputed views.
  • Colors, visualization settings, axis entities, and marker rankings when present.
mat.cluster(view="var", levels=[100, 500])
mat.write_zarr("clustered_matrix.zarr")

restored = dega.clust.Matrix.read_zarr("clustered_matrix.zarr")
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=restored)

Choose view levels appropriate to the number of features. Reloading restores the saved values and clustering without reclustering or repeating normalization. Values are written as float32 by default; dtype=None retains their existing precision. zarr_format=3 is the default, with version 2 also supported. to_clustered_adata() and from_clustered_adata() provide the same conversion in memory.

AnnData location Saved Matrix content X Matrix values, transposed to observations × variables obs / var Column / row metadata layers["size"] Optional size values, with the same orientation as X obsm["celldega_nodes"] / varm["celldega_nodes"] Column / row node records, including orders and attributes uns["celldega"]["linkage"] Row and column dendrogram linkages uns["celldega"]["views"] Packed arrays for precomputed views uns["celldega"]["meta_json"] Versioned format metadata, view descriptions, colors, visualization settings, and axis entities uns["marker_ranks"] Optional marker rankings

This is a regular AnnData Zarr store with Celldega-specific annotations. anndata.read_zarr() opens it; Matrix.read_zarr() restores the complete clustered object and requires those annotations. An arbitrary AnnData store is loaded through Matrix(anndata.read_zarr(...)) instead.

The browser renders the same clustered store without Python:

const cgm = await celldega.clustergram(element, {
    url: "https://your-data-host/clustered_matrix.zarr",
});

matrix_from_zarr() is another rendering entry point; network_from_zarr() returns the visualization network. The Matrix readers load the saved matrix into memory. Per-gene fetching applies to the single-cell Landscape reader, rather than these Matrix readers. See the Clust API and JavaScript API for usage.

Source: Matrix conversion, writer, and reader, browser Matrix reader, and browser rendering APIs.

docs.title: Point-Cloud DegaFiles
docs.text:
Written by celldega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset and rendered by CellCloud. There is no image pyramid or transcript layer; cells are points with 3D positions.

point_cloud_files/
├── cell_metadata.parquet               # cell key + geometry ([x, y, z] fixed-size list)
├── cell_metadata_<name>.parquet        # optional named position variants
├── cell_ids.parquet                    # original IDs once, in the optional indexed layout
├── cell_clusters/
│   ├── cluster.parquet
│   └── meta_cluster.parquet
├── cbg/<gene>.parquet                  # expressing cells only, keyed by cell name or row index
├── meta_gene.parquet
├── cell_cloud.json                     # manifest
└── landscape_parameters.json           # same manifest, for older loaders

The manifest has "technology": "point-cloud" and an "alignments" list naming the position variants. CellCloud(alignment="<name>") reads positions from cell_metadata_<name>.parquet while clusters and genes keep loading from the shared files, so several 3D alignments of the same cells share one dataset. Variant names may contain only letters, digits, ., _, and -, and default is reserved.

The writer supports two cell-key layouts:

Layout Geometry and cluster keys Expression keys Original cell identity Name-based, the existing default (use_int_index=False) String IDs in name String IDs in __index_level_0__ Repeated in the data files Indexed (use_int_index=True) uint32 row positions in name uint32 row positions in __index_level_0__ Stored once in cell_ids.parquet, whose name column follows canonical row order

For an indexed dataset, the manifest records "use_int_index": true and "cell_ids": "cell_ids.parquet". Geometry rows follow the canonical 0..n_cells-1 order. Appending an alignment requires exactly the same original cell IDs; the writer reorders its positions to match before writing. The browser resolves original IDs for selections and tooltips while reading expression by numeric row index.

Use coordinate_resolution=1.0 with micron inputs to round XYZ to the nearest micron and store int32 coordinates. This changes each axis by at most 0.5 µm. The manifest records the resolution. With the default None, coordinates remain float32. compression="zstd", compression_level=6 provides a compact Parquet alternative to the default Snappy codec. These options reduce data transfer and decoding costs; the number of rendered cells is unchanged.

See the CellCloud preparation examples.

Source: point-cloud writer, indexed identity reader, and cell initialization.

docs.title: Neighborhood-Cloud DegaFiles
docs.text:
Written by celldega.pre.write_nbhd_cloud_dataset from a cell-level AnnData plus a GeoDataFrame of per-slice neighborhoods (e.g. celldega.nbhd.alpha_shape_cell_clusters_by_slice), and rendered by NeighborhoodCloud.

nbhd_cloud_files/
├── nbhd_cloud/
│   ├── meta_slice.parquet              # slice_id, z, centroid_x/y/z, cell_count
│   ├── meta_neighborhood.parquet       # neighborhood_id, cluster_id, slice_id, color, area, cell_count, inv_alpha
│   ├── shapes/by_slice/slice_<id>.parquet   # one row per neighborhood, geometry_geojson (XYZ)
│   └── cells/
│       ├── by_cluster/cluster_<id>.parquet  # cell_id, x, y, z, cluster_id, slice_id
│       └── by_gene/<gene>.parquet           # optional top-expressing cells per gene
├── cell_clusters/meta_cluster.parquet
├── meta_gene.parquet
├── neighborhood_cloud.json             # manifest
└── landscape_parameters.json           # same manifest, for older loaders

The neighborhood GeoDataFrame needs unique ids (name, or neighborhood_id / nbhd_id) and slice_id, cluster_id, color, and cell_count columns. Geometry is stored as a GeoJSON string column rather than GeoParquet so the browser can hand it straight to a deck.gl GeoJsonLayer. cells/by_gene/ is written by celldega.pre.write_gene_cell_scatter, with cells/by_gene/available_gene_scatter.json listing the genes it covers.

docs.title: From Scanpy & Squidpy
docs.text: If you already analyze single-cell or spatial data with Scanpy and Squidpy, Celldega picks up where your notebook leaves off. It reads the same AnnData: your clusters, colors, UMAP, and expression. You explore them interactively, then bring selections and annotations back into the AnnData for the next step of your analysis.

docs.title: What Celldega reads from your AnnData
docs.text: AnnData Used for obs_names Cell IDs. For spatial data they must match the DegaFiles' cell IDs. obs["leiden"], or any categorical column Cell colors and the CELL bars, chosen with cluster_attr uns["leiden_colors"] The cluster palette, as Scanpy stores it; a palette is generated if absent Other obs columns Extra cell attributes for tooltips and queries, chosen with cell_attr obsm["X_umap"] The UMAP view obsm["spatial"] Cell positions for neighborhood analysis and 3D CellClouds; a spatial Landscape takes positions from its DegaFiles X or a layer Expression for Clustergram summaries; a single-cell Landscape reads a CSC layer from AnnData Zarr var_names Gene names; human gene symbols also get UniProt descriptions

docs.title: Choose a route
docs.text:
Is your data spatial?
   │
   ├─ Yes, and you have the instrument output (Xenium, MERSCOPE, Visium HD)
   │     └─► make DegaFiles, then Landscape(base_url=..., adata=adata)
   │
   ├─ Yes, but you only have an AnnData with obsm["spatial"]
   │     └─► write a point cloud, then CellCloud(zarr_url=...)
   │
   └─ No: single-cell RNA-seq
         └─► save AnnData Zarr with a CSC layer, then Landscape(zarr_url=...)
  • Spatial, with instrument output. DegaFiles hold the images, cell boundaries, and transcripts that make a spatial Landscape, and your AnnData supplies the clusters, colors, and UMAP. Follow Visualize Your Own Data.

  • Spatial, AnnData only. Without the images and transcripts, a CellCloud shows the cells as points, colored by cluster or gene. 2D coordinates work as a flat section:

    dega.pre.write_point_cloud_zarr(adata, "cells.zarr", cluster_key="leiden")
dega.viz.CellCloud(zarr_url="cells.zarr", cluster_attr="leiden")

  • Single-cell. No preprocessing beyond a CSC copy of the expression. See Single-cell Landscapes:

    adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.write_zarr("cells.zarr")
dega.viz.Landscape(zarr_url="cells.zarr", zarr_layer="counts_csc", cluster_attr="leiden")

docs.title: Scanpy and Squidpy plots, interactively
docs.text:
In Scanpy or Squidpy In Celldega sc.pl.umap(adata, color="leiden") The Landscape's UMAP view, with clusters you can select sc.pl.umap(adata, color="CD3E") Gene search, or click a gene's bar; several genes are combined sq.pl.spatial_scatter(adata, color="leiden") The spatial Landscape: the same cells over the tissue image, down to transcripts sc.pl.rank_genes_groups_dotplot(adata) Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden") and a dot-plot Clustergram, with views at several numbers of markers sc.pl.matrixplot(adata, markers, groupby="leiden") A Clustergram heatmap: Clustergram(matrix=mat, viz_mode="heatmap") sc.tl.dendrogram(adata, groupby="leiden") Hierarchical clustering of both the groups and the genes sq.gr.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key="leiden") A Clustergram of the enrichment z-scores (below) Enrichment with gseapy or Enrichr Enrich, linked to Clustergram selections

For example, to explore Squidpy's neighborhood enrichment as a Clustergram:

import pandas as pd
import squidpy as sq
import celldega as dega

sq.gr.nhood_enrichment(adata, cluster_key="leiden")
clusters = adata.obs["leiden"].cat.categories
zscore = pd.DataFrame(
    adata.uns["leiden_nhood_enrichment"]["zscore"], index=clusters, columns=clusters
)

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(zscore)
mat.cluster()
dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat)

The Scanpy–Squidpy Xenium pancreas tutorial links this Clustergram to a Landscape.

docs.title: Bring results back into your AnnData
docs.text:
The widgets share their state with Python, so what you select and draw becomes part of your analysis:

# Cells in the selected clusters or a drawn neighborhood
adata.obs["selected"] = adata.obs_names.isin(landscape.selected_cells)
subset = landscape.get_selected_cells(adata)

# Drawn neighborhoods, as a GeoDataFrame
landscape.nbhd

# Cells checked for review in a Yearbook
adata.obs["reviewed"] = adata.obs_names.isin(yearbook.selected_cells)

# Genes selected in a Clustergram, and clusters labeled in its category editor
cgm.selected_genes
cgm.manual_cat

See each visualization's "Python-backed interactions" section, for example Landscape and Clustergram.

docs.title: Plain objects or Collections
docs.text:
Celldega's analysis functions work on the objects you already use: AnnData, pandas DataFrames, and GeoPandas GeoDataFrames. For example, summarize the cell types in drawn neighborhoods and cluster the neighborhoods by composition. Celldega is also developing Collection classes that keep related results together, such as a neighborhood's geometry, its composition, its expression, and which neighborhoods border each other. Both approaches give the same results; use whichever fits your analysis.

Plain objectsNeighborhoodCollection 
gdf_nbhd = landscape.nbhd  # a GeoDataFrame

composition = dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_pop(adata, gdf_nbhd, category="leiden")  # AnnData
expression = dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_gene(gdf_nbhd, by="cell", adata=adata)  # AnnData

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(composition)
mat.cluster()
dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat)

nc = dega.nbhd.NeighborhoodCollection(gdf=landscape.nbhd, nbhd_type="drawn")
nc.add_mod("population", dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_pop(adata, nc, category="leiden"))
nc.add_mod("gene", dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_gene(nc, by="cell", adata=adata))
nc.add_relation("bordering", dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_bordering(nc, metric="binary"))

nc.mdata  # a MuData: one observation per neighborhood, one modality per summary

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(nc.mod["population"])
mat.cluster()
dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat)

The pancreas islet gradients example uses both, and the collection API describes the storage model.

docs.title: Common pitfalls
docs.text:
• Cell IDs don't match. Spatial readers such as spatialdata_io.xenium() can leave obs_names as 0, 1, 2, .... Set adata.obs_names = adata.obs["cell_id"].astype(str) so that cells match the DegaFiles; unmatched cells are drawn in a fallback color.
  • Scaled expression in dot plots. After sc.pp.scale, values can be negative, so "fraction expressing" (values greater than zero) is no longer meaningful. Build Matrix(adata, groupby=...) from normalized, log-transformed expression, and z-score rows in the Matrix instead.
  • Dense or CSR expression in AnnData Zarr. A single-cell Landscape reads one gene at a time from a CSC matrix; save a CSC copy, such as adata.layers["counts_csc"].
  • Remote notebooks and localhost. A local file server runs where the kernel runs. On a remote kernel, use a URL your browser can reach, or host the data; see Usage.
  • Google Colab. Link widgets with ipywidgets.jslink and display them in an HBox, as in the Quick Start.

docs.title: Python
docs.text:
Celldega supports Python 3.11 and 3.12. Install it into the environment used by your Jupyter notebook:

pip install celldega

For Scanpy-backed marker dot plots and marker ranking:

pip install "celldega[scanpy]"

For image preprocessing, including adding an aligned H&E background:

pip install "celldega[pre]"

Image operations also require a working native libvips installation. See preprocessing and aligned H&E for the relevant workflows.

See Usage for notebook, web, and desktop options, then follow Getting Started or open an example notebook.

docs.title: JavaScript
docs.text:
For an application managed with npm:

npm install celldega

import celldega from "celldega";

A standalone web page can import the built module or load it from a CDN such as esm.sh. See the JavaScript quick start for landscape, clustergram, and linked views.

docs.title: Visualize Your Own Data
docs.text:
This guide follows a public 10x Genomics Xenium human pancreas dataset from the instrument's output to linked views of your own analysis: your clusters over the tissue and in a UMAP, a marker-gene dot plot, and gene-set enrichment. The same steps apply to your own Xenium data. Run the code in a Jupyter or marimo notebook.

 Xenium output bundle
   │
   ├─ 1. pre.main ──► DegaFiles ──────────────┐
   │                                          ▼
   └─ 2. Scanpy ────► AnnData ──────────► 3. Landscape: clusters, UMAP
                         │                    ▲
                         │                    │ 5. linked
                         └─► 4. Matrix ─► Clustergram ─► Enrich

Each step's output for this dataset is already hosted, so you can start at any step. To explore the prepared data before installing anything, try the Quick Start.

docs.title: 1. Prepare DegaFiles from the instrument output
docs.text:
DegaFiles arrange the images, cells, transcripts, and expression so that the browser can load only what is in view. Preprocessing needs the pre extra and a native libvips installation:

pip install "celldega[pre]"

Download the Xenium output bundle from the 10x Genomics dataset page (a 5.7 GB zip), and unpack it:

mkdir -p data/xenium && cd data/xenium
curl -LO https://cf.10xgenomics.com/samples/xenium/2.0.0/Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE/Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs.zip
unzip Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs.zip -d Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs

Then write the DegaFiles:

import celldega as dega

dega.pre.main(
    sample="Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs",
    data_root_dir="data/xenium",
    path_dega_files="data/DegaFiles/pancreas",
    tile_size=250,
    image_tile_layer="all",
)

pre.main handles Xenium (including Atera) and MERSCOPE bundles; see the Atera preprocessing example. To view the DegaFiles, serve their directory over HTTP and pass the URL to a Landscape:

port = dega.viz.get_local_server(file_server_root="data/DegaFiles/pancreas")
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(base_url=f"http://localhost:{port}")
landscape

To share them, upload the directory to GitHub, Hugging Face, or a cloud bucket; see Host and share prepared data. The rest of this guide uses the hosted DegaFiles for this dataset:

base_url = (
    "https://raw.githubusercontent.com/broadinstitute/celldega_Xenium_human_Pancreas_FFPE/"
    "main/Landscape_Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs_webp"
)

docs.title: 2. Analyze with Scanpy
docs.text:
Read the cell-by-gene counts from the same output bundle, then cluster as usual with Scanpy:

import scanpy as sc

outs = "data/xenium/Xenium_V1_human_Pancreas_FFPE_outs"
adata = sc.read_10x_h5(f"{outs}/cell_feature_matrix.h5")
adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy()

sc.pp.filter_cells(adata, min_counts=10)
sc.pp.filter_genes(adata, min_cells=5)
sc.pp.normalize_total(adata)
sc.pp.log1p(adata)
sc.pp.pca(adata)
sc.pp.neighbors(adata)
sc.tl.umap(adata)
sc.tl.leiden(adata, flavor="igraph", n_iterations=2, directed=False)

This takes about two minutes for the 122,678 cells that pass the filter. Celldega links your analysis to the DegaFiles by cell ID: read_10x_h5 names cells by their Xenium cell IDs (such as aaaadnje-1), the same IDs the DegaFiles use. If you read the data another way, such as with spatialdata-io, set adata.obs_names = adata.obs["cell_id"].astype(str) first.

docs.title: 3. See your clusters in the tissue
docs.text:
Pass the AnnData to the Landscape. Cells take your Leiden clusters and colors, and the UMAP becomes available with the UMAP button:

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(base_url=base_url, adata=adata, cluster_attr="leiden")
landscape

Select a cluster in the UMAP, then switch to SPATIAL to see where those cells are in the tissue; see Spaces and embeddings, which shows this dataset's islet cells moving between the two views.

docs.title: 4. Find marker genes with a dot-plot Clustergram
docs.text:
Rank each cluster's marker genes, then summarize the cells by cluster. In the dot plot, color is a gene's mean expression in a cluster, scaled across clusters, and dot size is the fraction of the cluster's cells that express it:

import celldega as dega

sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="leiden")

markers = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden")
markers.filter_by_size(0.05)  # genes detected in at least 5% of a cluster's cells
markers.norm("row", by="zscore")
markers.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 3, 5, 10])

cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=markers, rank_dim=3)
cgm

cluster(view=..., levels=...) precomputes views with 1, 3, 5, and 10 marker genes per cluster; the DIM slider moves between them, and rank_dim=3 opens at three markers per cluster. See Clustergram for every interaction.

docs.title: 5. Link the views and interpret with Enrich
docs.text:
Link the Landscape and Clustergram, and add Enrich to look up the selected genes in public gene-set libraries:

dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm, enrich=True)

Clicking the islet cluster's column (9 here) in the Clustergram.

What happened 1 Clicking the cluster's column label selected it. Its markers, INS, GCG, and SCGN, mark insulin- and glucagon-producing islet cells. 2 The Landscape shows only that cluster's cells: the islets, scattered through the pancreas. 3 Enrich received the cluster's top marker genes and ranks endocrine and beta cell gene sets first.

Clicking a gene's row label colors the cells by that gene, and a row dendrogram branch sends a group of genes to Enrich. Your Leiden numbers may differ from this example's. See Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich for more linked workflows.

docs.title: 6. Save and share
docs.text:
Save the clustered dot plot so that it reopens without recomputing, in Python or in a web page:

markers.write_zarr("pancreas_markers.zarr")
restored = dega.clust.Matrix.read_zarr("pancreas_markers.zarr")

A notebook saved with its widget state can be published as an interactive report, as the example notebooks on this site are; see two ways to use a visualization.

docs.title: Next steps
docs.text:
• From Scanpy & Squidpy: what Celldega reads from your AnnData, and how to bring selections and annotations back into it.
  • Visualizations: every interaction in Landscape, Clustergram, and the other views.
  • Neighborhoods: draw regions, such as islets, and summarize the cells inside them.
  • Scanpy–Squidpy Xenium pancreas tutorial: add Squidpy's spatial neighborhood enrichment.
  • Chromium PBMC tutorial: the same steps for single-cell data, which need no DegaFiles.

docs.title: Screenshot sources
docs.text: The screenshot shows the hosted pancreas DegaFiles with the hosted Scanpy AnnData for this dataset, captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py. The code on this page was run with Celldega 0.28.0 on the 10x output bundle. Data: 10x Genomics, FFPE Human Pancreas with Xenium Multimodal Cell Segmentation.

docs.title: Technologies
docs.text: Celldega utilizes a suite of complementary technologies to develop an efficient web-based analysis and visualization toolkit for spatial and single-cell data.

docs.title: Visualization Technologies
docs.text:
Spatial transcriptomics (ST) datasets can be very large and difficult for researchers to analyze and visualize collaboratively. Additionally, visualization that is linked to analysis is key to extracting biological insights. To address these issues, we built the Celldega viz module to help researchers interactively visualize large ST datasets within notebook-based workflows on the cloud (e.g., Terra.bio).

The Celldega Landscape visualization method (see Gallery) utilizes novel vector tiling approaches to enable interactive visualization of large ST datasets in a notebook environment or as a stand-alone webpage. This approach allows Celldega to visualize larger datasets than currently available open-source tools (e.g., datasets with hundreds of millions of transcripts). We also utilize modern web image data formats (WebP) to reduce the data storage burden for interactive visualization. The resulting DegaFiles data format serves as a compact and highly performant visualization-specific data format.

docs.title: Terra.bio
docs.text: Terra.bio is a cloud-based compute and data storage platform that is being developed by the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard. We are utilizing Terra.bio to help Spatial Technology Platform clients access, analyze, and visualize their ST data.

docs.title: Manifold.ai
docs.text: Manifold.ai is an AI-powered cloud platform for life sciences research.

docs.title: Jupyter Widget
docs.text: We utilize the Jupyter Widget ecosystem to build interactive spatial and data visualizations that enable users to perform two way communication between JavaScript (front-end) and Python (back-end). We are utilizing the AnyWidget implementation to build our custom widgets.

docs.title: Deck.gl
docs.text: Celldega uses the GPU-powered data visualization library deck.gl to create high-performance spatial- and data-visualizations.

docs.title: Apache Parquet
docs.text: Celldega uses the Apache Parquet file format for storing vectorized spatial data and metadata. This file format in combination with the JavaScript library ParquetWASM and Apache Arrow in memory representation is used to build Celldega's high-performance vector tiling spatial visualization functionality (see GeoArrow and GeoParquet in deck.gl).

docs.title: ParquetWASM and Apache Arrow
docs.text: ParquetWASM is a JavaScript library for reading Parquet files into Apache Arrow memory and utilizes Web Assembly (WASM) to run Rust in a browser environment. The Apache Arrow in-memory format is a columnar in-memory format that is used for storing data from Apache Parquet files and efficiently passing to deck.gl. For more information please see GeoArrow and GeoParquet in deck.gl.

docs.title: WebP
docs.text: A modern image format developed by Google, offering efficient lossless compression and designed specifically for the web.

docs.title: Deep Zoom
docs.text: We utilize the Deep Zoom image schema, developed by Microsoft, to enable efficient visualization of large multi-channel microscopy images. Deep Zoom tile images are stored using the WebP image format.

docs.title: Clustergrammer Visualization Approaches
docs.text: The Celldega Matrix visualization builds upon the visualization approaches developed in the Clustergrammer project. This enables users to interactively explore high-dimensional datasets (e.g., single-cell gene expression data) alongside spatial data (e.g., cell distributions within a tissue).

docs.title: Scanpy and Squidpy
docs.text: Celldega is built to interface with the AnnData and SpatialData objects, which enables users to easily import analysis results from Scanpy and Squidpy, respectively, into Celldega for downstream analysis and/or visuaization.

docs.title: GeoPandas
docs.text: Celldega uses GeoPandas for efficient spatial operations and storing collections of spatial objects (e.g., neighborhood multi-polygons) as GeoDataFrames.

docs.title: LibPySal: Python Spatial Analysis Library Core
docs.text: Celldega uses the Python Spatial Analysis Library (libpysal) for spatial analysis - namely for calculating alpha shape cell type neighborhoods.

docs.title: Clustergrammer Data Analysis Approaches
docs.text: The Celldega Cluster module build upon the hierarchical clustering approaches developed in the Clustergrammer project. This enables users to perform hierarchical clustering on observations (e.g., single cells) and measurements (e.g., genes) and easily visualize these two orthogonal clustering results interactively using Celldega's Matrix visualization method.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text: Use Celldega in local or cloud notebooks, in a standalone web page, or through Celldega-App on your desktop.

docs.title: In a notebook
docs.text: Use Celldega downstream of single-cell and spatial analysis workflows, such as Scanpy and Squidpy, to interactively visualize the results. Bring cluster annotations, UMAP coordinates, gene expression, and neighborhood summaries from your analysis into linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich widgets.

docs.title: Example workflows
docs.text:
• Chromium PBMC: Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich — analyze single-cell RNA-seq data with Scanpy, then explore clusters, UMAP/XY landscapes, marker-gene dot plots, and gene-set enrichment in linked views.
  • Scanpy–Squidpy Xenium Pancreas — explore Scanpy clusters and expression patterns alongside Squidpy spatial neighborhood-enrichment results using Landscapes and Clustergrams.

See Example Notebooks for more workflows.

docs.title: Notebook options
docs.text:
• Local Jupyter — JupyterLab or Jupyter Notebook running on your own machine, following the standard Installation and Getting Started guides.
  • Cloud notebook services — hosted notebook environments such as Manifold.ai, Google Colab, marimo, and molab. Celldega installs like any other PyPI package (pip install celldega); widget rendering depends on the service supporting the Jupyter Widgets protocol.

docs.title: Prepare DegaFiles from instrument output
docs.text: For a spatial Landscape, start with the instrument's processed output bundle: cell-by-gene counts, cell positions and boundaries, transcript coordinates, and morphology images. Celldega arranges these into DegaFiles so that the browser can load the image tiles and spatial regions needed for the current view.

docs.title: 1. Install the preprocessing dependencies
docs.text:
pip install "celldega[pre]"

Image preprocessing also requires a native libvips installation. See Installation for the available extras.

docs.title: 2. Convert a sample into DegaFiles
docs.text:
Place your Xenium output folder at data/instrument/Xenium_Sample, then run:

import celldega as dega

dega.pre.main(
    sample="Xenium_Sample",
    data_root_dir="data/instrument",
    path_dega_files="data/DegaFiles/Xenium_Sample",
    tile_size=250,
    image_tile_layer="all",
)

pre.main detects Xenium (including Atera) and MERSCOPE bundles. The exact input files depend on the instrument; see the pre API and Atera preprocessing notebook. The output includes a manifest, cell metadata, gene expression, image pyramids, and tiled transcripts and boundaries. See DegaFiles for the layout and optional row-group storage.

To add a histology background to existing DegaFiles, follow the aligned H&E workflow. For an alternative cell segmentation, see the custom segmentation notebook.

docs.title: 3. View the prepared data locally
docs.text:
For the individual-tile layout written above, start a file server at the DegaFiles directory and pass its HTTP URL to Landscape:

port = dega.viz.get_local_server(
    file_server_root="data/DegaFiles/Xenium_Sample"
)

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url=f"http://localhost:{port}",
    height=600,
)
landscape

Keep the notebook kernel running while this server is in use. For remote notebook kernels, use the environment's browser-accessible forwarded URL. The local server notebook explains the working-directory and URL conventions.

Analysis and visualization preparation can run separately. Pass an analyzed adata to Landscape to supply cluster labels, colors, and UMAP coordinates; its cell IDs must match the DegaFiles. A single-cell UMAP/XY Landscape can instead use AnnData Zarr directly, without spatial DegaFiles.

docs.title: Host and share prepared data
docs.text:
Upload the complete DegaFiles directory, preserving its subdirectories, and set base_url to the browser-readable HTTP(S) URL of that directory. The root must contain landscape_parameters.json. Prepared Zarr stores are likewise served as directories containing their metadata and chunks.

Hosting option How to use it Local machine Serve the directory with viz.get_local_server as above for individual tile files. Other users need a shared host to view the same data. GitHub Use a raw-content directory URL, as in the Xenium example. Suitable for smaller prepared examples; consider GitHub's file and repository limits when choosing a host. Hugging Face dataset repository Upload the prepared files and use a https://huggingface.co/datasets/ORG/REPO/resolve/REVISION/FOLDER URL. See uploading datasets, our supporting data, and the PBMC notebook for hosted AnnData and Matrix Zarr examples. Cloud object-storage bucket Upload under one prefix and use its HTTPS endpoint, such as an S3, Google Cloud Storage, or Azure Blob endpoint. Configure browser access and, for packed row-group files, byte-range reads. S3's CORS guide explains one provider's configuration. Manifold-managed storage or bucket Use a browser-readable data endpoint supported by your Manifold workspace, with the workspace's access permissions. Manifold's Celldega example describes running Celldega on the platform; the bucket endpoint and access setup depend on the workspace.
