docs.title: spatial_clustergram(spatial, mat, width='600px', height='700px', *, enrich=False, row_enrich=True, col_enrich=False, enrich_kwargs=None, cluster_attr=None)
docs.text:
Display a spatial widget and a Clustergram widget side by side, linked so that clicking a Clustergram row/column updates the spatial widget.

Works with any of celldega's spatial widgets: Landscape, CellCloud, NeighborhoodCloud, or Yearbook. Landscape/CellCloud/ NeighborhoodCloud share an update_trigger trait and are linked via a front-end jslink (no round-trip through Python); Yearbook has no such trait and is instead linked by observing the Clustergram's click_info in Python and translating it into a front_end_query (same mechanism as landscape_yearbook_clustergram).

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default spatial Landscape | CellCloud | NeighborhoodCloud | Yearbook

The spatial widget to link.

required mat Clustergram

A Clustergram widget.

required width str

The width of the spatial widget. The Clustergram panel is sized to the Clustergram's canvas (its width plus ~100px for labels), widened if needed so its control panel fits.

'600px' height str

The total height of the spatial widget, including its control bar, and the default height of the Enrich widget. The Clustergram's height sets only its canvas; its controls and dendrogram add about 200px, so Clustergram(height=<height - 200>) lines the two up (e.g. the 700px default with height=500). The row stretches every widget to the tallest one.

'700px' enrich bool | Enrich

If True, create an Enrich widget; if an Enrich instance is provided, use it directly. If False, no enrichment widget is shown. Ignored for a Yearbook spatial.

False row_enrich bool

If True (default), run enrichment analysis when row dendrogram clusters are selected.

True col_enrich bool

If True, run enrichment analysis when column dendrogram clusters are selected.

False enrich_kwargs dict | None

Optional kwargs passed to Enrich when enrich=True.

None cluster_attr str | None

The cell attribute (adata.obs column) a clicked cluster refers to. Only used when spatial is a Yearbook; defaults to the Clustergram's own col_entity attribute (see _clustergram_col_attr).

None

Returns:

Name Type Description HBox HBox

Visualization display containing the widgets.

docs.title: Visualizations
docs.text:
Celldega's interactive views help you explore where cells are, how gene expression varies, and which biological processes distinguish a group. Use linked views to move between tissue context, expression patterns, and gene-set interpretation.

For desktop viewing, try Celldega-App, with linked Landscape–Clustergram panels, Yearbook cell portraits, and saved Clustergrams. Download the latest build or see the desktop guide and screenshots.

docs.title: Video tutorial
docs.text: This narrated walkthrough links a Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich to explore a Visium HD human colorectal cancer dataset. Follow along in the Visium HD Human CRC Landscape-Clustergram-Enrich notebook.

docs.title: Spatial visualizations
docs.text:
Explore cells and neighborhoods in physical space (x/y, and sometimes z) across a tissue section, or compare cells in a low dimensional embedding landscape (UMAP/XY).

  • Landscape: Where are cell types in the tissue, and which cells express a gene? Explore cells, transcripts, images, and neighborhoods over tissue, or switch to UMAP and gene-expression XY views.
  • Yearbook: What do individual cells look like? Compare a grid of cell portraits, each centered on one cell from the same spatial dataset, and mark cells for review.
  • CellCloud: How are cells arranged in 3D? Explore thick tissue and aligned serial sections.
  • NeighborhoodCloud: How do tissue neighborhoods extend across slices? Explore neighborhoods and their cells in 3D.

docs.title: Data visualizations
docs.text:
Compare measured values across cells, clusters, neighborhoods, or samples.

  • Clustergram: Which genes distinguish each cell group, and which groups are most alike? Find expression patterns in a clustered heatmap or dot plot, with dendrograms and gene/metadata labels.
  • Composition: How do cell-type proportions differ across samples, regions, or neighborhoods?

docs.title: Information visualization
docs.text:
Interpret the genes that distinguish a selected group.

  • Enrich: Which biological processes or cell types are associated with a set of genes? Explore gene-set enrichment against public libraries through Enrichr.

docs.title: Linked Visualization
docs.text:
Connect views of the same dataset to explore cell positions, expression patterns, and gene-set enrichment together.

  • Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich: connect tissue or embedding views with expression patterns and gene-set interpretation.
  • CellCloud–Clustergram: connect cells in 3D with expression patterns across cell groups.

Start with the Gallery for interactive examples or the Example Notebooks for complete workflows. Each visualization's guide explains what it shows and how to create it; the Python API reference covers constructor options and notebook controls.

docs.title: The control panel
docs.text:
Landscape, Yearbook, CellCloud, and NeighborhoodCloud share a control panel above the view. Clustergram, Composition, and Enrich have their own panels, described on their pages.

The Landscape control panel over a whole-transcriptome kidney section, showing glomeruli and tubules. Cells are colored by cluster over the DAPI, boundary, and RNA image channels.

Control What it does 1 View and image SPATIAL, UMAP, and XY switch between tissue, embedding, and two-gene views (UMAP appears when the data include an embedding). IMG shows or hides the image; each channel button toggles that channel, and its slider sets the channel's brightness. 2 CELL Shows or hides the cells; the slider sets their size. The bars rank cell clusters by count: click a bar to select that cluster, and shift-click to add more. 3 TRX Transcripts and gene expression. Zoomed in, TRX shows or hides individual transcripts and the slider sets their size; zoomed out, the slider sets how strongly cells are colored by a selected gene. The bars rank genes: click one to color cells by its expression. 4 NBHD Neighborhoods: shows supplied tissue regions, or lets you draw your own. Appears only when neighborhoods are supplied or drawing is turned on. 5 Gene search Type one or more gene names, separated by commas, to color cells by expression; clear the box to return to cluster colors. The box below describes the selected gene, from UniProt. 6 Celldega logo Opens this visualization's documentation page. 7 The view Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, hover over cells and transcripts for details, and click a cell to select its cluster.

Conventions shared across visualizations:

  • Blue button text means on; gray means off. A faded button is not available at the current zoom.
  • Scrolling over a Landscape, CellCloud, or Clustergram zooms it instead of scrolling the page. Move the pointer off the visualization to scroll the page.
  • Hovering shows details in a tooltip, without changing the selection; clicking selects. For genes, hovering shows a brief UniProt description and clicking shows it in the gene information box.
  • The Celldega logo in every control panel links to that visualization's page in this documentation.

docs.title: Two ways to use a visualization
docs.text:
Each visualization, such as a Landscape or a Clustergram, runs in your web browser. You can use it in two ways:

 Notebook widget (Jupyter or marimo)      JavaScript on a web page
┌────────────────────────────────────┐   ┌────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Python kernel                      │   │ Gallery, standalone web page,      │
│   AnnData, Matrix, your analysis   │   │ or notebook report (no Python)     │
│     │ options        ▲ selections, │   │                                    │
│     ▼ and data       │ drawings    │   │                                    │
│ Browser                            │   │ Browser                            │
│   Landscape ◄─link─► Clustergram   │   │   Landscape ◄─link─► Clustergram   │
└────────────────────────────────────┘   └────────────────────────────────────┘
                   ▲                                        ▲
                   └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘
                                       │
           prepared data (DegaFiles or AnnData Zarr), read over HTTP
  • As a notebook widget with a Python back-end. Create the visualization from your analysis in Jupyter or marimo. The Python back-end makes the widget stateful: selections, drawn neighborhoods, and annotations are available to your analysis, and Python can update the view. Links between widgets, such as a Clustergram click coloring a Landscape, run in the browser through the widget framework (jslink).

You can also embed visualizations in notebook reports: static HTML pages made from pre-executed notebooks saved with their widget state. The visualizations and their links stay interactive in the report, without a running kernel. The Example Notebooks on this site are shown this way. - As JavaScript on a web page, without Python. The Gallery pages, standalone pages built with the JavaScript API, and notebook reports all run the same visualizations in the browser. Every interaction and browser link works; there is no Python back-end to receive selections or annotations.

Each visualization's page describes its interactions, which are the same in both cases, and then what the widget's Python back-end adds.

docs.title: CellCloud–Clustergram
docs.text:
Link a CellCloud and Clustergram to compare 3D cell organization with gene-expression patterns. This is useful for thick tissue or aligned serial sections, where rotating the cell cloud reveals relationships across slices.

CellCloud shows cell positions in physical space. Clustergram compares expression across cell groups; its selections update the 3D view.

The Broad–Allen developing mouse brain: 3.8 million cells from 43 aligned Xenium sections in a CellCloud. Explore it in the 3D gallery, or link it to a Clustergram in the visualization notebook.

docs.title: What you can explore
docs.text:
• Select a cell group and inspect its distribution across the 3D dataset.
  • Click a gene to see where expressing cells occur while rotating or zooming.
  • Compare the expression relationships in the Clustergram with the physical arrangement of the corresponding cells.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Use point-cloud DegaFiles containing 3D cell positions and a matching cell-level AnnData, adata. Its obs_names must match the DegaFiles cell IDs; adata.obs["leiden"] supplies the cell-group labels used by both views.

The example assumes prepared, nonnegative expression in adata.X and uses celldega[scanpy] to summarize cells by group. Replace "leiden" in both groupby and cluster_attr to use a different cell annotation.

See the CellCloud guide for point-cloud preparation and File Formats for the layout.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Build the expression summary from the cells shown in the cloud:

import celldega as dega

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden")
mat.filter("row", by="var", num=min(500, adata.n_vars))
mat.norm("row", by="zscore")
mat.cluster()

cell_cloud = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    base_url="https://your-data-host/point_cloud_files",
    adata=adata,
    cluster_attr="leiden",
    use_adata_3d_centroids=False,
)
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat, name="cloud_clusters")

linked = dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(cell_cloud, cgm)
linked

Replace base_url with your point-cloud DegaFiles URL. use_adata_3d_centroids=False uses the saved 3D positions from DegaFiles while AnnData supplies the cell annotations. The Clustergram has genes as rows and cell groups as columns. Dot color shows row-z-scored mean expression and dot size shows the fraction of cells expressing each gene.

Use Clustergram advanced usage to prepare marker-ranked views or restore a previously saved Matrix instead.

docs.title: Try the linked selections
docs.text:
1. Rotate and zoom the CellCloud. Inspect the overall shape of the tissue or aligned sections.
  2. Select a cell group in the Clustergram. Its corresponding cells are highlighted in 3D.
  3. Click a gene in the Clustergram. CellCloud colors cells by expression, while you continue to rotate and zoom.
  4. Change the Clustergram's feature view. Explore a different set of genes when the Matrix includes precomputed views.

To add gene-set interpretation, pass enrich=True to the same helper:

linked_with_enrich = dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(
    cell_cloud, cgm, enrich=True
)
linked_with_enrich

See Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich for the enrichment interactions shared by these linked layouts.

docs.title: CellCloud
docs.text:
CellCloud shows cells in 3D, as points you can rotate and zoom. Use it for data with depth, such as thick tissue or serial sections aligned into a stack, to see how cell types and gene expression are arranged through the tissue. For 2D detail, such as images, cell boundaries, and transcripts, use a Landscape.

Loading an interactive preview…

Interactive preview: 76,356 cells imaged in 3D with thick-tissue MERFISH. Drag to orbit and scroll to zoom. Open the full-size view in the Gallery.

docs.title: Reading a CellCloud
docs.text:
Each point is a cell, colored by its cluster or by a gene's expression. The control panel matches a Landscape's, without the image and transcript layers, which have no 3D form.

3.8 million cells from 43 aligned Xenium sections of an E15.5 mouse brain, colored by cluster.

Control What it does 1 CELL The slider scales the point size, from 0 to twice cell_size. Click a cluster's bar to show only its cells; click again to show all. 2 Genes Click a gene's bar to color cells by its expression. 3 Gene search Color cells by one or more genes, typed by name. 4 Celldega logo Opens this page. 5 The view Drag to rotate, scroll to zoom, and hover for details.

docs.title: Rotating and zooming
docs.text:
Drag to rotate the cells around their center, horizontally and vertically, all the way around and past the poles. Scroll to zoom. Hover over a cell for its ID and cluster; tooltips pause briefly after the view moves, so that rotating stays smooth. Click a cell to select its cluster.

Turning the mouse brain fully around and tilting it, selecting cluster 2, and searching for SPARC, which outlines the meninges around the brain.

docs.title: Widget: Python-backed interactions
docs.text: A CellCloud responds to Python and to linked views: a linked Clustergram's clicks color or select its cells, and setting cell_size updates the point size. It does not send selections back to Python; use a Landscape of the same cells for that.

docs.title: Choose a data source
docs.text:
Use base_url for point-cloud DegaFiles or zarr_url for a cell-level AnnData Zarr store. The browser reads positions, categories, and the selected genes directly from either source; an in-memory AnnData is optional.

When testing the unreleased checkout, run npm run build and start the notebook kernel with CELLDEGA_LOCAL_ESM=1 before importing Celldega to use its new reader.

import celldega as dega

# Point-cloud DegaFiles served from a directory under the working directory.
port = dega.viz.get_local_server()
from_degafiles = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    base_url=f"http://localhost:{port}/data/cell_cloud_files",
    cluster_attr="cell_type",
    alignment="neighborhood",
    rotation_x=20,
)

# An AnnData Zarr store, served automatically when given a local path.
from_zarr = dega.viz.CellCloud(
    zarr_url="data/cells.zarr",
    cluster_attr="cell_type",
    alignment="neighborhood",
    rotation_x=20,
)

from_degafiles  # display this widget, or from_zarr

Both arguments also accept HTTP(S) URLs. Pass one source per widget. Zarr stores use CSC expression in X or a layer selected with zarr_layer. Positions come from obsm["spatial"] (XYZ), or obsm["spatial_<alignment>"] for a named alignment. Original obs_names remain the cell IDs used by tooltips, selections, and linked visualizations.

cell_size sets the default cell diameter (10 µm by default), assuming the centroid coordinates are in microns. The CELL slider scales this diameter from 0× to 2×; its initial midpoint is 1×. You can also update cell_cloud.cell_size after displaying the widget, preserving the slider's current multiplier.

Drag to rotate continuously around both orbit axes, including past the poles.

docs.title: Prepare either format
docs.text:
Start with cell-level adata: positions in obsm["spatial"] (XY or XYZ), an optional Z column such as obs["Z"], expression in layers["counts"] or X, and categories in an obs column.

# Compact Parquet files: retain original IDs once and use numeric indices elsewhere.
dega.pre.write_point_cloud_dataset(
    adata,
    "data/cell_cloud_files",
    name="neighborhood",
    cluster_key="cell_type",
    use_int_index=True,
    coordinate_resolution=1.0,
    compression="zstd",
    compression_level=6,
)

# A self-contained AnnData Zarr with CSC expression and the same positions.
dega.pre.write_point_cloud_zarr(
    adata,
    "data/cells.zarr",
    cluster_key="cell_type",
    alignments={"neighborhood": xyz},  # (n_cells, 3), in adata.obs_names order
    coordinate_resolution=1.0,
)

Here xyz contains the alignment's XYZ positions in microns. If spatial already has three columns and no separate Z column should take precedence, pass z_key=None to either writer. Omit alignment when displaying a store that contains only the default positions.

With micron inputs, coordinate_resolution=1.0 rounds each axis to the nearest micron (at most 0.5 µm of error per axis). Numeric IDs and compression reduce file transfer and decoding work while preserving original cell identity. The DegaFiles writer keeps its existing name-based defaults unless these options are selected. The Zarr writer requires a new output path by default.

Passing name="..." to the DegaFiles writer adds a named position variant. For an indexed dataset, appended alignments must contain exactly the same cells; the writer restores their canonical order. See the pre module API and File Formats.

CellCloud can also be linked to a Clustergram, exactly like Landscape — see dega.viz.spatial_clustergram.

For the full list of constructor arguments, see the Viz Module API reference.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: Explore the 3D developing mouse brain interactively, or follow its visualization notebook for a CellCloud linked to a Clustergram. The companion preprocessing and alignment notebook shows how to build the stack and write DegaFiles. For thick tissue, see the MERFISH notebook.

docs.title: Screenshot sources
docs.text: The screenshot and animation show the Broad–Allen developing mouse brain compact DegaFiles, captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py.

docs.title: Clustergram
docs.text:
Clustergram uses hierarchical bi-clustering to organize both axes of a high-dimensional matrix: genes/features by their expression patterns, and cells, clusters, neighborhoods, or samples by their similarity. The heatmap or dot plot makes these relationships visible alongside dendrograms.

For single-cell expression, a common workflow starts by identifying cell groups with tools such as Scanpy's Leiden clustering. Celldega can summarize expression within those groups, then hierarchically cluster the genes and groups to explore marker programs and relationships between cell populations.

Loading an interactive preview…

Interactive preview: top marker genes of 180 Tabula Sapiens cell types. Color shows mean expression scaled per gene; dot size shows the fraction of cells expressing the gene. Use DIM to change the number of markers per cell type. Data: Tabula Sapiens Consortium, via CZ CELLxGENE Discover · CC BY 4.0.

docs.title: Reading a Clustergram
docs.text:
A Clustergram arranges a matrix so that similar rows sit next to each other, and so do similar columns. In the marker dot plot below, rows are genes and columns are Leiden clusters of peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs). Each mark's color shows a gene's mean expression in a cluster, scaled across clusters: red is above the gene's average and blue is below. Its size shows the fraction of the cluster's cells that express the gene. The dendrograms on the right and bottom show how genes and clusters were grouped, so blocks of red reveal marker programs: B-cell genes such as CD79A in cluster 1, platelet genes such as PPBP and PF4 in cluster 8, and NK-cell genes such as GZMB and NKG7 in cluster 4.

Marker genes of nine PBMC clusters, five per cluster, as a dot plot.

Control What it does 1 COL / ROW Order each axis (CLUST, SUM, VAR, or INI), and cut its dendrogram with the slider. 2 DIM Choose how many genes to show, from views precomputed in Python; here, five markers per cluster. 3 CROP · UNDO · PROP · UNIT Crop to a region and undo the crop; switch dot-plot marks between proportional and full size. 4 Category bars Count the categories in view, such as clusters. Hover a bar to highlight its rows or columns. 5 Search Find a gene and zoom to it. The box below describes a clicked gene. 6 Celldega logo Opens this page. 7 Column labels Cluster names, above a colored strip for each column category. 8 Row labels Gene names. Hover for a description; click to send the gene to linked views. 9 Matrix One mark per gene and cluster. Hover for its values. 10 Dendrograms The row (right) and column (bottom) clustering trees. Hover or click a branch to select its group.

Many of these interactions build on Clustergrammer (Fernandez et al., Scientific Data, 2017), whose interaction guide describes the original designs. For stacked cell-type proportions across groups, use Composition.

docs.title: Motivation for Clustergram and Matrix
docs.text: We usually describe Clustergrams with cells and genes, but the analysis is generic: any matrix of observations and dimensions can be explored this way.

docs.title: Clusters of observations and of dimensions
docs.text: Graph-based clustering, such as Scanpy's Leiden clustering, assigns each cell to a cluster but does not show how the clusters relate to each other or which genes they share. A Clustergram hierarchically clusters both axes. Clustering the Leiden clusters' expression signatures gives a meta-clustering that groups related clusters, such as T-cell subtypes. Clustering the genes finds programs of co-expressed genes, such as the NK-cell cytotoxicity genes above, and shows which cell groups share them.

docs.title: A viewer for a DataFrame or an AnnData
docs.text: dega.clust.Matrix prepares a pandas DataFrame or an AnnData for hierarchical bi-clustering: it holds the values, the row and column annotations, the clustering, and any precomputed views. A Clustergram displays a Matrix, so you can think of it as an interactive viewer for your DataFrame or AnnData, with clustering on both axes.

docs.title: Observations as columns
docs.text:
A Clustergram shows observations as columns and dimensions as rows, the transpose of AnnData's observations × variables:

AnnData Clustergram Observations (obs_names): cells, clusters, samples Columns Variables (var_names): genes, proteins Rows obs columns, such as leiden or sample Colored strips above the columns var columns Colored strips beside the rows X The matrix, transposed

Observations usually carry more annotations than dimensions: cluster, sample, condition, cell type, and so on. With observations as columns, each annotation becomes a horizontal band of color above the matrix, and a stack of horizontal bands is easier to read than a row of vertical ones. Celldega transposes for you when it reads an AnnData and when it saves a Matrix.

docs.title: Views of marker-gene rankings
docs.text: Scanpy's rank_genes_groups ranks marker genes for each cluster, and a marker plot usually shows one choice of how many genes to include. Celldega precomputes views at several levels, such as 1, 3, 5, and 10 markers per cluster, each clustered on its own. The DIM slider then lets you move between them interactively. See views at different feature resolutions.

docs.title: Dot size: the fraction of cells expressing a gene
docs.text: Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden") summarizes cells by group: color is the group's mean expression, and dot size is the fraction of its cells with expression greater than zero, as in Scanpy's dot plots. A gene can have a high mean because a few cells express it strongly, or because most cells express it moderately; dot size tells these apart. See the marker-gene dot plot example.

docs.title: Saving the results in AnnData
docs.text: AnnData has no standard place for hierarchical clustering of observations and variables. When you save a clustered Matrix with Matrix.write_zarr, Celldega stores the dendrograms, node orders, views, and colors in an ordinary AnnData Zarr store under Celldega-specific keys (uns["celldega"], obsm["celldega_nodes"], and varm["celldega_nodes"]). Python and the browser can both reopen the same store without reclustering. Separately, for a single-cell Landscape, Celldega reads cell-level expression from a CSC copy of the expression matrix, which lets the browser fetch one gene at a time. See File Formats for both layouts.

docs.title: Beyond cells and genes
docs.text: The same methods cluster any observations and dimensions. The Atera breast cancer neighborhoods tutorial clusters tissue neighborhoods by their cell-type composition, and the Scanpy–Squidpy Xenium pancreas tutorial clusters cell types by their neighborhood enrichment.

docs.title: Zooming and panning
docs.text:
Scroll to zoom and drag to pan. When a Clustergram has many more rows than columns, zooming first spreads the rows apart until the marks are about square, then zooms both axes. Scrolling over the labels or dendrograms zooms from that edge of the matrix. You cannot zoom out beyond the whole matrix.

Scrolling spreads the rows apart first, then zooms both axes; dragging pans; scrolling back out returns to the whole matrix.

docs.title: Hovering for details
docs.text:
Hovering shows information without changing anything:

  • A mark: its gene, column, value, and, in a dot plot, its size.
  • A gene label: the protein name and a description from UniProt, for human gene symbols.
  • A dendrogram branch: the members of that group (dimming the rest).
  • A category tile: its category, with matching tiles highlighted.

The platelet gene PPBP in cluster 8: its scaled mean expression (value) and the fraction of cells expressing it (size).

Hovering a gene label shows its UniProt name and description.

docs.title: Reordering rows and columns
docs.text:
The COL and ROW dropdowns order each axis by CLUST (the dendrogram), SUM (total value), VAR (variance), or INI (the original order). The reordering is animated so that you can follow the rows and columns. Dendrograms appear only in CLUST order.

Double-click a gene's label to sort the columns by that gene, from highest to lowest; the label turns blue and COL reads CUSTOM. Double-click a column label to sort the genes by that column, or double-click a category title, such as leiden beside the strip, to group that axis by category.

Double-clicking GZMB sorts the clusters by its expression (NK cluster 4 first); ROW → SUM sorts the genes by total; CLUST restores the dendrogram order.

docs.title: Dendrograms
docs.text:
Each dendrogram slider sets where its tree is cut into groups. While you drag it, a preview draws the whole tree over the matrix, with a blue cut line and the number of groups. Release the slider, or press Esc, to hide the preview. The slider is unavailable while that axis is cropped.

Moving the ROW slider cuts the gene tree into more or fewer groups.

Hover a branch, the gray trapezoids along the right and bottom, to see its members and dim everything else. Click it to select the group: a gene group colors linked cells by the genes' combined expression and can be sent to Enrich. Click it again to clear the selection. Double-click a branch to crop to that group, and double-click again to restore the axis.

Hover the platelet branch to see its genes, click to select it, double-click to crop to it, and double-click again to restore the rows.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Colored strips beside the labels show each row's or column's categories, such as its Leiden cluster. The category bars in the control panel count the categories in view. When an axis has more than one category, choose which to show from the dropdown. Hover a bar or a strip tile to highlight the matching rows or columns.

To annotate interactively, create the Clustergram with manual_col_cat="cell_type" (or manual_row_cat). Clicking a column's category tile then opens an editor where you can name its category and choose a color, for example to label each cluster with a cell type. The annotations are available in Python as cgm.manual_cat.

docs.title: Cropping
docs.text:
Click CROP, then drag a rectangle over the matrix to keep only the rows and columns inside it. CROP stays unavailable until you click UNDO, which restores the whole matrix. To crop one axis to a dendrogram group, double-click its branch.

CROP, then drag a rectangle: the Clustergram keeps the monocyte, platelet, and NK-cell genes across all clusters. UNDO restores the matrix.

docs.title: Changing the number of dimensions
docs.text:
When a Matrix has precomputed views (see views at different feature resolutions), the DIM (dimensions) slider steps through them, ending with all rows. The readout shows the level, such as 5/clust for five marker genes per cluster; hover it to see how the genes were ranked. Each view is clustered on its own, so the order of the columns can change.

Stepping DIM from 1 to 50 marker genes per cluster (9 to 310 genes), then back to 5. Each view is clustered on its own.

docs.title: Proportional or full-size marks
docs.text:
In a dot plot, PROP sizes each mark by its size value, such as the fraction of cells expressing the gene. UNIT draws every mark at full size, keeping the colors, which makes weak or rare expression easier to compare.

UNIT draws full-size marks, revealing weak and negative values; PROP restores sizes by the fraction of cells expressing each gene.

docs.title: Searching
docs.text:
Type a gene name in the search box and press Enter, or choose it from the suggestions. The Clustergram zooms to the gene and bolds its label. Searching does not select the gene; click its label to send it to linked views.

Searching for GZMB, then CD79A: the Clustergram zooms to each gene and bolds its label.

docs.title: Linking to other visualizations
docs.text:
Linked to a Landscape, CellCloud, or NeighborhoodCloud, and to Enrich, a Clustergram drives the other views:

In the Clustergram Landscape or CellCloud Enrich Click a gene label Colors cells by that gene; click again to return to clusters — Click a column label Selects that cluster's cells Receives the column's top marker genes Click a column dendrogram branch Selects those clusters' cells — Click a row dendrogram branch, or crop rows Colors cells by the genes' combined expression Receives those genes Click a mark Colors cells by that gene within that cluster —

Selecting an Enrich term turns its genes' labels blue in the Clustergram, and clicking a gene in Enrich zooms the Clustergram to it. Selections made in a Landscape do not change the Clustergram. See Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich for a complete linked example.

docs.title: Widget: Python-backed interactions
docs.text:
As a notebook widget, a Clustergram also shares its state with Python:

  • Selections: cgm.selected_genes, cgm.selected_rows, and cgm.selected_cols hold the latest selection; cgm.enrichment_genes holds the gene set sent to Enrich; and cgm.click_info describes the last click.
  • Annotations: categories assigned in the manual category editor are in cgm.manual_cat.
  • Updates from Python: for example, cgm.viz_mode = "heatmap" switches a dot plot to a heatmap.
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat, manual_col_cat="cell_type")
cgm

# After clicking a dendrogram branch and labeling some clusters:
cgm.selected_genes
cgm.manual_cat

Links made with dega.viz.spatial_clustergram and dega.viz.clustergram_enrich run in the browser, so they keep working in a notebook report without a kernel. Links to a Yearbook use Python and need a running kernel.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
This example assumes that adata.X already contains prepared expression values. Filtering and normalization are explicit:

import celldega as dega

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(adata)
mat.filter("row", by="var", num=min(5000, adata.n_vars))
mat.norm("row", by="zscore")
mat.cluster()

cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat)
cgm

Row z-scoring emphasizes each gene's relative expression across the columns. For large single-cell datasets, summarize cells into groups as below before hierarchically clustering the columns.

docs.title: A marker-gene dot plot after Leiden clustering
docs.text:
Assume that adata.obs["leiden"] holds the first-round cell labels and adata.X contains nonnegative, log-normalized expression, before cell-level z-scoring. This example requires celldega[scanpy].

import scanpy as sc
import celldega as dega

# Rank markers using the same expression values that will be summarized.
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="leiden", use_raw=False)

# Columns become Leiden groups; rows remain genes.
markers = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden")
markers.filter_by_size(0.05)
markers.norm("row", by="zscore")
markers.cluster(
    view="rank_genes_groups",
    levels=[1, 3, 5, 10, 25],
)

dotplot = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=markers, rank_dim=5)
dotplot

Before row z-scoring, the color matrix is each group's mean expression. Dot size is the fraction of its cells with expression greater than zero. filter_by_size(0.05) keeps genes detected in at least 5% of cells in at least one group; row z-scoring changes the color values while preserving those fractions. A Matrix carrying size values opens as a dot plot automatically.

Matrix reuses matching rank_genes_groups results. Alternatively, pass rank_genes_groups=True when constructing the Matrix to calculate missing rankings. See Scanpy's marker-ranking documentation and aggregation documentation for the underlying operations.

docs.title: Generate views at different feature resolutions
docs.text:
cluster(view=..., levels=...) keeps the full matrix and precomputes smaller feature sets. Each set is independently clustered on both axes, so the column order can change as different gene programs come into focus.

view How rows are chosen Meaning of a level "rank_genes_groups" Union of each group's top-ranked marker genes Markers per group "var" Highest row variance Total rows "sum" Highest row sum Total rows "mean" Highest row mean Total rows

In the dot-plot example, level 5 means up to five markers per Leiden group. Shared markers are counted once, so the total displayed rows may be less than 5 × number of groups. The DIM slider switches among the computed levels and all, which restores the full matrix.

Metric views also work without marker rankings, including bulk and other high-dimensional data. For example, compare the most variable genes across Leiden-group means:

variable = dega.clust.Matrix(
    adata,
    groupby="leiden",
    rank_genes_groups=False,
)
variable.cluster(view="var", levels=[100, 500, 1000])

heatmap = dega.viz.Clustergram(
    matrix=variable,
    viz_mode="heatmap",
    rank_dim=500,
)
heatmap

Metric rankings use the Matrix's current values. Use un-z-scored normalized values for variance views: row z-scoring makes row variances equal. Choose levels smaller than the feature count. Levels that select the whole matrix, too few rows, or duplicate another feature set are omitted.

One Matrix stores one view family at a time. Build separate Matrices to compare marker-ranked and variance-ranked views. rank_dim chooses the initial level; it does not compute a new view. The browser switches among precomputed levels.

docs.title: Save the clustered views
docs.text:
markers.write_zarr("marker_dotplot.zarr")
restored = dega.clust.Matrix.read_zarr("marker_dotplot.zarr")
reopened = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=restored, rank_dim=5)

The store preserves values, optional dot sizes, metadata, dendrograms, precomputed views, colors, and marker rankings. See Matrix storage for what is saved before and after clustering, and File Formats for the AnnData Zarr schema and JavaScript readers.

docs.title: Examples and source code
docs.text:
Link a Clustergram to a Landscape, CellCloud, or NeighborhoodCloud with dega.viz.spatial_clustergram. Gene clicks color cells by expression, and group selections highlight their corresponding cells.

The Chromium PBMC tutorial demonstrates marker dot plots and saved Matrix stores. The Visium HD tutorial demonstrates linked Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich views.

For constructor options, see the Viz API. Source: Matrix clustering and views, Clustergram widget, and browser view controls.

docs.title: Screenshot sources
docs.text: Screenshots and animations show the PBMC 3k marker dot plot that the Chromium PBMC tutorial saves with Matrix.write_zarr (pbmc3k_leiden_markers.zarr), from 10x Genomics PBMC 3k data. They were captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text: Composition is a Clustergram variant for comparing category composition across groups — e.g. cell-type proportions across samples or conditions — rather than a general-purpose heatmap. It shows the count or relative proportion of categories within each group, and compares those compositions across groups.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Each group (e.g. dataset or sample) as a stacked bar, whose segments are the categories (e.g. cell types) that make it up.
  • The same column-attribute tracks and reorder buttons (ini / sum / clust) as Clustergram.
  • A PROP / COUNTS toggle in the control panel to switch between relative proportions and raw counts.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

# Cell types across samples, straight from a cell-level AnnData
dega.viz.Composition(
    adata, groupby="sample_id", category="cell_type", group_attrs=["condition"]
)

With groupby, the cells are cross-tabulated into groups x categories and colored from adata.uns[f"{category}_colors"]. Composition also accepts a precomputed group-by-population matrix: an AnnData (groups as obs), a MuData modality, or a plain DataFrame (e.g. from dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_pop), or a DatasetCollection / SetCollection with a population modality. See Clustergram for the shared heatmap controls, and the Viz Module API reference for the full set of constructor arguments.

docs.title: Example
docs.text: The Atera kidney tutorial uses Composition to compare cell populations across neighborhood gradient bands.

docs.title: Enrich
docs.text: Enrich interprets a list of genes, such as the marker genes of a cluster, by looking them up in public gene-set libraries through Enrichr. It answers questions such as "which cell types or biological processes are associated with these genes?"

docs.title: Reading Enrich
docs.text:
Enrich shows the top-ranked gene sets, or terms, for the current gene list, and the genes themselves.

The top 20 marker genes of the pancreatic islet cluster, looked up in CellMarker 2024. With the Alpha Cell Pancreas Human term selected, its genes are highlighted in the gene list.

Control What it does 1 Library Choose the gene-set library to search, such as CellMarker_2024 for cell types; the default list includes cell-type, pathway, and tissue libraries. 2 Terms The top terms, ranked by Enrichr's combined score; the bar length shows the score. 3 Gene list The genes being looked up. 4 Gene information The name and description of a clicked gene, from UniProt. 5 Source, CLEAR, and Enrichr link Where the genes came from, a button to clear them, and a link to the full results on the Enrichr website. 6 Celldega logo Opens this page.

docs.title: Interacting with terms and genes
docs.text:
• Hover a term for its full name, combined score, p-value, adjusted p-value, odds ratio, and overlap with your gene list.
  • Click a term to highlight its genes in the gene list; the other terms are dimmed. In a linked Clustergram, the term's genes turn blue. Click the term again to clear it.
  • Hover a gene for its UniProt description and how many of the shown terms include it.
  • Click a gene to bold it and show its description below the list. In linked views, the Clustergram zooms to the gene and a Landscape colors cells by it. Click it again to clear the focus.
  • CLEAR empties the gene list.
  • Choose a library to look up the same genes in another library.

Hovering a term shows its statistics; selecting the delta and alpha cell terms highlights their genes, such as SST and GCG; clicking GCG shows its description.

Enrich queries Enrichr from your browser, so it needs an internet connection. Gene descriptions come from UniProt and are available for human gene symbols.

docs.title: Where the genes come from
docs.text:
Set the gene list from Python, or link Enrich to a Clustergram so that selections there update it:

In the Clustergram Genes sent to Enrich Click a column label That column's top marker genes Click a row dendrogram branch The branch's genes Crop rows The cropped genes Click a column dendrogram branch Its top marker genes, when col_enrich=True

Clicking a single gene in the Clustergram focuses it without replacing the enrichment gene list. See Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich for a linked example.

docs.title: Widget: Python-backed interactions
docs.text:
As a notebook widget, Enrich shares its state with Python:

  • enrich.gene_list sets or reads the genes, and enrich.background_list an optional background.
  • enrich.inst_lib is the selected library.
  • enrich.selected_term and enrich.term_genes hold the selected term and its genes.
  • enrich.focused_gene is the clicked gene.

The links to a Clustergram run in the browser, so they keep working in a notebook report.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

enrich = dega.viz.Enrich(width=650, height=650)
enrich.gene_list = ["INS", "GCG", "SST", "CHGA", "PCSK2"]
enrich

Link it to a Clustergram with dega.viz.clustergram_enrich(cgm), or to a Landscape and Clustergram with dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm, enrich=True). For the full list of constructor arguments, see the Viz Module API reference.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The Visium HD tutorial and Chromium PBMC tutorial connect Enrich to a Clustergram and Landscape.

docs.title: Screenshot sources
docs.text: The screenshot and animation show the top 20 Scanpy marker genes of the islet cluster in the hosted Xenium pancreas AnnData, captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py.

docs.title: Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich
docs.text: Link a Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich to move between where cells are, which genes distinguish them, and what those genes mean. The Landscape shows the cells, in tissue or in a UMAP; the Clustergram organizes expression across genes and cell groups; and Enrich interprets a selected group of genes through gene-set enrichment.

docs.title: How the views connect
docs.text:
In the Clustergram Landscape Enrich Click a gene label Colors cells by that gene; click again to return to clusters — Click a column label Shows that group's cells Receives the group's top marker genes Click a row dendrogram branch Colors cells by the genes' combined expression Receives the branch's genes Click a mark Colors cells by that gene within that group — In Enrich Clustergram Landscape Click a term Its genes' labels turn blue — Click a gene Zooms to the gene Colors cells by the gene

Selections made in the Landscape do not change the other views. The links run in the browser, so they keep working in a published notebook report.

docs.title: Spatial data
docs.text:
For spatial data, the Landscape shows the tissue from DegaFiles, with your clusters from an AnnData.

Xenium pancreas: clicking INS colors the islets in the tissue; clicking the islet cluster (9) shows its cells and sends its markers to Enrich; clicking the INS–GCG–SCGN branch sends those genes to Enrich and colors cells by their combined expression; and clicking a term turns its genes blue in the Clustergram.

import scanpy as sc
import celldega as dega

sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="leiden")
markers = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="leiden")
markers.filter_by_size(0.05)
markers.norm("row", by="zscore")
markers.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 3, 5, 10])

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url="https://your-data-host/DegaFiles",
    adata=adata,
    cluster_attr="leiden",
)
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=markers, rank_dim=3)

dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm, enrich=True)

The AnnData's obs_names must match the DegaFiles' cell IDs, and the Matrix's groupby must be the Landscape's cluster_attr. Color is each group's mean expression, z-scored across groups; dot size is the fraction of the group's cells that express the gene. Visualize Your Own Data walks through this example from the instrument output.

docs.title: Single-cell data
docs.text:
For single-cell data, the Landscape shows the UMAP from an AnnData Zarr store, read directly in the browser, with no DegaFiles. The linked Clustergram adds a higher-dimensional view: which genes distinguish the clusters you see in the UMAP.

Tabula Sapiens, 1.1 million cells and 180 cell types:

  1. Zooming toward the spermatids updates the CELL and gene bars to the cells in view, and PRM1 colors the spermatid swirl; zoomed out, PRM1 stays confined to it.
  2. Dragging the column dendrogram slider previews the cell-type tree and its cut, then selecting column dendrogram branches highlights meta-clusters of cell types in the UMAP.
  3. Double-clicking the spermatid column ranks the genes by spermatid expression, selects the spermatids, and sends their top markers to Enrich, which ranks Germ Cell Testis first. Zooming into the top rows and clicking PRM1 colors its cells.
  4. Clicking the plasma cell column selects plasma cells across tissues, and Enrich ranks plasma cell gene sets first.

Follow along in the Tabula Sapiens tutorial, or explore the atlas in the Gallery.

adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.write_zarr("cells.zarr")

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    zarr_url="cells.zarr", zarr_layer="counts_csc", cluster_attr="leiden"
)
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=markers, rank_dim=3)  # markers as above
dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm, enrich=True)

A Clustergram can also show individual cells instead of cluster summaries, for example a single-cell Clustergram of a selected population; the Chromium PBMC tutorial links both kinds to UMAP Landscapes.

docs.title: Try the linked selections
docs.text:
1. Click a gene in the Clustergram. The Landscape colors cells by that gene's expression, in tissue or the UMAP.
  2. Select a cell group in the Clustergram. The Landscape shows those cells, and Enrich receives the group's top marker genes.
  3. Select a gene group with the row dendrogram. Enrich looks up the genes in the selected library.
  4. Select an enriched term. Its genes are highlighted in the Clustergram.
  5. Click a gene in Enrich. The Clustergram zooms to that gene and the Landscape colors cells by its expression.

A focused gene and the enrichment gene set are kept separate: inspecting one gene does not replace the multi-gene enrichment query.

docs.text:
• Visium HD tutorial: a complete spatial Landscape–Clustergram–Enrich workflow.
  • Narrated walkthrough: watch the linked spatial workflow.
  • Chromium PBMC tutorial and Tabula Sapiens tutorial: single-cell UMAP Landscapes linked to Clustergrams and Enrich.
  • Python linking API: layout and enrichment options.
  • CellCloud–Clustergram: the same linking for cells in 3D.

Source: linking helpers.

docs.title: NeighborhoodCloud
docs.text: NeighborhoodCloud is a 3D, orbit-camera view of precomputed tissue neighborhoods — one alpha-shape polygon per cluster/slice, so it stays cheap to display regardless of dataset size. It replaces Landscape's older technology="neighborhood-cloud" mode.

docs.title: What it shows
docs.text:
• Neighborhood polygons: one alpha-shape region per (cluster, slice), rendered in 3D with the same orbit camera as CellCloud.
  • On-demand cell detail: real cell centroids load in only when a neighborhood is selected, instead of being loaded up front.
  • A slice control for stepping through multi-slice datasets.

Draw and edit neighborhoods in spatial, UMAP, and XY views with Landscape. NeighborhoodCloud displays precomputed neighborhoods across slices.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

nbhd_cloud = dega.viz.NeighborhoodCloud(
    base_url="https://your-landscape-files-url",
    adata=adata,
)
nbhd_cloud

Build the underlying neighborhood-cloud DegaFiles from per-slice alpha shapes:

gdf = dega.nbhd.alpha_shape_cell_clusters_by_slice(
    adata, cluster_attr="leiden", slice_attr="slice_id", z_attr="Z"
)
dega.pre.write_nbhd_cloud_dataset(
    adata, gdf, "path/to/dega_files",
    cluster_attr="leiden", slice_attr="slice_id", z_attr="Z",
    max_cells=50_000,  # cap the cells written per cluster for large datasets
)

Shape colors come from adata.uns["leiden_colors"] (or pass meta_cluster= with a color column); without either, each cluster gets a distinct fallback color.

See File Formats for the layout. NeighborhoodCloud can also be linked to a Clustergram, exactly like Landscape — see dega.viz.spatial_clustergram.

For the full list of constructor arguments, see the Viz Module API reference.

docs.title: Yearbook
docs.text:
Yearbook shows a grid of cell portraits: small, zoomed-in views of the tissue, each centered on one cell. Use it to compare many individual cells side by side, such as the cells with the highest expression of a gene or a sample of a cluster, and to mark cells for review.

Loading an interactive preview…

Interactive preview: kidney cells with the highest expression of the podocyte marker NPHS2, from the same Atera kidney section. Page through the portraits, scroll to zoom them together, or query another gene or cluster.

docs.title: Reading a Yearbook
docs.text:
Each portrait shows the image, cell boundaries, and transcripts around one cell, using the same layers and colors as a Landscape. The portraits share one zoom level, so cells of different sizes are compared at the same scale.

Podocytes (cluster 16) ranked by their expression of NPHS2.

Control What it does 1 Image IMG shows or hides the image; each channel button toggles a channel, and its slider sets the channel's brightness. 2 CELL Shows or hides the cells; the slider sets their size. The bars count the clusters of the cells shown; click a bar to show only that cluster's cells. 3 TRX Shows or hides transcripts; the slider sets their size. Click a gene's bar, or shift-click several, to show only those genes' transcripts. 4 Gene search Choose genes by name, as in a Landscape. 5 Query Cells Find cells by cluster, gene, or both; see Querying cells. 6 Pages Move between pages of portraits. 7 Celldega logo Opens this page. 8 Portrait One cell, centered. Hover a cell for its ID and cluster. 9 Review checkbox Marks the cell for review; see Marking cells for review.

docs.title: Zooming and panning
docs.text: Scroll over any portrait to zoom all portraits together; each stays centered on its own cell. Drag a portrait to look around its cell; the view re-centers when you zoom or change pages. Double-clicking does not zoom.

docs.title: Querying cells
docs.text:
The Query Cells box finds cells in the browser, without Python:

  • Cluster only: a random sample of that cluster's cells.
  • Gene only: all cells, ranked by their expression of the gene, highest first; the portraits are colored by its expression.
  • Cluster and gene: that cluster's cells, ranked by the gene.

Type a cluster or gene, choosing from the suggestions, and click Query or press Enter. The status line reports how many cells were found. Clear empties the boxes without changing the portraits.

Querying cluster 20, the glomerular endothelium, ranked by the endothelial marker EMCN, finds 3,967 cells. Zooming out shows each cell's glomerulus; checking cells on two pages and returning to the start shows that the checks are kept.

docs.title: Paging
docs.text: The page indicator shows the current page and the total, such as 1 / 8. Use ◀ and ▶ to move one page, or START, MID, and END to jump.

docs.title: Marking cells for review
docs.text: Click a portrait's checkbox, at its bottom right, to mark or unmark its cell. Checked portraits have a blue border. The checks belong to the cells, not the page, so they are kept when you change pages or run another query. Build a review set this way, such as possible doublets or segmentation errors, and read it in Python.

docs.title: Widget: Python-backed interactions
docs.text:
As a notebook widget, a Yearbook shares its state with Python:

  • Review set: yb.selected_cells, or yb.get_selected_cells(adata) for an AnnData of the checked cells. Set yb.selected_cells = [] to clear every checkbox.
  • Portraits: yb.cells lists the cells being shown, and yb.front_end_query the last query run in the browser.
  • Pages and zoom: yb.current_page, yb.zoom_level, and the methods next_page(), prev_page(), and go_to_page(n).
reviewed_ids = yb.get_selected_cells()  # same IDs as yb.selected_cells
adata.obs["yearbook_review"] = adata.obs_names.isin(reviewed_ids)

# Or get a copy of the marked cells for downstream work.
reviewed = yb.get_selected_cells(adata)

# Clear every review checkbox, including those on other pages.
yb.selected_cells = []

A Yearbook linked to a Clustergram with dega.viz.spatial_clustergram, or to a Landscape with dega.viz.landscape_yearbook, updates its query through Python, so these links need a running kernel.

docs.title: Choosing which cells to show
docs.text:
There are three ways to choose which cells Yearbook displays, in increasing order of power:

  1. An explicit id list: cells=["cell_1", "cell_2", ...].
  2. A back-end selection: selection=..., accepting a celldega.select.Selection, a JSON-ready selection dict, or a plain id list. This is the recommended way to drive the grid from a Python AnnData object.
  3. A front-end query: front_end_query=..., evaluated in the browser against the dataset's DegaFiles, needing only a base_url and no Python AnnData.

Use selected_cells= to initialize the review checkboxes. The selected list stores original cell IDs independently of the current page and query.

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

yb = dega.viz.Yearbook(
    base_url="https://your-landscape-files-url",
    front_end_query={"gene": "NPHS2", "max_cells": 50},
    rows=2,
    cols=4,
)
yb

For constructor arguments, see the Viz Module API reference.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text: The Atera kidney tutorial includes a Yearbook for inspecting individual cells alongside a Landscape. The Atera kidney Yearbook review uses dega.select to build a candidate queue, inspect portraits across pages, and retrieve checked cell IDs for follow-up.

docs.text: The screenshot and animation show the Atera whole-transcriptome kidney DegaFiles, captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py.

docs.title: Landscape
docs.text:
Landscape shows where cells are and what they express. In spatial data, it draws tissue images, cells, transcripts, and neighborhoods together, so you can ask where a cell type sits in the tissue, which cells express a gene, and which cells neighbor each other. The same cells can also be shown in a low dimensional embedding, such as a UMAP.

Spatial Landscapes read DegaFiles, loading the image, cell, and transcript tiles needed for the current view. This page covers the spatial view. UMAP and XY covers embeddings and single-cell data, and Neighborhoods covers drawing and using tissue regions and gates.

Loading an interactive preview…

Interactive preview: an Atera whole-transcriptome kidney section. Scroll to zoom into glomeruli, tubules, and individual transcripts; drag to pan; and click a cluster or gene. Open a larger view in the Gallery.

docs.title: Reading a Landscape
docs.text:
Close up, a Landscape layers the microscopy image, each cell's segmentation boundary and centroid, and every detected transcript. Cells are colored by cluster, and transcripts by gene. The bar graphs in the control panel summarize what is in view: the CELL bars count cells per cluster, and the TRX bars count transcripts per gene.

A glomerulus in a whole-transcriptome kidney section. Podocytes (cluster 16) lead the CELL bars and the podocyte gene PODXL leads the TRX bars, because they are what is in view.

Control What it does 1 View and image SPATIAL, UMAP, and XY switch views; IMG shows or hides the image; each channel button toggles a channel, and its slider sets the channel's brightness. 2 CELL Shows or hides cells; the slider sets their size. The bars rank clusters by the number of cells in view. 3 TRX Transcripts and gene expression. Its button and slider depend on the zoom; see Genes and transcripts. The bars rank genes. 4 Gene search Color cells by one or more genes. The box below describes the selected gene. 5 Celldega logo Opens this page. 6 The view Scroll to zoom, drag to pan, hover for details, and click to select.

The control panel is shared with Yearbook, CellCloud, and NeighborhoodCloud; see the control panel.

docs.title: Zooming and panning
docs.text:
Scroll to zoom and drag to pan. A Landscape uses semantic zoom: what it draws, and what its controls do, change with the zoom level.

  • Zoomed out, each cell is a dot colored by cluster or gene expression, over the whole tissue.
  • Closer in, the image appears at higher resolution, and TRX can load the transcripts and cell boundaries in view on request.
  • Close up, transcripts and cell boundaries load automatically for the tiles in view.

Because a Landscape only loads the tiles in view, it stays responsive even for datasets with over a billion transcripts. See Performance.

Scrolling into a glomerulus: cell boundaries and transcripts load as the view narrows, and the TRX button becomes active.

Double-clicking does not zoom. The zoom stops slightly beyond the whole tissue and at about 10 µm across the view; min_zoom and max_zoom change these limits.

docs.title: Images
docs.text:
IMG shows or hides the image. Each channel, such as DAPI or a membrane stain, has a button to show or hide it and a slider for its brightness. When an aligned H&E image has been added to the DegaFiles, an FLR / H&E selector next to IMG switches between the fluorescence channels and H&E; see Add aligned H&E to DegaFiles.

Hiding the cells, turning off the boundary and RNA channels, adjusting DAPI brightness, and restoring them.

When you select a cluster or gene while zoomed out, the image is hidden so that the selected cells stand out. It returns when you zoom in close or clear the selection.

docs.title: Cells and clusters
docs.text:
CELL shows or hides the cells, and its slider sets their size. Click a cluster's bar to show only that cluster; click it again to show all clusters. Shift-click more bars to add clusters to the selection. Hover a bar for its cell count. You can also click a cell in the view to select its cluster.

Selecting podocytes (cluster 16) outlines every glomerulus in the section; shift-clicking adds glomerular endothelial cells (cluster 20).

Selecting a cluster clears any gene selection.

docs.title: Genes and transcripts
docs.text:
Click a gene's bar, or type its name in the gene search box, to color cells by its expression. Type several names separated by commas, or shift-click several bars, to color cells by their combined (summed) expression; up to the 20 highest-expressed genes are combined. Clear the search box, or type cluster, to return to cluster colors.

Searching for the podocyte marker NPHS2 and the endothelial marker EMCN lights up every glomerulus across the section; zooming into one shows the two genes' individual transcripts.

docs.title: The TRX controls change with the zoom
docs.text:
The TRX button and slider are an example of semantic zoom:

Zoom TRX button TRX slider Close up Blue or gray: shows or hides transcripts, which load automatically Transcript size Closer in Gray: click to load the transcripts and boundaries in view Cell expression opacity, once a gene is selected Zoomed out Faded: transcripts are not available Cell expression opacity, once a gene is selected

Zoomed out, a selected gene colors cells, and the slider sets how strongly; the gene box shows the expression that reaches full color, such as Full opacity at ≥ 145. Close up, the same selection shows only those genes' transcripts, each colored by gene, and the slider sets their size.

Zoomed out: cells colored by the combined expression of NPHS2 and EMCN. Every glomerulus stands out; the fainter signal elsewhere fits EMCN in endothelial cells outside the glomeruli.

Close up, with cells hidden: NPHS2 transcripts (teal) along the podocytes and EMCN transcripts (yellow) in the capillaries, two orthogonal markers in one glomerulus.

The gene box describes the selected genes using UniProt (human gene symbols). Clicking a transcript selects its gene.

docs.title: Sequencing-based spatial data
docs.text:
Sequencing-based technologies such as Visium HD measure expression in a grid of small bins rather than as individual transcripts. To show this as transcripts, preprocessing creates one point per count in each bin and adds a small random offset, or jitter, so that a bin's points spread out instead of drawing on top of each other. Zoomed in, each bin then shows the mix of genes it detected, in their gene colors, and the same gene controls work as for imaging data. The positions within a bin are a visual aid, not measured locations.

Visium HD colorectal cancer: zooming from the whole section into normal crypts reveals jittered transcripts, and the TRX bars are led by plasma-cell genes (IGKC, PIGR, JCHAIN). Selecting IGKC and hiding the H&E shows its transcripts in the plasma cells around the crypts; zooming out shows IGKC across the section.

Celldega's preprocessing writes these points with pre.write_pseudotranscripts_from_sbg, whose jitter argument sets the range of the offset; see the pre API. The Visium HD colorectal cancer tutorial explores this dataset with a linked Clustergram and Enrich.

docs.title: Spaces and embeddings
docs.text:
The same cells can be shown in more than one space: their positions in the tissue, and a low dimensional embedding, such as a UMAP computed from their expression. Pass an AnnData with obsm["X_umap"], for example from Scanpy, along with the DegaFiles, and UMAP and SPATIAL move the cells between the two spaces. The move is animated so that you can follow the cells. Select a cluster in one space, then switch to the other to see where those cells are.

Xenium pancreas: zoomed out on the tissue, the cells move into their Scanpy UMAP. Selecting the islet cluster (9) highlights it in the UMAP, and switching back to SPATIAL shows the islets in the tissue.

In both spaces, the bar graphs describe the cells in view, so zooming into a region is a way to query its neighborhood: a tissue region in the spatial view, or a group of similar cells in the UMAP.

The Scanpy–Squidpy Xenium pancreas tutorial computes this UMAP with Scanpy and passes it to the Landscape. The AnnData's cell IDs must match the DegaFiles:

adata.obs_names = adata.obs["cell_id"].astype(str)  # Xenium cell IDs
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(base_url=base_url, adata=adata, cluster_attr="leiden")

See UMAP and XY for more about embeddings.

docs.title: Hovering for details
docs.text:
Hover over a cell for its ID and cluster, and its expression when cells are colored by a gene. Hover over a transcript for its gene, with the protein name and description from UniProt.

Hovering a transcript shows its gene, here NES (Nestin), with a description.

docs.title: Single-cell Landscapes
docs.text:
For single-cell RNA-seq, a Landscape needs no DegaFiles. Save your Scanpy AnnData as an AnnData Zarr store with a CSC copy of the expression matrix, and the browser reads the cells, their UMAP, and one gene at a time directly from the store. Add a Clustergram of cell-type marker genes for a linked Landscape–Clustergram. Spatial data needs one more step, preparing DegaFiles for the images, transcripts, and boundaries, but single-cell data goes straight from an AnnData:

import scanpy as sc
import celldega as dega

# Cells: a CSC copy lets the browser read one gene at a time.
adata.layers["counts_csc"] = adata.layers["counts"].tocsc()
adata.write_zarr("cells.zarr")

# Cell-type marker genes as a dot plot, clustered on both axes.
sc.tl.rank_genes_groups(adata, groupby="cell_type")
markers = dega.clust.Matrix(adata, groupby="cell_type")
markers.norm("row", by="zscore")
markers.cluster(view="rank_genes_groups", levels=[1, 3, 5, 10])

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    zarr_url="cells.zarr", zarr_layer="counts_csc", cluster_attr="cell_type"
)
cgm = dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=markers, rank_dim=3)
dega.viz.spatial_clustergram(landscape, cgm)

In a single-cell Landscape, the bars describe the cells in view. As you pan and zoom, the CELL bars count the cells of each type in view, which gives the local cell-type proportions. With cell-type signatures, the gene bars estimate the mean expression of the cells in view from those proportions, and TRX turns purple. See viewport estimates.

Zooming in therefore queries the local neighborhood you are looking at, in data space here just as in tissue space for spatial data: which cell types are in this part of the UMAP, and which genes characterize them. Click a gene from those bars, then zoom out to see how localized its expression is.

Tabula Sapiens: zooming into the swirl of spermatids at the top of the UMAP, the CELL bars narrow to spermatids and spermatocytes, and TRX turns purple. Selecting the top estimated gene, RGMB-AS1, and zooming out shows its expression concentrated in the swirl.

Explore the 1.1-million-cell atlas with its linked marker Clustergram in the Gallery, or follow the Tabula Sapiens notebook to build the Landscape, Clustergram, and Enrich from AnnData Zarr stores. The Chromium PBMC tutorial walks through the same steps from a Scanpy analysis.

docs.title: Multiple datasets
docs.text:
Pass a list of DegaFiles URLs to switch between datasets in one Landscape. A dropdown after IMG lists them, and switching keeps the selected clusters, genes, and view where possible:

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url=["https://host/sample_a", "https://host/sample_b"],
    dataset_names=["Sample A", "Sample B"],
)

Each item can also be a dictionary with url, label, and short_label.

docs.title: Linking to other visualizations
docs.text: Linked to a Clustergram with dega.viz.spatial_clustergram, a Landscape responds to Clustergram clicks: a gene colors cells by its expression, a cluster selects its cells, and a gene group colors cells by the genes' combined expression. See the Clustergram's linking table. Selections made in the Landscape do not change the Clustergram.

docs.title: Widget: Python-backed interactions
docs.text:
As a notebook widget, a Landscape also shares state with Python:

  • Selected cells: landscape.selected_cells holds the cells of the selected clusters, a drawn neighborhood, or cells highlighted from a linked Clustergram. landscape.get_selected_cells(adata) returns them as an AnnData.
  • View: landscape.landscape_state is "spatial", "umap", or "xy".
  • Neighborhoods: drawn regions are available as landscape.nbhd; see Neighborhoods.
  • Updates from Python: landscape.update_cell_clusters(...) recolors cells with new cluster labels, and landscape.highlight_cells(...) highlights cells.

The zoom, pan, slider positions, and selected genes are not sent back to Python.

docs.title: Use it from Python
docs.text:
import celldega as dega

landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url="https://your-landscape-files-url",
    adata=adata,
    ini_zoom=-5,
)
landscape

The optional adata supplies cell attributes, cluster colors, and UMAP coordinates; its obs_names must match the DegaFiles cell IDs. The segmentation shown is chosen when the widget is created, with segmentation=.

To add an aligned H&E background to prepared DegaFiles, use dega.pre.add_aligned_he("data/DegaFiles", "sample_he.ome.tif", alignment="sample_he_imagealignment.csv"), then reload the Landscape. See Add aligned H&E to DegaFiles.

For constructor arguments and methods, see the Viz API. For web pages without Python, see the JavaScript API.

docs.title: Source code
docs.text:
• Python Landscape widget: constructor, AnnData metadata, signatures, and selection/neighborhood methods.
  • Browser initialization and Landscape renderer.
  • Pseudo-transcripts for sequencing-based data.

docs.title: Screenshot sources
docs.text: Screenshots and animations show the Atera whole-transcriptome kidney DegaFiles from the Atera kidney tutorial, the Xenium pancreas DegaFiles and AnnData from the Scanpy–Squidpy pancreas tutorial, the Visium HD colorectal cancer DegaFiles from the Visium HD CRC tutorial, and the Tabula Sapiens atlas (Tabula Sapiens Consortium, via CZ CELLxGENE Discover, CC BY 4.0). They were captured with Celldega 0.28.0 using scripts/docs_screenshots/capture.py.

docs.title: Neighborhoods
docs.text:
Celldega helps you identify neighborhoods of cells, both in physical space, such as a structure in the tissue, and in data space, such as an island in a UMAP or a population in a two-gene XY plot. You can draw them in a Landscape or create them in Python, for example with alpha shapes around a cell type. Drawn neighborhoods keep their state: they are saved with the widget, available in Python as a GeoDataFrame, and can be saved to a file and loaded again.

Neighborhoods then connect to Celldega's neighborhood analysis. The nbhd functions summarize the cells inside each neighborhood, such as their cell-type composition or gene expression; a NeighborhoodCollection keeps the geometry and summaries together; and a Clustergram compares neighborhoods by those summaries.

docs.title: Drawing a neighborhood
docs.text:
Create the Landscape with nbhd_edit=True, then:

  1. Click NBHD to turn on editing.
  2. Click SKTCH, or press S with the pointer over the view.
  3. Drag around the cells you want; releasing the mouse closes the shape.
  4. Name the neighborhood, choose a color, and click Apply (or press Enter).

Drawing a neighborhood around a glomerulus and naming it "glomerulus". It appears in the NBHD bars, and its cells become the Landscape's selected cells.

Press Esc to stop sketching. While sketching, tooltips and cell clicks are paused. New neighborhoods get unique default names, such as nbhd_spatial_1; the editor checks custom names for duplicates.

docs.title: Drawing in UMAP and XY
docs.text:
The same tools work in a UMAP or XY view, where a neighborhood acts as a gate around a population of cells. Each neighborhood belongs to the view in which it was drawn, and only the neighborhoods of the current view are shown. An XY neighborhood also records its genes and scale.

Pressing S over a PBMC UMAP and drawing a gate around the monocytes.

A gate drawn in a UMAP selects cells by their expression profile rather than their location. With spatial data, switch to SPATIAL to see where those cells are in the tissue.

docs.title: Editing neighborhoods
docs.text:
With editing on:

  • Click a neighborhood to edit its shape: drag a vertex, or drag along an edge to add a vertex. A red DEL button deletes the neighborhood. Click the neighborhood again to finish.
  • Double-click a neighborhood to rename it or change its color.
  • Click a neighborhood's bar to select it and its cells.

docs.title: Viewing supplied neighborhoods
docs.text:
Neighborhoods made in Python, such as alpha shapes around each cell type, are passed with nbhd= as a GeoDataFrame. The NBHD button shows or hides them, its slider sets their opacity, and the bars list them by area; click a bar or a shape to select it. Start in this view with landscape_state="nbhd".

gdf_alpha = dega.nbhd.alpha_shape_cell_clusters(adata, cat="leiden")
landscape = dega.viz.Landscape(
    base_url="https://your-landscape-files-url",
    adata=adata,
    nbhd=gdf_alpha,
    landscape_state="nbhd",
)

See the alpha-shape and gradient example for building neighborhoods from cell types.

docs.title: Using neighborhoods in Python
docs.text:
As a notebook widget, a Landscape keeps every neighborhood available to Python:

  • landscape.nbhd: a GeoDataFrame of neighborhoods from all views, with name, space, coordinate_space, geometry, and, for drawn neighborhoods, cell_ids and cell_count. landscape.nbhd_polygons holds the same polygons.
  • landscape.get_selected_cells(adata): an AnnData of the currently selected cells, such as those in the last drawn or selected neighborhood.
  • landscape.save_nbhds("neighborhoods.geojson") and landscape.load_nbhds("neighborhoods.geojson") save and restore them; landscape.select_nbhd("nbhd_xy_1") selects one, restoring its view.
  • Passing nbhd=landscape.nbhd to another Landscape of the same dataset shows them there too.

Spatial geometry uses the tissue's coordinates, while UMAP and XY neighborhoods keep their display coordinates. Filter to the space you need before calculating areas or distances, then summarize the cells inside with the nbhd functions:

tissue_nbhds = landscape.nbhd.loc[landscape.nbhd["space"] == "spatial"]

# Cell-type composition of each drawn neighborhood.
composition = dega.nbhd.calc_nbhd_by_pop(adata, tissue_nbhds, category="cell_type")

mat = dega.clust.Matrix(composition)
mat.cluster()
dega.viz.Clustergram(matrix=mat)

adata.obsm["spatial"] must use the same coordinates as the DegaFiles. The Atera breast cancer neighborhoods tutorial compares neighborhoods by their composition, and the pancreas islet gradients example stores geometry, summaries, and relationships in a NeighborhoodCollection.

How saved neighborhoods stay tied to their data

A fingerprint of ordered cell IDs and coordinates (or expression, for XY) keeps saved gates tied to their original data, even if a local server URL changes. UMAP and XY geometry is stored in display coordinates with Y increasing downward; UMAP records axes.y.reversed=True because increasing X_umap[:, 1] is displayed upward. Matching saved UMAP polygons from the previous orientation migrate automatically, and cell IDs remain unchanged.
